Half-Life Source is a slightly enhanced version of the 1998 classic.
This supposed remake retains most of the original game's textures, models and animation but favours towards the better world effects available from the new Source engine of the time. Half-Life Source has a Havoc powered physics engine with enemies and objects obeying Newton's three laws, picture-quality water reflections and expanded scenary - now built as geometry rather than painted on backdrops. Also, the sound and presenetation now borrows heavily from Half-Life 2.
My opinion of Half-Life Source is rather mixed, befuddled even. HL: Source feels very sloppily put together and thrown over. Valve could of and should of done a complete overhaul of the game. It's lukewarm reception from the many alienated players of the game led to the creation of Black Mesa Source, a total conversion set to unofficially reimagine the first game on the source engine. I implore you to wait for it instead. Otherwise, buy the original.

I can't truly express how disappointed i am to see the sequel of one of the best first person stealth games of all times to be released in this state.
I made an exception with Dishonored 2 and pre-ordered it because Arkane Studios always delivered quality in the forms of excepcional gameplay, interesting plots and good optimization for PC. Now that is over.
The gameplay might still be as exquisite as Dishonored 1, the artistic design as breathtaking and the plot as interesting. None of that matter when you can't play the game properly due to a few, but critical, technical problems.
Unfortunately some of them will never be fixed like the mouse sensitivity tied to your framerate, making your mouse aiming absolutely random at all times depending to where you are looking at. This one is real nightmare for me personally. Also, even if you disable mouse smoothing and friction, the mouse still feel unprecise and unresponsive due to some kind of hard-coded filter on it, that along with the FPS-mouse-tied problem i said above makes you feel more like drunk octogenarian grandpa than the most lethal assassin of the empire, destroying inmersion and any moments of joy this game could give you in the way.
The optimization on the other hand, is even worse (if that's possible). I'm running the game on a 970 OC, 2600k 4.4ghz, 16gb ram on Windows 10 Pro at 1080p. As soon as i got outdoors my framerate just wont go higher than 40FPS while looking at the open. No matter if i'm on Ultra, Very High or High, with filters or without them, the framerate varies maybe 5FPS, which is absurd to say the least. On Low i get over 50 and near 60 sometimes, but for some reason the game feels that it's playing at 30 FPS even if it's at 80. All this optimization problems are probably happening because of Denuvo's, Arkane having no clue how to optimize IdTech 5 engine, and being a console port designed for pad instead of mouse and keyboard. When you go to the controls tab in the options the first screen you get is to config your pad instead of your mouse. The mouse options are in the third tab. Priorities i guess. Mouse problems like this are very common in console ports with the sticks stuff really hard-coded in the game affecting the way the mouse should work, because it's usually emulating or dealing with stick filters instead of just being raw input.
Stay way from Corvo and Dunwall, for now. Let my broken heart and wallet teach you this lesson the easy way.

In my campaign to give critically-panned games a chance of redemption, I've stumbled onto this little gem of a game. Despite the harsh reviews, Watchmen: The End is Nigh does manage to get some things right.
Sometimes, you just want to play a short and mindlessly fun game. Watchmen offers both with its brief 3 hour campaign and rewarding button mashing.
The game opens with an option of playing as either Rorschach or Nite Owl, each with his own unique attacks. This divergence, for those curious enough, does promote replayability. Your character will unlock new combos just frequently enough ensure combat stays fresh.
For me, the most impressive aspect here is the aesthetics. They're not the best visuals to date, but they're still nice to look at. The environments are detailed and the combat animations are smooth. Overall, Watchmen is extremely easy on the eyes.
If you've got the change to spare, Watchmen will provide you (and maybe a friend) a few hours of enjoyment.
Grade: C+

Super Meat Boy is a game that needs no introduction. Its notoriety comes from the sheer difficulty of its platforming, and having played many platformers at this point, it certainly lives up to its reputation. Not only are the levels themselves challenging, there's time trials for each level, collectibles to find (which unlock new playable characters), and secret levels to unlock (i.e. there's a lot to do in the game). Along with this, a weird (but hardly profound) little story, and great music (wonderful, since you'll be hearing some of the same tracks over and over), you've got yourself a worthy entry into the pantheon of platformer games.
This is recommended for hardcore platformer fans who thirst for a true challenge. This will test the very limits of your ability to time your movements and ensure that they are accurate. There is very little margin for error here, so take a deep breath, get yourself adjusted to how the game controls, and prepare for a LOT of trial and error. Good luck.

If there's one thing you should know about SteamWorld Dig is that it stems from a handheld console. The Nintendo DS family of consoles specifically.
While many would be turned off at this fact as it indicates some limitations that wouldn't otherwise exist if it were a console or PC release. However, don't let that discourage you from giving SteamWorld Dig a serious look.
I first picked this game up on my 3DS and put a good amount of time into playing the game, so naturally when I saw SteamWorld Dig on a sale I decided "Why not?".
The game is very visually pleasing for both the 3DS and even more so on the PC release. Everything looks nice and crisp and clean for both versions, but even more so on the PC version since you will be viewing it on a larger screen than you would on the 3DS.
Gameplay wise SteamWorld Dig only falls short in one area. The first hour or so of gameplay can feel really slow and pointless as you will find yourself slowly plinking away with your pick axe trying to gather minerals to return to town. However, you'll find that after getting the first couple of upgrades and abilities that SteamWorld Dig really picks up in its pace as long as you can push through the initial grind.
There are plenty of upgrades to collect and work for. From buying bigger pouches to allow you to stay underground longer and carry more loot, to buying better pick axes, or buying bigger water tanks to power your special abilities. SteamWorld Dig is great for people who have a compulsion to collect everything and upgrade everything.
Ever play a game and you finally get a new ability to feel accomplished and happy only to turn around and learn that the ability has a limited use or is only useful in certain sitations? Forget all that, Steamworld Dig does a good job at making sure that each new ability enhances your ability to explore and is actually useful. From an ability that charges up your boots and releases a burst of steam to allow you to jump higher, to an ability that allows you to cross large gaps that would normally be inaccessable. No ability goes unused.
My only gripe with the game is that the upgrading system could have a little more depth. As it stands all you have to do to upgrade is to gather minerals, take it to town to exchange it for money, then buy the upgrade. A great improvement that could be done for future SteamWorld games would be to make the individual ores a requirement for building the upgrades in the same way that Minecraft or Terraria do.
Despite the shallow upgrade system and initial feeling of "Why am I even doing this?" SteamWorld Dig is a great all around simple and addicting game that would be great for anyone who is a fan of these sorts of games. And for a measly entry price of 10 bucks its a very accessable game that is well worth a shot to anyone whos looking to kill some time or even looking for a great handheld game to download. SteamWorld Dig can also be found on the Nintendo eShop for $5 bucks (the price when I bought it for my own 3DS system).
Regardless of whether you buy it here on Steam or you buy it for your 3DS you'll find a great game in SteamWorld Dig.

For those thinking about getting the game, dont. Well, not yet anyway. The game is incredibly poorly optimised for PC, something that seems to be a recurring problem with new releases. The game feels clunky and slow in comparison to the first game, but that may be due to the fact that the game suffers from stutters and crashes at the most random times.
I believe the game has potential, its a bethesda game so it obviously does, however it may be worth waiting a week for some patches to be released.

Where do I start? From the main menu it is immediately noticable that the mouse cursor moves as if through oil. I have a computer that can run The Witcher 3 on max settings at 1440P resolution at 50-60 fps, sitting at 60 the majority of the time. Crysis 3, all maxed settings except AA options, and so on.
From the opening scenes of the game I was pulling fps ranging from the high 20's to low 40's, and that's with half the settings on very high rather than ultra. There is NO way this game is more graphically intensive than the latest Deus Ex game, which I can run very smoothly at 45-60 fps with a mix of maxed and high settings.
After noticing the poor mouse movement and framerate issues, it was a serious blow to first enter into the open'ish world only to encounter pathetically bad lod meshes. Other than some superior lighting and shadow, visually this game is a pretty big step back compared to the first game. Trust me, the moment you leave the beginning area you will be shocked at just how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ the gameworld looks.
This game was clearly made for consoles, with pc's receiving a very poorly optimized version. The art direction alone REEKS of console limitations, which reeks even more of the game being rushed, or the developers being lazy in not implementing proper graphics scaling options to account for pc capabilities. Parity across platforms has it's limits.
Do yourself a favor and either refund this game or sit on it for awhile until it gets better optimization.

As a lover of point and click adventures, I'm ashamed to say that I'd never played a Sherlock Holmes game before. So in an effort to correct this, I started playing Versus Ripper without much pre-knowledge of what the gameplay or quality of the game was actually like. Oh boy, was I in for a surprise?
I loved this game. Although some of the production values may now be rather dated, I feel that they added to the charm. The puzzles weren't difficult, but just hard enough to make you feel that you actually had something to solve. While the voice acting over all was nothing compared to a AAA nowadays, the characterizations of Holmes & Watson perfectly fit into everything you could wish for. The Ripper story itself took a fascinating perspective on the historical events.
Apparently this is one of the best of the Sherlock games, so it's all downhill for me from here (though I'm definitely going to play through the whole series), but I would wholeheartedly recommend this to anybody that likes point and click adventures, murder mysteries, or just generally doesn't need AAA production values to appreciate a game.

I will base this review off the ask:
10$ for a 4-5hour game on a platform where similar, mining/adventuring games exist.
Let me start that, having completed the game (within 4h), Steamworld Dig isn't a bad game. I just wouldn't recommend it because it lacks the stuff to be a good one.
The first 1h is REALLY boring. You can barely jump/mine and all enemies are EXACTLY alike.
If you're able to suffer through it, underneath it all, you'll *start* to have fun after you find a first few upgrades (drill, jump, etc.).
But that's the problem with this game: it all ends as soon as it gets started.
Within 3hours, you've found all the upgrades and FINALLY you can start to enjoy the game, right?
Not really, because the game ends as soon as you find the good stuff (double jump, etc.).
Conclusion:
The developper abandonned his creation just as it got started.
Let's compare alternatives
Terraria/Starbound vs Steamworld Dig
Plenty of enemy AIs
vs only 2/level (3levels)!
10+ bosses
vs 1
Perfect controls
vs weird floaty controls
Useful and divers power-ups
vs Useless Powerups (game ends as soon as you get them, so you can't use them)
Clearly : get Terraria, then Starbound... then if you're REALLY BORED out of these 2, get this.

Darksouls is a visually astounding action RPG that rewards cautious playstyles and planning over brute force. There are plenty of unforgiving moments, but there are also bosses that leave you shaking, enemies oyu can overcome that you never thought you could, and when you do the game makes sure to reward you in kind.
After the last port disaster, this one is imrpoved greatly, although still suffers a few smaller port flaws.
While the Singleplayer - Multiplayer bits, where you can leave messages and see ghosts is still awesome, the co-op is terrible.
All in all, this game improves upon Dark Souls 1 in many ways, many more for PC users, however it is a trip down the same unforgiving lane that you traveresed once before.
The Good:
-60 FPS, smooth visuals with HD textures, much better port than DS1
-Many visually remarkable places to see, gear to collect, and enemies to fight.
-Skill combat that revolves around timing your moves, dodges, parrying, and using everything you have just to stay alive a little bit longer than you did the previous time.
The Bad:
-The fact that it is extremely hard is also a downside, there is no difficulty settings, and casual gamers will most likely want to avoid this. There is no shame in doing so, and the people insulting others because they have a hard time or get frustrated and quit, need to lay off. Enemies sometimes swarm you, or knock you down over and over in a row until you die, and you lose all your souls unless you can reclaim them.
-Co-op is technically there, but it may as well not be. Wasn't able to play with my friend yet if at all because they made it so you have to jump through a bunch of hoops, meet a bunch of requirements, and even then it might not let you. This shoudl not have been a feature that they made hard to do, people enjoy playing with friends, they should never have handicapped this feature.
-It can be easy to get lost and end up wandering around clueless, since there is no real story progression, its mostly a quiet dark brooding game.
-Game is made for controller, if using a keyboard the controls are still better than Ds1, however icons for a controller still pop up everywhere and such, as well as the controls still being hard for keyboard.
7.8/10

This game played a key role in the transition to full 3D in first person gaming. After the richness and depth seen at the climax of the '2.5D' era, the move to full 3D seemed to throw all that advancement out the window. Whereas the 2.5D era had reached a point where such depth was near inherent, successors like Quake and Quake 2 showed a simplicity that while enjoyable, left an undeniable lacking. And gone were so many of the innovations defined by the previous era. On consoles, a game named Golden Eye brought many of those past innovations kicking and screaming, into the 3D space; On PC, at the forefront of the charge, rode the mighty Half Life. Aftermath has a lot of promise, but at the same time it is lackluster in comparison to other zombie games. It is hardly the best zombie survival game available on Steam, and I wouldn't recommend it to those who enjoy playing this kind of game with a diversity of modes and features or to those who prefer more realistic visuals and features. However, it certainly has a lot of potential for a free-to-play game since it has only been out for a short period of time. Of course, the game also needs a great deal of improvement. This game is in beta, so play at your own risk.
Pros:
- Visuals are somewhat good (for a game barely two months old)
- a diverse array of craftable items (including craftable weapons and ammo)
- farming is possible (beets, tomatoes, broccoli...)
- PVE and PVP modes (where PVP has easy, medium and difficult levels)
- base-building is available with a modest amount of defensive features
Cons:
- Has a tendency to crash a lot (lacks optimization)
- sound effects aren't very realistic
- Mostly limited to survival-focused objectives (could use some more activities to really draw more people)
- Market is unrealistic and irrelevant (most necessary items are craftable and free, where market items are overpriced)
- spawn items largely useless (only a flashlight spawns after you die)
- safe zones lack collectable items
- the environment is monotonous, lacks biome diversity and creatures/predators to fight and hunt
- predictable map layout (many abandoned camps interspersed by larger yet fewer safe zones)
- game is essentially limited to one map
- character appearance is customizable, but lacks fully customizable features (height, mass, etc.)

As a big fan of Sherlock Holmes, and having played some of Frogware's previous games in the saga, I bought this game on a sale for just $2.49, and if you can get it at that price, I heavily recommend you do.
The adventure game focuses on the murders of low-class sex workers in Whitechapel, London, by an individual known by the public as "Jack the Ripper". Here, you control (alternatively) Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson, in order to investigate these murders and catch the person responsable. You can play in either 3rd person, point-and-click manner, or in 1st person.
The game presents you with all sorts of puzzles that you must solve in order to progress through the immersive story. I've found many of these puzzles to be rather confusing and certainly difficult, and had to resort to using walkthroughs in order to solve them. And in one occasion, I had to draw an elypsis on a map, which despite having done so many times, the game wouldn't register as correct. So I had to go online an download a save file, or otherwise start all over again.
Despite the problems mentioned above, I greatly enjoyed my hours playing this game, and do recommend anyone who is a Sherlock Holmes or adventure games fan, to get it.

As I have less, and less time to enjoy gaming as I grow older I am slowly gravitating towards a particular style of games. The common elements of these are:
1. They must have a competent story.
2. They cannot be very long, a 8-12 hours game works perfectly.
3. They need to steadily provide me with enjoyment, and feeling I am working towards a goal.
4. (optional) It is great to play games with my girlfriend, who enjoys mystery/puzzle games (we had lots of fun playing Professor Layton on a 3DS).
So if you are in a similar situation, then this game will be right for you. It is a bit clunky, and you can see budget limitations, but Sherlock Holmes games were never made to be mass-appeal AAA games. The story in this one is fascinating, and there are some great gameplay mechanics, especially those related to deductions and recreations of Jack the Reaper murders.
Nothing to say more. Grab it for 10EUR, or wait for Steam Sale to go even cheaper.

If you want to learn how to play fighting games, this is perhaps the best place to start.  It's tutorial is indepth, from basic mechanics to tactics against certain characters.
Also the plot is pretty great.

GUILTY GEAR Xrd -REVELATOR- is, in short, a fluid and fantastic fighting game that is easy to learn but hard to master. The game is very accessible to new players and boasts a ton of replay value with plenty of characters to learn and collectibles to earn. I would definitely recommend this game to people who are looking to get into fighting games or are just looking for a good fighting game to sink their teeth into.
To go a bit more in depth, starting off with characters, all of them are unique in their own style, whether it be look, personality, or playstyle. No two characters play the same, each with their own unique styles of play and gimmicks which allow each character to provide a different experience for old and new players. The characters are all very balanced, with one character not really being objectively "better" than another, due to the fact that it's not really about which character is "better" overall, but about matchups between two characters, as a character could be really bad at fighting one character, but would matchup really well with another.
The gameplay has been fine tuned to near perfection when it comes to fast and fluid fighting game goodness. Although it may be a bit rough at first to learn the button layout, once you learn it becomes easy to learn new moves and combos for each character. Through combinations of punches, kicks, and slashes you can perform either short or long combos to really keep your opponent guessing. Learning what moves can chain or cancel into others and what matchups work can really help in getting better at the game.
The art style and look of the game is where Guilty Gear Xrd -Revelator- really shines above all the other fighting games. By using cell shaded 3D animation the team behind Xrd was able to capture a style that looks exactly like something straight out of an anime, but with 3D models. All the characters are crafted beautifully with hyper detailed model work and animation that keeps the snappy look of regular sprite based fighting games but with a very nice hand drawn-esque twist to really bring out the best in a fighting game's look. The environments are no exception, with stunning detail going into the backgrounds, all locations being unique and beautiful in their own right.
And obviously, the highlight of any fighting game, the online play. The online for Guilty Gear Xrd -Revelator- is much improved from -SIGN- with the frame delay being very accurate and the game being able to maintain smooth gameplay. Note: however, while the online can be really good, I would strongly recommend trying to stick to local play for those with non-stable internet connections, as the frame delay and frame rate drops dramatically with bad connections on PC.
As stated before, this is a great, high quality fighting game for the price point and anyone who wants to get into fighting games or is looking for a great fighting game, and I would strongly recommend picking this up for those looking for a great time.
Note: If you haven't heard this already, I would strongly recommend getting the "GUILTY GEAR Xrd -REVELATOR- (+DLC Characters) + REV 2 All-in-One" for the definitive and best version of Guilty Gear Xrd -Revelator- as the Rev 2 DLC improves online and adds a lot more content to the base game.

With a total of 17 hours as of writing this review, I can't say the game's getting boring.
For a game this early in development, there is a LOT of content. However it's far from perfect, but defenitly enjoyable. Here are the key points of the game broken down and examined:
OPTIMIZATION: Meh... On an i7 6700K and GTX 970 FTW+, the early game is silky smooth but once you've built up a substantial base the lag seems to set in when your in the vicinity.
SCENERY: The games are style (as you can probably tell from the screenshots) is very No Man's Skyish, but the planets will present variety in biomes across a SINGLE planet (unlike NMS which had single biome planets) The different planets in the system will not only present different scenery, but planetary sizes, gravity, weather patterns and resources.
MULTIPLAYER: Fairly buggy to get working in the first place, but once it is working it goes pretty much without a hitch, multiplayer also definitly adds to the replay value.
DIFFICULTY: A very easy game with little to no violence, just watch your oxygen!
GAMEPLAY: The ability to mould the world enables some forme of base customisation, but at the end of the day the bases will all look pretty much the same, it can be a lot of fun building up trading systems, scouting with rovers and visiting other planets, but without multiplayer after 2 or 3 run throughs it can get a little boring as your essentially following the same order with very little freedom to progress a different way.
OVERALL SCORE: 8/10 - For a game in the development stage it is, it feels more complete than NMS, and a great way to kill time, all though I will say this game gets a bit boring after a while if you only do singleplayer

If "The Awakened" was the most disturbing and dark chapter of the saga I have to say this one is the most raw chapter because of the crimes we're called to investigate: Jack the Ripper's victims.
This chapter is kind of chilling if compared to the previous ones and poor Dr Watson's stomach or patience is often tested. At a certain point even Sherlock Holmes remains speechless when confronting the last victim corpse. Nothing excessively gruesome is being shown but it's all about Jack the Ripper, a formidable figure of whom nobody knows or saw anything for sure and you must investigate deeply to find the way to the truth behind his identity and nature.
Just like the previous chapter this is a point'n'click adventure, originally designed in 1st person View, but now presented with the possibility to play in 3rd person view and obviously with a remastered Graphic. The interface is almost the same as in previous titles but there's few very important innovations in this chapter's gameplay which have quickly become the key moments that best represent a game dedicated to Holmes and Watson adventures: The deduction schemes, reconstructions and experiments. The best inno are simple moments that require you to order your ideas and clues, link them and choose the right conclusions to better understand the next direction for your investigations. Reconstructions involve both Holmes and Watson trying to replicate the murder after a accurate analysis of the crime scene and the corpse. Experiments are exactly what the name says, simulation of situations or reactions to determine the murder weapon or other particular conditions or clues. These innovations are implemented in the classic gameplays elements so there are dialogues, riddles and puzzles, and errands... maybe a bit too many errands, compared to the previous chapters, but I liked the gameplay so much that I simply didn't mind too much.
They didn't waste too much effort in music as there are still the classic melodies from the previous chapters and one or two new tracks, but still they fit as they rarely pretend to stand in the gameplay unless the cutscene requires it to better represent the events.
The game takes place once again in London but this time we won't see any of the great marvelous buildings so typical of the city, but we'll be wandering back and forth in Whitechapel, the most squallid neighbourhood which is well represented as it's full of life with people and workers wandering on the roads, beggars, streetwalkers (seems like pro stitutes is a censored word... -.-), ill people and whatever. The Remastered engine shows nicely the alleys we'll be visiting (even though it has some heavy loads moments due to and excessive abuse of effects on water and reflections) but we won't be able to admire any particular example of level design except for some occasional office or internal ambients.

Sherlock Holmes may not be the best in Frogware's Sherlock Holmes series, but I definitely think it's the most interesting of the lot. Where most games in the series are based in fiction, Sherlock Holmes vs Jack the Ripper is based on actual history, and it sticks to it surprisingly well. Almost every character in the game was an actual person involved in the case, and the game follows a possible interpretation of the events (which, interestingly, actually goes against Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's own theory which speculated that the Ripper could actually be female) pretty closely. The Whitechapel regions are also recreated fairly well, though they do reuse a lot of obvious models from the previous games in order to fill the larger street population.
This does cause the potential issue of it not being interesting enough, however; the game is historically accurate enough that it does a pretty effective job of killing the mythological status that Jack has gained through most works of fiction about him, which may or may not disappoint fans of his story - this game is very much a story of the man, rather than the legend. The real-life inspiration also leads to the game being a bit less gorey than previous games like Sherlock Holmes: Awakened, with most of the corpses in this being replaced by slightly tamer drawings to give respect to the real victims - the final victim isn't even shown on screen except in a clay replica back at Holmes's office, due to the extent of damage that the real-life Ripper did to her.
Overall, while I can't say this game is my favorite in the series, it's still pretty great, and while its portrayal of the Ripper might not please everyone, I thought it was interesting to see the case from a historic perspective instead of being heavily fictionalized.

Despite a lackluster beginning, the burden of silly "adventure game" tropes, and one or two unreasonable puzzles, this is an enjoyable story.  Building the case piece by piece is a pleasure, and though progress feels plodding at times, the deduction mechanics are great fun, and it all builds to a satisfying conclusion.  The plot didn't dazzle me with its cleverness, but it did cast a suitably horrifying light on the awful crimes committed by the villain.  A diverting way to spend a few evenings.

For better or for worse, Xenonauts is a tribute to the original X-Com/UFO:Enemy Unknown released by Microprose in the early 1990s. It copies virtually all the gameplay elements, essentially being a game that is 90% turn based tactical combat pitting your soldiers vs aliens from outer space on a varied isometric map. Added to this are some light RPG elements and more important, a research system that lets you use newer and better gear.
Some of the fiddly bits from X-Com have been removed or streamlined (such as having to build weapons for your interceptors), but it keeps much of the quirkiness that makes the game both frustarting and fun. For instance, your soldiers are terrible at start. Only if they survive will they become decent and even then, you'll facepalm a lot when they miss an easy shot.
One thing is lacks is X-com's use of actual UFO folklore. To a certain extent, most the enemies in this are inspired by ones from the original X-com, but different enough that they bear no resmblance to UFOlogy.
The graphics are somewhat awful in the static screens, particularly the soldier equip screen, but the actual in combat graphics for the tactical map are really quite excellent. The sound is lacking compared to the original X-com, where you could track aliens by their movement sounds.
This game probably isn't for those that didn't already love X-Com or have at least played it. It's not well explained nor is it very forgiving. It's also very slow paced. But if you loved the original X-com and didn't like the remake so much, this is a great alternative

there's something very wrong with the hit calculations for this game, and I'm not talking about BS RNG hit chances. Enemies will routinely attempt to fire and often do hit you behind solid walls, especially when you are near corners.
The AI also very obviously cheats and knows exactly where you are in tactical mode, even when facing non-psi units like androids. They will hide in a blind corner and not move and only come out to shoot when they know you are within distance for them to move and shoot in one turn. They will also know exactly how many people you have within their target that has action points left to react to their movement. Have too many guards around and they won't come out. They also can tell whether or not  your unit is behind cover, and will not come out if you move the same unit behind strong cover. They can also tell whether your units are close enough to be a good grenade target. They'll come out if you are packed together, and stay hidden if you spread out.  They know all this information by hiding behind a box in a blind corner, even robots and androids with no psi ability. Oh, and I've had aliens throw grenades at me behind a wall over the wall to hit a unit of mine before it has even seen one of my units.
the larger multilevel ufos also have sometimes have bugged vision where you can see through floors and walls or the layers don't hide properly so the graphics are messed up to the point of unplayable.
vision is also very inconsistent in places where you and the enemy are on opposing ends of cover (not even touching, so not corner peeking), and they will have vision/shoot angle of you and you don't have vision of them.
air combat control is severely limited. You don't have the ability to break up squadrons and send individual planes to different areas once you have sent a squadron out. Not gonna lie, got it to practice for Dragon Ball: FighterZ. However, I ended up having more fun than I thought I would! Arc System Works put a lot of love into this game, and it shows in the overall quality. Surprised that this game is not as popular as it should be.
+ Gorgeous anime-style graphics: excellent character animation and nice backgrounds.
+ Interesting (and over-the-top) characters. I had to try all of them, and I'm glad to report that they felt balanced, and their playstyles are pretty unique.
+ Decent story mode, which plays out like a visual novel
+ Deep combat system with nice ultimates. Incredibly satisfying to learn the mechanics, let alone master.
+ One of the best tutorials ever seen in a fighting game. Close to what I saw on the new Killer Instinct.
+ Cool soundtrack
- Not many playing online. To find someone, I suggest getting REV2 upgrade, and doing player matches. That's what others suggested, and it works for me.
- Even if you get "REV2 upgrade + All DLCs bundle", you are still required to buy characters with real money like Dizzy and Haehyun, if you want them. Sucks.
- Story cutscenes play in some weird framerate. Animations in there look slow also. Not sure if it was intended. Action scenes during the cutscenes does not have this oddity.
- Nitpick: the extra costumes are just color swaps

This game is incredibly fun. I picked this game up for 49 cents on sale (originally a dollar), thinking it would be just an ordinary indie shooter with subpar graphics and clunky movement/gameplay. I couldn't have been more wrong.
• Stunning graphics, thanks to Unreal Engine 4. They're smooth and shiny!
• Customization! Though it's minimal with really only helmets for now, it makes up in skins, hats, etc..
• Wide array of "Guardians" to choose from, filled with their own loadouts and abilities to help the team.
• Fun gamemodes! Harvest; you guide a Harvester to collect materials while fending off the dinos/occasional robots, for ten rounds. Survival is exactly how it sounds. Surivive for ten rounds!
• Lastly, squading up with people is hands down a great experience. Playing solo can become tedious and depressing, but with friends, I'll play this game more often.
• Occasional lag drop spikes. This normally occurs on the space station. (likely because of syncing all the players together in one instance)
• Easy and Medium difficulty feels the same (easy mode), plus they give same rarity of loot. Hard mode, however, does feels like a hard mode.
• Partying up is difficult with your friends on Steam. The four of us tried many ways, but apparently praying you spawn on the same station so you can invite to party in-game, is the most efficient way to do so. Steam invites have really only worked 65% of the time..
• Not so much a complaint, but it would be nice to be a male recon class. I thought putting on the male mesh would convert it for each class, but apparently not. Don't get me wrong, it doesn't bother me to play as a female, but it just opens that door for class diversity, which to me, would be cool.
• The shotguns in the game can snipe and it's really scary. My friend can shoot pteradactlys out of the sky from a long distance. Increase spread??
• On a funny note, Assualt class can be annoying. Why did he
to say, "look at me go!!!!", every time he used the jetpack.. In what world would anyone say that? (It is a very fun class to use, though!)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
These are a small amount of cons that I'm confident will come to be fixed over time. This game is fun to play with friends and looks like it has a promising future. Definitely worth the 49 cents on sale! (1 dollar without the sale.) I will recommend to anyone!

We have to go deeper!
So what are you waiting for? Grab that pickaxe and start digging!
Steamworld Dig is a funny little mining game that gave me the same feeling as Minecraft: you just want to keep exploring in hopes of finding something awesome. The game feels really polished and there are some very nice mechanics in it. For example, that you need to use water to fuel your special abilities (you are a steam powered robot, duh).
Especially in the beginning you need to do some careful planning for each "haul", because your light will run out in a minute or two which means you need to make your way back to the surface to recharge your lamp. While you're back there, you can sell your precious minerals and buy some upgrades for your silly little robot in return.
Add a few small puzzle rooms and some pop cultural references on top of that and you have a great game that will entertain you for about 7 hours. The only downside I could think of are the enemies, since they are not really a threat once you know how to deal with them. But digging your way down a seemingly endless cave makes up for that.

I've been a junkie of the X-Com franchise since the original.  The review from @DerpsWithWolves hits it on the head and I have to agree with everything DWW posted.
TL; DR
This game takes the original X-Com idea and makes it better in every way.  This game is deeper, richer, and more "real" than the original.  I got it on sale and having played ten hours so far, I could have bought it at full price and it would be worth it to me.
Having multiple bases across the globe mutually supporting each other is fantastic.  Being able to send injured team members out into combat showcases the desperate times.  I love that there are no countdown timers on missions.  The missions are not a breeze either.  Hunting down ten or twenty aliens in urban terrain is a pain for a new player with green troops.
The alien AI is actually a little surprising.  Maybe it is only the first ten hours but the AI in X-Com has always been predictable in tactical combat.  I find this AI tosses me curveballs regularly.
Overall, I am really enjoying this game.   If you are a fan of the original or the franchise I believe you will enjoy it too.

This game is simply put excellent. You play as Cj who returns to los santos after receiving the news of his mothers death only to be dragged into the gang life he once left. The whole atmosphere of this game feels like a 1990s rap music video. It captures 90s California perfectly. The music is excellent and covers vast variety of genres, it's as good as vice city's soundtrack. The sound design in general in this game is solid for its age. The gameplay is vastly improved compared to its predecessors. With added rpg elements and improved combat. This game is one of the most ambitious games I have ever seen. Don't let the low amount of play time mislead you, I played Guilty Gear Xrd Rev2 a lot on PlayStation 4. The reason why I also own this on PC is because I think it's easily the best fighting game out there. Don't get me wrong, I'm still a scrub and online I lose most of the time. Still, I think this game taught me more about fighting games than Street Fighter ever did before.
Guilty Gear might be one of the most complex fighting games in existence, but I've enjoyed my time with it a lot more than with Street Fighter V. Which is a nice game as well, Guilty Gear Xrd just appeals a lot more to me. The graphics are, after countless hours of play, still amazing to look at. The soundtrack is great if you like rock and metal (and who doesn't like to sing along with Birthday Train?). The story, I don't understand any of it, but it's great to dive into if you have the persistence.
But the characters are what stands out the most to me. Most of these have been tweaked and improved for more than twenty years. Yeah, it's all anime, but it's great anime. Anime done right and I love it. All of the characters have their own traits and play very different from each other. It's proof of Arc System Works craftsmanship that these characters are balanced so well. Sure, there is a tier list, but a good player can still do a lot of damage with a low tier character. It might only matter in truly high level gameplay, something you shouldn't worry about if you never played Guilty Gear before.
The thing I dislike is the low popularity of this game. Since this title has been out for a while there is a small group of high level die-hard players always playing online. For a new player this could become a frustrating experience. Sure, everyone is nice enough most of the time, but I doubt you'll learn anything if the difference of skill is too big. Also due to the small amount of players nobody in the US and Europe plays ranked matches (while Japan still does). It's all player rooms, which is designed really well by Arc System Works (and will be used in a similar way for Dragon Ball Fighters), but it's sometimes hard to find a proper room or someone to play with.
Before I forget, for new players the game should be very interesting, because it basically has multiple tutorials where it teaches you how to play a fighting game. It really is something no other Japanese fighting game did before (Killer Instinct also has a great tutorial) and it truly teaches you techniques from low level to high level stuff. You can't blame the developers for trying to get new blood on board of the (Birthday) train.
All in all, just get Guilty Gear Xrd Revelator with the Rev2 DLC if you want to dive into a fighting game. Beginner or expert. I'm sure there are a lot of SFV players who are looking for something with more depth to chew on. This game is what you should get.

This game surprised me. I bought a HumbleBundle and SteamWorld Dig was part of it. I don't like the steampunk genre, from the screenshots I didn't like the game color tones like warm/desert stuff and the gameplay seemed, well, like a rehash of other games.
I still registered the game to my account even though I was about to gift it. Then I tried it real quick expecting a shït little game.
How wrong was I.
This game is actually very good. It's very addictive thanks to a progression mechanic: you dig, find ore, sell them, and after a certain amount of ore has been sold, the town's people can create upgrades for you using them. Obviously you will have better pickaxes but not just that. You can buy teleport beacons thingy to go back in the main cave in no time for example.
Sometime while digging, you will encounter small caves. Entering them will present you a puzzle like environment where you need to reach a specific area. Some caves are part of the game story, and completing them will grant you new abilities, like double jump or using your fist and stuff.
Using those new skills you'll be able to reach ore inaccessible before. You see, our dude can only dig one tile around him. Some ore are sometimes across a pit or something. You'll be like "damn that's too far." So you'll keep digging and upgrade more and more. It is very rewarding.
The story of the game is... well average. The graphics, the drawings are nice. Animation is good too. Nothing else to report.
The difficulty is awesome. It's progressive but never too hard or too easy. Very nice.
Finally the game controls are just very good. I played this using a DS4 pad and DS4Windows. All the movements are smooth and I had no trouble moving my dude around. I changed however the dig button to right trigger so I could hold that stuff down for long time.
The only 'problem' with the game is its replayability: levels are not randomly generated :/

But tru dat we have leaderboards and achievements like finish the game in less than two hours and stuff. I guess the whole game becomes a real crazy puzzle if you wanna speed run. Yep I can't even imagine that. BDSM style :D
Well I recommend the game, it is well made, has lots of details, never crashed, and is... just good you know. 10 hours of that game were required to finish it, after having explored everything and taking care of looking stuff around. Definitely worth it.

The only thing I feel keeping a lot of dedicated Infestation players away, is the animation of the player character. I'm assuming this will be fixed. It feels super janky, and uncomfortable to play with. The running animation kills it for me.
At the end of the day, what makes a survival game great for me, is the PVP with a blend of quirky encounters with random players. With Infestation it was like this in the first month, but after that it went and turned into a straight deathmatch. If Aftermath's dev team can get the right mix between the two they will make a great contender to all the other survival games on the market.
[ My backstory with WarZ ] If you are reading this and thinking.. this guy barely played Infestation... consider the fact that I have almost 1500 hours on steam. Remember that War Z was not even released on steam until a few months after it's alpha release. I played War Z since day 4 of it's initial alpha release. You are going laugh at me when I tell you I had never played PC games until War Z. I was obsessed with DayZ Mod videos before I came across War Z's trailer by "MrJoeTrocious" on youtube. That video is what made me go out and by a $700 HP desktop so I could play The War Z. I loved it till around the time DayZ Standalone released. Then it was a back and forth battle. I eventually stopped playing the game and moved onto trying other games like WoW and more ARMA mods. Nothing has hooked me like Infestation hooked me. When all of the emulators came out and Thai ISS I just could not bring myself to play them. All I wanted was the original game. For some reason it felt like cheating on my girlfriend or something.
I recommend Aftermath on the pure fact that it is free and has the potential to be the true successor to War Z. I have noticed a lot of the aftermath community is fresh to this game and I appreciate that. I just hope the developers can make the game great and create the community that I was once a part of. Bring back the fun and addiction that was once called The War Z... It's a new game, but it will always be "The Second Chance" game that it is today. If you guys do it right this time around you earn the right to be called a good game development team. Goodluck, Goodnight, and Have Fun. DustyZ out...
PS, I imagine this review may have not helped anyone, but I felt I had to give my insight as one of the players who was most invested in the previous game. I will not down vote a game just because it's past was ♥♥♥♥♥♥. I have it in my library and will chime in from time to time. If the game becomes what I, as a player enjoy playing, then I will invest my time into it. As would anyone who enjoys any game. Give it a chance, it's free, you're not paying for anything. If you don't enjoy, leave it alone, come back in a few months and maybe it will be better. If not, don't play. My recommendation is if you enjoy it, enjoy it as much as you can because you never know when the enjoyment won't be there any longer.

My back line soldiers make reaction shots into the backs of their allies standing in front of them.*
*People keep helpfully commenting on my review to tell me to position my soldiers so this doesn't happen, and if you choose to dedicate yourself to playing this game, of course this is what you will do. But if you have limited patience for design flaws you may not want to commit your time.
I'll try to make this review a little more helpful. There is a lot of tactical depth here if you choose to explore it. But here are some pointlessly confusing things that will frustrate new players and discourage investment:
1. Little control over your units' reaction fire. Of course you can't fire through friendly units but I think it is not too much to expect units to not attempt reaction shots with a chance to hit an ally. You could at least check this as an option during your turn. I have seen some players suggest instructing your units to drop their weapons at the end of their turn and pick them up again next turn. You could also of course just walk back and forth until your unit doesn't have enough AP to fire. If you don't do these fiddly interface screws, your units might kill each other. This really is a basic issue that the designers should have foreseen. "Won't our players just drop their weapons or run back and forth to avoid shooting their allies?" "Yeah, let's just give them an option to suppress reaction fire, or not shoot their allies." But what do I know.
2. Confusing AP costs. The interface provides a guide for how much AP to reserve each turn in order to fire at various levels of precision, and you can use a slider to set a reserve amount of AP for firing, but if you use the AP reserve and walk to the edge of your range, you will often find that the cost to fire is actually 1 or 2 greater than has been reserved, leaving your unit exposed and helpless in sight of the enemy that you planned to kill with the AP you didn't have enough of. Again, restart, or lose a unit to pointless interface issue. After this happens once (maybe twice if your attention wanders) you will learn to always reserve slightly more than the AP reserve function would if you want to fire on your enemy, making that function misguiding and useless.
3. Various other interface screws, like needing to equip a medkit as a weapon in order to use it, poor tooltips throughout, etc... It is already a game that requires patience to play, so a smooth interface is important. Just make the medkit a click-to-use item that prevents reaction fire that turn, and give it an AP cost in line with the cost of equipping and using it. Seems obvious.
There is good stuff, like, it's X-COM, there is a perfectly good tactical game underlying all this junk, and its strategic and tactical layers have good interplay. Firefights feel like fun when something random and unintuitive doesn't happen. But after 2 hours I had the impression of a game that would not respect my time, and I returned it. If none of this stuff would bother you too much, Xenonauts is a pretty cool strategic & tactical game where you kill some aliens. It lacks a lot of polish though and I'd rather play something else.

Another gripe is the alien's tendency to hide in their spaceship, leaving you with only the options of sacrificing soldiers or a prolonged seige, waiting for them to poke their heads out.
Despite all of this there is a good game trying to get out, which will certainly scratch an itch if you miss some of the more involved strategy elements in xcom classic. It's just unfortunate that a dogmatic attachment to classic mid 90s design has ultimately hampered the experience.

Update 1: So far, after playing for 9-10 hours as I'm writing this, my only complaint(s) are these. The Good:
- Combat feels better - weapons feel weightier, dual wielding adds another layer of depth, and there are a lot of cool new weapons.
- The game is longer - it took me probably 15-20 hours longer on my first playthrough of this game than my first of Dark Souls.
- The late-game is better than the early-game - unlike Dark Souls where it could be argued the best moment was Anor Londo and it went downhill from there, in this one it stays constant, and arguably increases in quality later.
- NG+ has more purpose - NG+ only items and enemies, as well as less of a restriction in online connectivity.
- It's more Dark Souls. More Dark Souls is good.
The Bad:
- Soul Memory - A mechanic in which every soul you have ever gained is counted up, and is the only factor in connecting online - sounds good on paper, but in practice, cheating players can be SL500 and mod their soul memory to 0 abd invade anyone, and a player that limits their character to SL100 for PvP will be punished for playing their character longer and not levelling.
- Boss design - There are few bosses in this game on the same level as Ornstein and Smough, Artorias, Kalameet, etc - a lot of bosses are just dudes with swords, which are alright but it gets somewhat repetitive.
- No Patches.
The Ugly:
- Keyboard controls are pretty terribad still.
- If you have a VAC ban from any game on Steam you will be unable to play online - they are supposedly looking into this but it puts a damper on it when people have VAC bans from Modern Warfare 2 where cheaters leveled you up to max level without you being able to stop it.

So much eye candy.
Really, the thing that's the most striking was their attempt - and success - at making 3D work look like 2D animation. While anime isn't everybody's cuppa, their hard work at doing hand-adjusted animation and "inbetween" models really makes it stand out from the crowd. It's easily the best-looking fighting game in my opinion, if not one of the best looking games in general. They avoid the tendency for costume and character overdesign you see in other series, but the level of detail in outfits is striking, from little rivets to even tiny bits of text you can only spot during certain animations. It really is something else.
"But how is the game?" Well, it's a very refined high-mobility 2D fighting game that sticks to its roots, largely for good and to a lesser extent for worse. Characters have fast, big, and creative attacks, a wide variety of strategies and strengths, and are loaded with personality and visual flair. There are several ways to try and turn games around, from increased damage on supers at low life to "bursts" that knock enemies away. However, if you're not into doing half-circles followed by a direction reversal, you might find this more than a little intimidating. While it's not the worst old-school fighting game motions I've seen, there is the occassional 360 degree joystick motion or quarter-circle plus half-circle archaic notions that, unfortunately, keep games like Guilty Gear targeted squarely at their default audience. However, it does feature one of the best training modes in the genre, so if you're willing to dig in, the game will teach you some surprisingly pro techniques.
The story is pure word salad nonsense at this point, concluding the story from Guilty Gear Xrd #SIGN and the barely-played-by-anybody Guilty Gear X2 Overture. Having played the series since the original Guilty Gear game on the Playstation 1, I can only imagine what it would be like to come in at this point in the story. The arcade modes set up endings for each of the characters which plays into a straightforward anime movie / visual novel mode without any actual gameplay. And while it's pretty (and the story is enjoyable for those already invested in it), I wish they had come up with a way to engage the player better. Still, it is very, very easy on the eyes. And the soundtrack is an an amazing collection of hard rock, albeit with some questionable english lyrics at times...
While it doesn't really push the fighting genre forward at all game-play wise, Guilty Gear Xrd #REVELATOR is an extremely refined and tuned entry in the series. It's nearly the Platonic ideal of what it strives to be. If you like anime or metal and you like fighting games, get on top of this. It isn't going to change videogames, but it's a great entry in an already very original and memorable series.

Mindless fun. Not very challenging, but scratched an itch. In short you go into a mine, dig up gems, avoid or attack monsters, return to the surface, sell gems, buy upgrades, and dig deeper into the mine. Repeat. There are little puzzle sections to progress to the next section of the mine that are probably my favorite part of the game, mainly because it's pretty much the only part of the game you really need to think a little.
That said, there are some interesting hazards throughout the different levels of the mines that make you think about where you're digging. You also quickly learn to not just dig willy-nilly so that you don't accidentally make some gems impossible to reach. Art style was cute, story was practically non-existent, and sound design was good. Not an incredible game by any stretch, but well worth it as part of the Humble Bundle.

Steamworld Dig is Everything I wished Motherload was, but wasn't. Multiple weapons, likable characters, Puzzle aspects, hidden areas, running out of fuel doesnt cripple you, there are actually enemies to fight, you can dig up (to an extent), you have spells and abilities, necessary tech doesnt require grind, you can buy permenant checkpoints that teleport you to the surface. I havent played this game to completion yet, but so far it's in good standings to sire my children.
The one thing Motherload has Steamworld beat on is its rogue-like elements. Steamworld's puzzle rooms are static (obviously) and don't change from playthrough to playthrough, and it's downwards path is pretty linear. If you're okay with this, pick this game up.

I love the Frogwares game series based on Sherlock Holmes. I am a Sherlock Holmes fan, a Lovecraft fan and deeply interested in Ripper-lore as well, and if I didn't know better I'd think that Frogwares are going out of their way to please me.
The games are by no means perfect, and this one is no exception, but if you are as into the protagonist and subject matter as I am, you'll forgive the flaws.
The pros:
-The voice acting for the characters of Holmes and Watson are very close to how I have always imagined them from the stories
-The story is very well researched; the developers have obviously spent a lot of time collecting materials and connecting them with the story as it unfolds. This also means that, like the other Holmes games from Frogwares, there are lots of documents to read. That may be a plus or minus, based on your preference.
-It feels like you are actually solving the crime in a good whodunnit
-The conclusion is far from the worst take I have seen. And for the most part, I think the game treats the evidence astutely.
-The puzzles related to the murders (decuctions, conclusions etc.) are fun, if rather easy.
The cons:
-The game is
linear and holds your hand a lot of the time. When you need to check out a new location, Holmes will tell you precisely that, whether it was obvious or not. And you can't leave locations until your work there is done ("No, I haven't discovered everything yet"), nor can you go back to locations where your work is already done ("I have no reason to go that way"). It would make the game a lot more challenging - and immersive - if you were allowed to go wherever you pleased. That would make the game a lot harder, of course, and the first play-through would certainly take a lot longer.
-The puzzles in this game are for the most part arbitrary and irrelevant to the case (fix a gas leak, fixing an electric winch by connecting wires , fishing out a necklace from between floorboards in a slide puzzle etc.), though challenging and entertaining enough
-Some puzzles are just... odd ("Oy vey, I would lend you my mask, but unfortunately it is in that cobra cage for some reason, so you will have to figure out a way to get the snake out first"). Brings a bit of levity to the game, though.
-Tedious errands ("I will tell you what I know if you do such and such for me")
-The quality of the voice acting varies.
Still, all in all, I thoroughly enjoyed this game, warts and all, and if your interests are at all similar to mine I can definitely recommend it.

Dishonored despite being a single player game, I've replayed it countless and countless of times, the game was simply just too fun to not replay.
So let's go onto Dishonored 2.
Being a huge fan of Dishonored, I obviously pre-ordered Dishonored 2, got real excited and hyped to play the game the moment it came out and here is how it turned out: (IT WASN'T A NO MAN'S SKY)
At the start, the downloading and loading screen were a huge disappointment, downloads and downloads, over and over again, all taking quite some time. This is not the game's fault.

I solved the problem and wen in game. The FPS was just 5-10fps.

I kinda wished it was like what the Developers said, that super different perspective what not, disappointed by this as I kinda wished they were like working on their own thing at some different place and have different stories, welp, suck it up, the gameplay makes up for it.
The plot twists, weren't really plot twists, so the story gets a little boring and in the end, the ending.
The ending wasn't as impactful as Dishonored's endings. It felt a little off. That doesn't seem right.
When I played Dishonored 2, I felt something strange.
Like my soul had some kind of void.

And then I realised.
Dishonored 2, can never, never ever replace the original Dishonored. The classic you could say.

Honestly, it was kind of stale. Essentially it is a slightly streamlined remake of the original X-Com UFO Defense. It plays exactly the same with an identical core game loop, with some of the edges polished off and some nice high res Americana for the art.
But in the streamlining they ended up cutting as much meat as they cut fat. Some odd balance choices made some of the late game interceptors and soldier weapons functionally useless, and psionics were completely cut from the late game arsenal (the aliens still have them). Where the original X-Com ended with a bang in an intense two-part mission, Xenonauts ends with a whimper with a casual stroll down a single corridor (with an optional objective in two rooms immediately to each side).
I'm curious what they're going to do in the upcoming sequel, being less chained to strict adherence to the original, but I can't really recommend going after this one.

Flowchart tl;dr recommendation:
-Fast and fluid high-paced gameplay.
-Decent amount of offline content and unlockables.
-Surprisingly good tutorials and missions to get at least started.

(Begin walloftext)
Guilty Gear is a long running 2D fighting game dating originally back to 1998. I can only speculate it began when someone watched too much shonen anime while playing wildly mistuned guitar in a garage and decided to put them both in a blender and I dare to say some folk may have encountered the name purely due to its pretty rocking soundtrack. It is perhaps the first (?) example of a fighting game where air is equally common place to duke it out as the ground due air mobility, leading to a common term "airdasher" to describe Guilty Gear and some other anime-style fighting games as well. Another notable aspect is how basic combo structure is more lenient than in several other entries combined, which on very basic level makes it easier to pick up and play without need to read a fighter jet manual how to combo several attacks. It boomerangs back later in another form however.
Like in any other fighting game, the purpose is to beat the living crap out of the opponent before the same happens to yourself. Aforementioned airdashing adds another element to it as the to the casual observer, the gameplay often appears as if two angry bees trying to hit eachother. Each character has their own moveset of normal moves and special moves, and some have unique movement options or even restrictions as well: someone has teleport dash instead of regular ground dash, someone has no real ground dash but it instead functions as air-hoverdash, one character cannot dash at all and so on. Characters' unique selling point often makes up a good part of their gameplan or tools of trade they can use. Mechanically the game provides good set of universal options, ranging from reducing chip damage and pushing the opponent back to blitz shielding to "parry" an attack essentially to simple "get off me" in form of a burst, to double jumps and instant kills - which are mostly used to either goof around or swag round-enders in certain conditions - and whatnot.
Perhaps most bizarrely (for the genre) the game actually has functional and understandable tutorial which teaches you plenty of basics how game works roughly, followed by plenty of missions where you can learn how some other characters work or prefer to use in without need to consult the fighter jet manual just yet. Multiplayer lobbies allow 8x players total playing on either four separate "cabinets" or lining up as they see fit, there is a training room so you can do a quick check of x or y before picking up a cabinet, spectate-only is possible and whatnot. Feature-wise quality of life Guilty Gear is a gold standard that should be put on a pedestral. For those who are more interested in offline content or unlocking something, there are unlockables in form of artwork, extra background music from older games or new tracks introduced in Xrd, voice actor messages, colour palettes for characters and whatnot. The main story of the game is more like a low-key anime OVA (if not outright visual novel minus naughty bits) and as far as the story goes, all I was able to decipher is that apparently in alternate universe Freddie Mercury was a scientific genius who also engineered some weapons of mass destruction with someone after magic appeared in the world and destroyed most of the ye olde tech, and then as expected something went wrong and apparently some Christians formed a resistance against newfound weapons of mass destruction taking over the world and then new crusades happened and... something something fastforward nearly 20 years of games to the actual story of Revelator. At least I found it quite entertaining and consistent.
For all the hype of quality of life, the game has pretty notable learning curve. It is nothing too uncommon in fighting games nor I would consider it a bad thing at all, but Guilty Gear is rather technical to the point you will eventually have to consult a fighter jet manual to understand what is going on, and simply practice proper (and sometimes outright rigid) procedures how to deal with various situations. Some of them are easy to search or try out in training, mode others are really convoluted and bizarre until you simply memorise what the deal was in the first place. Depending on the character in question, character matchup and other variables it can range from simple answers to the need to memorise several very specific circumstances and having only one real option to deal with it, where even tiniest mistake can mean instant loss. The game is also heavy on setplay, which is about forcing knockdowns into circumstances where they retain the advantage and ensure the opponent has as few options as possible to keep it their turn. The overwhelming amount of "you are not allowed to do anything" hits very hard and improving in the game is a pretty long road to deal with, especially for those with no former genre experience or more casual background. Another notable aspect is the game's playerbase. Random lobbies do exist but due to variable connections, where on Earth you live and GG being bit of a niche in already not-necessarily-that-popular-genre, your best bet may to find people to play with either by Steam or Discord or [insert something here]. Preferably with a touch of masochism while at it.
It is a very solid package of fluid gameplay and a good example how a fighting game's quality of life should be handled to ensure in spite of requiring a fighter jet pilot training to understand it on deeper level, all the necessary information how to get started is actually in the game as opposed to hidden on a 1990's 28k dialup optimised webpage on the Internet archive.

Instead, now they pad every monster with overtuned attacks and eratic AI to try and make a castlevania 1 style game. Character animations, especially while walking or using a torch are amateur at best. its hard to believe that dark souls 1, which came out in 2011, has better animation quality for its player characters, than its successor.

Metroid and Dig Dug had a baby!
Fun and satisfying.
7.5 / 10
Cons:
- Once you dig fairly deep into one of the mine locations, it becomes a chore to climb back out to save and re-supply.
- The game has only one boss at the very end of the 3rd Mine location. It would have been nice to have at least one for each location.
Pros:
- The game is a platformer and puzzle solver. Just exploring the mines and digging for valuables is a puzzle in technique so that you don't get stuck, miss something, or make it hard to access something later. You have to think each time you swing your pick.
- Metroid style upgrades that give your character powerful and fun new abilities keep the game exciting, while upgrades to your new equipment can be purchased by mining for valuables, making it less of a grind.
Tips:
- Death isn't that bad... Unless you're hording cash. Dying takes away 50% of your cash for repairs! It does NOT take your minerals or orbs (though your minerals will be dropped where you die and you will have to go back to get them). So make sure that when you cash in your ore for money, SPEND AS MUCH OF IT AS POSSIBLE IMMEDIATELY. This way, if you die, you'll lose some pocket change and not a paycheck, and there is only so much money to be gained in the game.
- Don't buy teleporters. They cost orbs, which are rare and even more limited than ore. There will be more short-cuts and teleporters to the surface the deeper you go, so be patient and save those orbs for upgrades.

I like the fact how simple this game is, you can grasp all the main concepts in a few minutes. Still, even though being that simple, it is very much enjoyable. Especially for us, collectors and perfectionists, it's very charming to be able to dig through the world and try to find every single last precious ore nugget that is out there.
The game length is 6 - 10 hours, and that's a benefit for me. The worlds were quite different and they introduced new concepts, which is great, one would never feel bored.
The only thing I disliked about this game is the "light" game concept. It seems to be that it was introduced in order to make the game less plain, to make the game mechanics more complex. Which I agree with, it would be way too simple otherwise. But it's not designed properly. With current design, you simply have to go above ground every few minutes, even though your bag is almost empty and you have no other reason to return, just to refill the light lamp. That often means spending up to several minutes traversing the mine to the top. That's crazy, and it's annoying as hell. Some possible improvements to this concept include: a) an ability to refill the oil from the (eternal) lamps scattered through the level, maybe at the expense of extinguishing that lamp forever b) an ability to purchase and take with you an extra flask of oil, maybe even at the expense of one of the inventory slots. With this approach, you have immediately made the game less painful and also more interesting, because there is very interesting choice to be had - spend more money and have less inventory space, but have longer and more convenient light? Those are exactly the right tough question every game should offer. Sadly, in this case, it was not though out well.
Except for the single issue mentioned above, I very much enjoyed how the game looked and played, and recommend it to everyone enjoying this kind of casual exploring/digging/a bit puzzle and platforming genre.

It is every bit as fluid and functional as the original Dishonored with slight tweaks in basic mechanics (sliding, vaulting over obstacles, etc) providing more variety in range of motion. The original Dishonored was a masterpiece in my opinion and the sequal contains everything I loved about the first and more! It doesn't just capture and replicate the winning formula however, it innovates in both major and subtle ways. It's everything a good sequal should be and honestly, who can argue with that?
The long and short of it is: "If you loved the first, you'll love the second. It's more of same but with fun and interesting innovations to keep it feeling good and entertaining. Not to mention it looks incredible. Aces all around".

The game feels something of a combination of  The Secret of the Silver Earring and The Awakened, with on one hand a dark subject matter and lots of realistic detective work, and on the other high reliance on the player's own ability to connect the right clues to draw the correct conclusions. Many of the suspects were actual people who have been suspected of the killings at one point or another. Unfortunately, the story only barely holds together, with lots of running back-and-forth and long-winded, badly acted dialogue.
Ultimately, the player needs to choose between half a dozen possible suspects. I couldn't even remember who one of them was, and another had already been cleared of suspicion. Apart from one the rest I had never even considered suspects, and the actual guilty party stuck out like a sore thumb. There had been more credible suspects earlier in the game, but these had been proven innocent, perhaps unwisely, as this made the conclusion of the game feel quite patronising.
Also patronising was how instead of more realistic depictions of the victims, the player has to make due with caricatures or even dolls -- even when Sherlock is examining the victims in person. One can't help but feel the game has been cleaned up for larger audiences -- The Awakened had featured significantly more gruesome imagery. Despite its flaws, the game is still worth a play, if only barely.

Take literature's most famous detective, Sherlock Holmes, and make a crossover with the most feared serial killer of the Victorian London era, Jack the Ripper. Sounds awesome, right? Well, I think so since I'm a geek. For the most part, this was an enjoyable adventure game even with its flaws.
+ Seriously, I've always thought this crossover would've been a great idea, glad to see it actually happened.
+ The deduction boards were probably the best puzzles, at least in my opinion; they were fun and required some thinking.
+ 1st person view addition, I already prefer this over 3rd person view for adventure games.
+ Good story, provides some suspense and thrills through out.
+ Not too challenging, and not exactly easy either. Progressive difficulty is done right for the most part.
+ Analyzing victims is lots of fun lol.
+ Dat ending.
- Errands, bleh. I'm fine with that in GTA, Skyrim, etc. But here, not exactly the most fun time.
- Graphics are crap for a 2009 game.
- Every now and then, you'll find grammatical errors in the subtitles. It annoys me.
- Voice acting isn't exactly the greatest.
- Some puzzles are dumb; for example, why does Sherlock need a "pivot" and a stick to move a barrel? Is he weak? lol.
- Some puzzles are annoying when it comes to registering your solution, such as the one where you narrow down Jack's "comfort zone" and the final deduction.
If you're a fan of Sherlock, or interested in Jack the Ripper case, I recommend this. Heck, if you love mysteries, or enjoy solid adventure games, then get this game.

This game is more like Xcom than the Xcom reboots are. If you want the nostalgia of the classics, but with some modernization for more convenient play (like knowing how many time units you will have left after a move, or being able to give a soldier a riot shield), I would highly recommend Xenonauts.
This is much more user friendly than the Open Xcom project (which aims to be more like a source port to allow the game to run on modern machines, with little focus on making the game more intuitive). That being said, it does still maintain the classic difficulty the series is known for (one of the many things it actually does better than the also amazing reboot series).
If Enemy Within and Xcom 2 didn't feel enough like XCom for you, I can fully recommend this game.
Important note: There is a bug where the game does not shut down correctly, and Steam logs it as play time. This continues even when restarting steam, and no Xenonauts related stuff shows up in Task Manager to kill the process. This has apparently been present since as far back as 2014 according to a quick google search. If you have too much play time logged, you are not eligible for a refund. While I like this game (and wasn't planning a refund), I think it is important for people to know this. And its also pretty shady on Goldhawk Interactive's part, since this has existed for so long and will explicitly make you unable to refund the game if you don't like it but don't catch it fast enough.
Second Edit: I found the solution! If you view the manual for the game from the launcher, steam thinks Xenonauts is still running until you kill Adobe Reader.

If you are a fighting game fan that has only stuck to what you've grown up with, then I highly recommend you come out of your shell and give this a try. The game has a great tutorial for beginners and a high level of depth due to how different all the characters and the options that they all have.
Gameplay wise, the game was made a bit easier so that it's more acessible to new comers. For example, the Roman Cancel system doesn't require strict timing for FRC anymore. Now you have YRC which is your new FRC and it's way easier to perform. However, just because the game was made easier doesn't mean it's any harder to master. You still need a solid understanding of fighting games to be good. Guilty gear has had an emphasis on the more aggessive side of things with mechanics such as negative penalty which removes all your meter for not fighting or back dashing too much. Also, you're rewarded with meter by attacking and moving forward. That doesn't mean that defense is completely butchered (SFV, I'm looking at you!). You have an alpha counter that you can use for half meter, DP, Burst, back dash, Faultless Defense, Blitz Shield and back dash.
On the more technical side of things, I would like to say that the PC version has the lowest input lag of all the platforms because you can turn a bunch of the fancy graphics settings. As for netcode, it can be a bit iffy if you don't have a good connection with your opponent because it's delay based (GREED SEVER) but most of the time it's playable.
Unfortunately, we're missing a few of the classic characters such as Bridget, Testament, Zappa and Anji. However, I do think that this game is totally worth it.
