So far is everything a sequel should be. It keeps the spirit and core of the first game, while improving upon the AI, the ability system, the amount of content, and the depth of the world. If you liked the previous Dishonored then this game is a no-brainer.
I do personally prefer the first game's aesthetic, I've always been a fan of grimy streets and dark corridors. However, this game looks undeniably pretty. It's much brighter and more populated, with actual people you can talk to, rather than plague infested corpses. The graphics can hog your machine, however. I'm running an 8 gig RX 480, which is a decent card, and can sit it at high-very high with infrequent frame drops.
The chaos system feels more fleshed out, rather than just a good-bad scale. You grow slowly more cynical the more you kill, and different people will add different layers of chaos. There used to be moments in the previous game where it seemed absurd that killing such a corrupt, evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ would equal killing some innocent guard, but that is now balanced.
The AI is some of the best I've seen in a stealth game to date, which was something I wasn't expecting. They react to the environment, notice empty doors opening, buddy up to search and get in formation/surround you while in combat. This makes the hardest difficulty espescially punishing. If you get caught your best option is to dissapear as quickly as you possibly can.
Corvo's powers are much the same but, once more, deeply fleshed out. Each power now has a mini upgrade tree, and you have the ability to create bonecharms to fully customise your build. Have not yet tried Emily but have seen that she's a completely different experience.
Story feels a bit reminiscent of the original game, giving a Star Wars VII vibe almost. Still, it adds new characters, new environments and new obstacles, which is all you really need in a stealth-based action game. Also Corvo has a voice, which I'm not actually sure I like. You definitely feel like you've inherited a personality more in this game, which may be a positive or negative depending on the player.
Overall, about 3-4 hours in and really enjoying it. As someone who has always been wary of sequels, espescially ones made with to be BIGGER and BETTER (Deus Ex c'mon), it did not dissapoint at all.
5 bags of popcorn and a little mask to put on while playing.

One of the best board games i have ever played.

Here's my video of one entire game versus the computer AI and a basic explanation of how it works and plays:
Wow!  There's quite a few of these little dice and card games available, but none of them that I have played are nearly as much fun and as well designed as this game.
This game is just early in development when it launched today on October 22, 2015, but it already plays and runs like a finished game with lots of pizazz and glimmer.  This game is as cleverly designed as it's own name of the game is.. "Dicetiny.. Destiny" - get it? Hehe.
Okay, imagine a board game where you roll dice to move in the opposite direction around the board as your AI opponent, each of you having a goal to knock or see your opponet's health drop to or below 0 health points.  So you take turns rolling the dice to move around, getting more powerful and aquiring more gold every time you pass your starting square on the board (Think Monopoly passing Go rewards).  In the special locations on the board you might land on the temple where you can spend your gold for very nice attack bonuses, health boosts, or action point increases!  Other corners you might land on with your dice roll could be a hand store to buy a very special card to hold in your hand, or a dungeon where you battle an increasingly more difficult monster each time it's defeated, but each also rewarind the winner with more rewards.  There are also trapped locations or occupied spots where you must either fight or hire random creatures to aid you in taking out your opponent.  This game offers a great balance of strategy with all of the choices you make, the gold you spend, when to spend it and what to spend it on, as well as luck with dice rolls and the timing of cards drawn etc.  Think RPG, Magic the gathering, and Monopoly all mixed into a perfect combination with a nice touch of humor and unique artistic style.
To be honest, this is a brilliant little game that offers a HUGE bang for your dollar.  You can build your decks, customize your decks, choose and win different cards and heroes, and play a game that will vary so much that each game will ever be the same as the one before.
My score even this early in it's development is a very solid and impressive 87%.  Watch my video to get a better understanding of why and how I came up with my score... or better yet just buy this game now and thank me later!  :-)

Once more down the hole, for old times' sake.
If you've ever been gripped by a game before, you've no doubt wondered what you'd find if you were to press just a bit further into the unknown. SteamWorld Dig uses the exhilaration of morbid curiosity and discovery as it's main mechanic; You're always wondering what else lies deeper beneath.
You're Rusty, the new miner in Gold Rush-esque Tumbleton (pop. 3). Your single purpose in life is to exploit the natural resources of the world for personal gain and development. Dig for minerals and precious metals, have them appraised, then use the funds to outift your character with new weapons and abilities so you can dig further.
The major difference between this game and other notable games with pickaxes and digging, is the experience here is much more pointed (story based linearity). I completed the storyline in roughly 9 and a half hours which is likely on the higher end of clock-in times-to-completion (I tend to overstay my welcome in most game worlds).
While I enjoyed the time I spent with it, the unfortunate reality is there isn't much replayability once you've finished the main story and unlocked all the upgrades. Randomly generated this is not, so if you're on the fence about getting this game, know that you'd be buying it primarily for the storyline and that it's pretty much a one shot deal. An endless challenge shaft with unique and otherwise inaccessible upgrades or something would have given this game that extra something worth playing over and over for.
As it stands, SteamWorld Dig is worth checking out as a moderately short, single player, story-based narrative. I'd have loved to stamp this with a pun about being a well-oiled machine but there are creaks here and there (especially as it relates to the lack of replayability). Hopefully the developers will expand upon this game with future installments or DLC.

Video version of this review:
Super Meat Boy is a platform game with a fairly high level of difficulty. Your girlfriend, Bandage Girl, has been captured by Dr. Fetus. Hey, whenever you’re hungry, do you yell, “Feed us”? And when you get tired of walking, you sit down and rest your “Feet-us”? Alright, I’m out of fetus jokes.
You have to do a lot of quick and tricky platforming to get around a bunch of obstacles. There are all sorts of stuff to avoid, like saw, lasers, needles, monsters, and so on. Don’t expect your first time playing to be a cinch. You will die… a lot. Every time you beat a level, they show a replay, showing every attempt you’ve ever made all at the same time. I died so many times on one level, I broke the replay, and had to exit to the map in order to continue on.
As angry as I have gotten, the bosses are actually quite fun. They’re very challenging, but still possible to beat. I kept getting hand cramps from all the intense platforming I was pulling off. I sure had one hell of a time with the race at the end of the Salt Factory. You have to escape as quickly as you can before the salt can reach you. No thanks, Dr. Fetus, I’ve already been plenty salty at this game. So anyway, I spent a total of thirty minutes on this level, and boy, did I get mad. But it wasn’t until a while after I beat it that I started to realize how somewhat fun it was. Because as hard as it was, and with all the times I kept saying it was stupid, it was still fair. You just have to find the best method for speed.
In some of the levels there are bandages to pick up. I haven’t really bothered to pick them up, because they are difficult to get. Besides, all they really do is allow you to get new skins. You can also get new skins in other ways. I got Commander Video from one of the warp zones in the first world. He moves slower than Meat Boy, but he can hover in the air if you hold the jump button. But playing as him didn’t really work out for me, so I switched back to Meat Boy.
Some of the really intense platforming can be really fun to do. But others are not, especially when you have to do them over and over, and you can’t figure out a way to get past some areas. I’ve certainly had my fill of rage, especially in one of the Hell levels where you have to ride a platform and avoid being hit by these flying mouth things. But I have died so many times from them, I literally was screaming. But it wasn’t just that that made me angry, what made me even angrier is this one glitch where I keep dying while the platform is moving under a narrow space. This has happened several times, and ONLY in the Hell chapter.
When it comes to glitches, the Rapture chapter has been such a problem that I haven’t actually beaten it, and ended up rage-quitting. There’s a level I had no choice but to skip because I kept on glitching through the descending platform, and landing right on the saws. There was no way to avoid the glitchiness of this level, so I went somewhere else. There was even a level where I ran straight into the floor, like, I was literally in the floor.
I’ve seen forum threads talking about the exact same problem that made me rage-quit: unresponsive jumping. This is a problem I’ve had throughout the game, but it was never as bad as it was in the Rapture chapter. Probably 90% of my deaths in this chapter were a result of unresponsive jumps. This problem actually ruins the game, because you only need to play a certain amount of levels to fight the boss, but with the levels I actually had to skip because of the broken jumping controls, and that one elevator glitch, there is no way I’m gonna be able to get there.
I can’t really say I recommend this game 100%, solely because of the glitches and jumping problem. But I think I can still recommend it because it is actually a lot of fun to play. I’m not usually one for games of high difficulty, but I will say that I think this is a great challenge for anyone who loves platformers as much as I do.

The strategic layer revolves around shooting down UFOs, deploying to ground battles and managing the direction of your forces. You have to build the bases and recruit the personel while also researching and building new toys to reduce the mortality rate amongst your soldiers.

I have really enjoyed my playthroughs and I am looking forward to Xenonauts 2.

At release this game had a few issues - crippling bugs and horrible balance issues that went well past making the game challenging to tedious.
Over 3 years later, this is now a solid, enjoyable and ultimately a good game.  Largely as a result of community contributions to the community branch.
The developers realized that their game did not offer the best modding support and that they didn't quite have the resources to fix a game that untimely was never all that popular.  So they did something almost no other dev does - they shared the code with the community.
The result is the community branch and a mod manager that not only fixes the bugs but improves game balance and further lets you easily install mods that allow you to fine tune your game.
This is not X Com Enemy Unknown or X Com 2 - it's far harder, far more brutal and admittedly more frustrating. Yet the reward for enduring the often unfair gameplay is the sense of success and tremendously deep gameplay.
Yes this game is hard, yes I suggest playing with numerous mods that tune the difficulty down, yes it's not pretty, and your soldiers will never become superheros like they do in the XCom of today. There are no 'super powers' like dodging shots or being a guaranteed a miss. You will always be at the mercy of RNG and you will lose your troops at all stages of the game rather than having them become vastly more powerful than the aliens.
In short - give this game a shot, hit up the community to figure out which mods you want and what strategies to use to deal with the aliens as the game will not hold your hand and expect to reload often or fail often.

There’s a formula to the game that having played 
 at any time prior to this, which should make any 
 player comfortable with how things go. There’s the base building, the air game, and the ground game.
Your eight-man squad can be made up of anyone you choose. You’ll have the privilege of naming them, as well as equipping their weapons and classes. This adds a personal touch that makes you care more about each decision you make when moving them on the ground against their alien adversaries.
On the geoscape, or world view, you’ll scan for alien activity. A scout will appear, and you can send ships to intercept. Compared to
, the air game here is expanded.
The game has an old-style aesthetic that is appreciated and clear to see. However, the hand-drawn visuals, bright colors, and wonderful animations set it apart from anything out there today. This, coupled with the built-in Xenopedia shows off more of that great art in alien and ship design. 
It can be punishingly difficult, tense, and absolutely overwhelming. But the game’s sheer depth and level of control, makes it a rewarding and fulfilling experience, even if you have to start over multiple times.

Pay to win items in this game include fast cars and premium firearms far deadlier than the stock firearms which otherwise would have taken days to weeks to earn, if at all. Pay to win elements should never award any significant advantage over the default elements. If it does, the quality of gameplay is flushed down the toilet and it's not a real game anymore.
In summary, the only way to be good in this game is to buy the deadly premium weapons on which the company has unabashedly placed exorbitant pricing, and apparently most players do so every day. It is the only way to have any amount of fun in this game, unless you enjoy being unfairly DM'ed.

Unless you are willing to spend hundreds of dollars a month on this one game, I strongly suggest looking elsewhere to satisfy your daily cravings of online shooter fun.

An amazing game for the ludicrously low price, but very bare-bones at the moment, with noticably wonky animations. Otherwise, it's a surprisingly competent cooperative shooter with a number of character classes, weapons, and stat-boosting gear items available. You can switch beween third-person, first-person and even top-down views at will. It has two modes currently, Harvest and Survival, the main difference being that Harvest ends after ten waves and a boss fight, as in say, Killing Floor, with a variety of maps. The jetpack-equipped Assault, healing Support, and cloaking Recon classes are available from the start, while others must be purchased using "Trek" currency, which can be obtained in-game through achivements and quests, and also exchanged for the other currency "Ion", albeit at a slow rate. Other cash shop items include armor colors, hats, pets, XP boosts, etc. There is an experience and level system with skill trees, allowing you to get things like increased sprint speed or shorter cooldowns for your class grenade. Everyone can also perform a short distance teleport move and a more mundane dodge roll. There's a zany variety of enemies, including robots, aliens and goddamn dinosaurs.
According to the various trailers there's a startling array of content planned for this game, including pilotable vehicles, a hub city with vendors, personal spacecraft, and some form of open-world gameplay transforming the overall experience into a type of shooter-MMO, perhaps vaguely similar to what Destiny should have been. It remains to be seen if the developers can meet these goals but I wish them luck in doing so.

So far is everything a sequel should be. It keeps the spirit and core of the first game, while improving upon the AI, the ability system, the amount of content, and the depth of the world. If you liked the previous Dishonored then this game is a no-brainer.
I do personally prefer the first game's aesthetic, I've always been a fan of grimy streets and dark corridors. However, this game looks undeniably pretty. It's much brighter and more populated, with actual people you can talk to, rather than plague infested corpses. The graphics can hog your machine, however. I'm running an 8 gig RX 480, which is a decent card, and can sit it at high-very high with infrequent frame drops.
The chaos system feels more fleshed out, rather than just a good-bad scale. You grow slowly more cynical the more you kill, and different people will add different layers of chaos. There used to be moments in the previous game where it seemed absurd that killing such a corrupt, evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ would equal killing some innocent guard, but that is now balanced.
The AI is some of the best I've seen in a stealth game to date, which was something I wasn't expecting. They react to the environment, notice empty doors opening, buddy up to search and get in formation/surround you while in combat. This makes the hardest difficulty espescially punishing. If you get caught your best option is to dissapear as quickly as you possibly can.

The best PC port of Souls series for now. Let's put an emphasis on "for now" part.
Even though I can spot some translation errors on my Korean version, the experience is hardly affected by it. DS2 has better mouse and keyboard controls compared to DS1, but I'll just stick to my faithful gamepad to transcend from death.
Graphic wise... actually I'm disappointed. Only difference of PC and console version is textures and framerates. No dynamic lighting, awesome area effects, or w/e we were able to see and get excited about were added for PC version. If only going 1080p and 60fps was Fromsoft's idea of graphical improvement for PC port, then they should give themselves a backstab. This should've been achieved back in when DS1 was ported to PC for the first time and not for DS2. Fromsoft should've known that players already expected 1080p and 60fps to be on PC port of DS2 since DS1 and were expecting more. To be honest, I didn't give a single "thing" about texture of console versionof DS2 since I've already knew that last gen consoles cannot achieve much with graphics. But we are talking about a PC version, a medium that can be pushed to the limit. If DS2 wasn't going to have a PC port, then I would've not even bothered with this BS. But DS2 has pc version and I already have expectations of having better experience of DS2 on PC than console "overall".
Combat wise... PC version still have those gawd awful delays of running, perrying, and using items. May be later two would've been my personal issue with the game, however, delays on the character to shift to running mode? Why backstab is not a backstab but rather a stab in the back of the side of the back???? Yea I understand backstab hitbox is smaller and requires more precise hit, but why not activated when my character is too obviously and directly standing at the back of the enemy? But then why can I get a backstab activated when i'm like on the side of the back of the enemy? I dunno what Fromsoft did to these mechanics. (BTW I'm not criticizing the new perrying mode or shield bashing. I rather like them more than the old way)
Environment wise... I don't know why but PC version seems more lighter than console version. Overall environment hasn't changed but I just don't know why. May be 'cause dynamic lighting's back? No? No...
Gameplay performance wise... I like it. I'm using the laptop with slowarse 5600rpm HDD but I still get 3 second loading screen time. Character customization screen updates the character faster than console version. No more 10~15 sec wait after you moved a tick of slider to the side to see what's changed. My character's motion is butter smooth (mostly because of 60fps part I assume), Don't see much of random frame drops, (though I still experience them due to my outdated hardware...), and better lighting effects (I said better...)
Interface wise... Same deal as the console. Simply awful. Where's my DS1 and DeS interface that actually worked for me...?

This is the best game, you guys.
Just to get it out of the way, I haven't had any of the crashing/startup/etc issues other people have been experiencing. I guess being a power-user with a trimmed/optimized OS has its perks :P
Also, PLAY USING A GAMEPAD. FROMsoftware doesn't know what a mouse and keyboard are, so just don't bother with them. Seriously, get a gamepad, they're dirt cheap on amazon. If you don't, and decide to use K+M, you'll look like an idiot when you start complaining about the controls. Get a gamepad, don't be a♥♥♥♥♥♥ All the talk about "THEY PROMISED GOOD CONTROLS *hyperventilating*" is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The absolute majority of their dev work on the PC version went into graphical tech and engine stability. Again, the devs don't know what a keyboard and mouse is, stop crying.
ACTUAL REVIEW PART:
The visuals are amazing. Not crysis 3 good, but very well done. You'll be sucked in instantly. The lighting is very good (albeit dated tech). Shadows add to the bleak and melancholy theme of the world. Textures are sharp and detailed. Animation is fantastic; everything flows together to make the characters more natural (and at times, unnatural).
Sound design is nothing short of masterful. The music dims out during times of peaceful respite or when you're deep in a dungeon. It really helps sell the "I could get murdered at any second by something from any direction" feel of the game. This system really shines during boss fights, where the music hightens into a symphony of desperation once a boss is near death. You really FEEL your struggle, and this makes victory feel even better.
Gameplay-wise, it's a *souls game. The recipe has been refined and moulded with bits and pieces added or removed, but at its core it's still a *souls game. This is a good thing. The UI has been significantly improved. Menus are quick (sometimes too quick), there's no hiccups when you're blasting through your inventory trying to equip another weapon in place of your broken one while a group of undead are rushing at you. Oh yes, there's no pausing; better find a bonfire. Combat is fast paced, but methodical and strategic just like the previous games. The various subsystems (e.g. magic, upgrading, durability, fast travel, leveling up, etc) have been redesigned. Things are more straight-forward and it helps alleviate the notorious learning curve that this series has.
Even if you haven't played the previous games, you should play this one. If you're a fan of dark fantasy and love a good challenge, this is it. Just get a ♥♥♥♥ing gamepad.

If your looking for a 2d exploration platformer thats not too difficult, and has a medium length to it, then this would be a good choice. I completed it in around roughly 8 hours and the best way I could describe Steamworld is if Digdug and Metroid had a baby. The art style is very pleasing to the eye and I really enjoyed the music. The characters are likable and the story, while not original, isn't bad. Like I said before the game isn't very difficult, the times I died were due to my own impatience or lack of paying attention, and the only penalty for death is half your money, which is no big deal as by the end game money comes in fairly easy.

The main mechanic of the game is to explore underground and mine for precious ore while trying to discover what happened to Rusty's, the main characters, uncle. You bring the ores back to the surface and sell them to buy upgrades, that in turn allows you to reach new areas. After you get deep enough that trecking back to the surface is a chore, you discover teleport pads that take you right back to the surface, and when your done with the shops return you to where the pad is underground. There are a few pads already placed but you can buy your own and place them where you wish as well. I really enjoyed Steamworld Dig and highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys 2d platformers or exploration games.

SteamWorld Dig is as the name implies, a game about digging... and that's pretty much all there is to it.
The game is incredibly short (I've beaten it in about 5 hours, including bonus levels that are spread around), and between the extremely repetitive, dumb enemies and the incredibly simple mechanics, there is almost no challenge involved, with the exception of the
, which can be mildly challenging.
There is little consequence for failure: die and you will be revived. Your lost loot will stay there so you can pick it back up and keep going. Healing and refilling your
which you acquire fairly early in the game are both very easy to do.
Speaking of the loot though, all you can find is different types of ore (which are only used for money) and special orbs with are used in more expensive purchases that improve your character: You can dig faster, have more health and so on. There are upgrades spreaded around here and there that WILL change your character, such as a
or a
, but ultimately, even they do little to improve the game's overly simple mechanics.

It is sad that I can´t recommend this game. Taking the original XCom, improving its graphics and adding new features sounds good, but the devs totally destroyed the gameplay implementing AI cheats.
Don´t get me wrong, I know that because of limitations of AI, the computer player must have some advantages over the human player. All games do that. But one thing is giving advantages to the computer, and other thing is giving it the ability to cheat.
Computer´s soldiers in this game have better aiming than yours, better morale than yours, better resistance than yours, they heal better than yours, they have better weapons than yours , they have more specialized units than yours, and they have psychic abilities that you can´t have. All  those things are advantages.
BUT, having the ability of knowing where each one of your soldiers is, at all times, by all of their soldiers, that is not an advantage, that is clearly cheating.
Advantages make a game challenging, cheats make a game frustrating.
You can´t make ambushes, you can´t run and hide, you can´t flank and take the enemy by surprise, you can´t infiltrate. Why? Because the computer constantly knows where your soldiers are.
And I know that the computer MUST know where your soldiers are, because it is controlling the program after all, but in good games, the computer player behaves like all positions of your soldiers are unknown to it.
Imagine a exploration game where the computer player, taking advantage of the fact that positions of all treasures are in its memory, goes directly to take all of them, giving the human player no chances of taking any. Something like that happens in this game. That cheat totally ruins the gameplay.

Let's start it with stating that I have played most of UFO games.
Except some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ FPS, I did all the classics, Aftermath, Firaxis versions, even UFO A.I. (free remake).
When you compare xenonauts to them, Xenonauts simply suck.
Here is why:
- no geoscape. Flat map that stutters when you move it around, visibly and annoyingly
- imbalanced weapons and armors and vehicles
- imbalanced research
- imbalanced base construction
- imbalanced item production
- buggy cover
- buggy AI
- game breaking bugs like your soldiers suddently can't move
- shooting and grenade throwing mechanics
- idiotic concept of TUs
- very poor morale on soldiers
- parts of environment are not destructible
- can't breach ufo hull
- no unit training outside of the mission
I will be honest with you.
This is X-Com mechanics, messed up to annoy you.
First, upkeep and production cost.
In order to produce an item, say lowest armor, you have to pay money for production, build workshop (cost you money), pay upkeep costs for workshop, hire engineers (costs you money) pay montlhy salary to them.
And when you try to sell the item, it sells at half production cost.
Meaning you cannot make profit from anything you construct.
I modded that out, halving construction costs and times and salaries, and upping sale costs a bit, but FFS is the vanilla so unrealistic and stacked against having fun from the game.
Second, tactical part is so crappy, it is insulting.
If you have played any ufo games or games like Fallout1/2/tactics, you do know the concept of Action Points.
Here, there are time units. Any action that is not related to firing weapons takes defined amount of TUs (I have modded it down again), but SHOOTING YOUR GUN TAKES PERCENTAGE.
What does it mean?
Two soldiers, one with 50 TUs and other with 100 TUs, move 20 TU in one direction. You would expect that first will shoot once, but another will shoot many times.
You are wrong.
Firing LMG will cost 30 TUs for first soldier, but 60 TUs for a second one.
Developers had tested and tried mechanics done many times before, instead their opted for this stupidity.
I am virtually certain, that If I was fast enought to run extra ten meters in the same time as another guy, I would also be able to pull the trigger at least one extra time. Again, I had to lower that to make game playable.
Apart from that accuracy and damage is atrocious. Aliens always need one or two hits to kill your soldiers, initially unarmored soldier is one hitter for an alien handgun, later on heavily armored soldier will be blasted off from plasma cannon. Armours don't reduce damage done - they have a chance to stop it completelly at the expense of armour HP, which are getting used as the damage is received. But there is no indicator your armour is down and next shot will kill your trooper.
And accuracy always sucks. Pistols are fantastically unaccurate, missing from point blank range.
And damage has 50% random element to it (+/-), meaning that even if you shoot you might not harm enemy.
And then there is psionics and panic. Psionic attacks can reach your soldiers from anywhere on the map, regardless of distance and obstacles. Panic attacs can happen to your most experienced veterans, if they survive alien shots, they usually panic or bleed to death. Or panic and run away from your medics, and bleed to death.
Third, and most important, game is tedious, frustrating and boring.
You do not have alien infiltration turning some organisations against you. You do not have multiple landing missions (they happened very rarely for me), just aliens floating around and bombing countries lowering your approval and funding.
Interesting thing is that you loose the game if 1/3 of the world stops funding you. I had to mod this to at least half, because I think it was silly.
There is no soldiers training when idle. Menu is difficult to navigate sometimes. Research is boring and proffesor comments on your engineers (he calls people building plasma cannons monkeys, brutes and primitives; why this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ angle in the game?) is pretty messed up.
There are few races of aliens, there are many classes of aliens, but alien classes are not mentioned. I would love to have some entries in xenopedia, but apparently that was too much work.
Also aliens are usually camping in the last room in downed ufos, ready to return reaction fire at your grunts.
Technology is standard, with no fancy things to them: for example you meet small alien scout drones, but game never lets you build your own.
Tanks etc have 2x hitpoints of your soldiers (seriously?) and die way too soon.
Also, while you can recover wreck of a downed plane, you cannot fix your destroyed tank.
All of the above and more adds up to the game that is completelly devoid of any charm.
It's not challenging, it's just brutal.
For example one might think that developing alien based technology would make countries interested in paying you trucks of cash just to boost their defences against invasion, instead you sell it at a loss.
Many small things like that add up to big pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥that is really not worth playing.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas still holds a very special place in my heart even after all these years and multiple entries in the franchise.
Rockstar really outdid themselves on this game. (even though you could say that about most Rockstar games).
The world is big and ambitious, and even has more things to do and see than most open world games does today.
While the map is nothing compared to let's say Grand Theft Auto V in size, since the game features 3 large cities and plenty of small towns, forest areas, mountains, and deserts the world feels massive. It's one of the few games where I can just hop into a vehicle and drive just for the sake of exploring and not get bored. Nearly 150 hours on Steam alone (And I've previously played on the Original Xbox, Playstation 2 & Playstation 3) and I still feel like there's more to explore and see, and during my recent play-through I found locations and secrets I didn't even know were in the game.
The soundtrack is on point, that feeling of driving from one city to another and then all the sudden a song like "Hold the line" goes on and it instantly makes my day better.
It is pretty clear however that I have a strong nostalic feeling towards the game, but looking at the game and trying to put those feelings aside the game does hold up to this day. (well, maybe not the graphics but there are plenty of mods to fix that).
A big open world, a huge variety of weapons and different types of vehicles, a great storyline about following trains, betrayal, and brotherhood really makes San Andreas a timeless classic.

Have you asked yourself what would happen if an alien invasion happened during Cold War? No? Well, me neither, but the point is Xenonauts are the answer for that question!
Xenonauts are in my opinion one of the best turn-based tactical strategies.
There are many different types of aliens, each of them fights in its own way, making it hard to win every time with use of the same old tactics. You need to adjust your moves and equpiment to the situation you find yourself in:
You will fight differently with aliens that can heal themselves, and with aliens that can only bite, but if they bite you... Well, it would be better off if they don't.
But aliens are not the sole thing you have to worry about. Half of your victory goes to making a good use of terrain you're fighting in. You will act totally different depending on a place where combat takes place:
On a farm you have many open spaces and only few good spots for cover. That means you will need to act fast, in order to have an upper hand. However, in an industrial part of the city, where you have countless buildings with more than one floor, you will go carefully, moving from one wall to another. You don't want to carelessly open every single door, because sometimes there's something right behind them.
So, you already know how to be careful on the battlefield and how to kill an alien scum? Well, you don't. There's also third thing you have to keep your eye on: Morale. Your soldiers aren't the terminators. These are normal people, with fears of their own and you have to keep their morale high, otherwise they can panick. They can freeze in fear, they can start running away from the place of danger (often right onto the enemy), and in the most serious situations, they can get PTSD and start shooting around with high probability of killing one of your other soldiers.
Last but not least, Xenonauts have many awesome mods. You think that there are too few types of aliens? No problem, just install the mod that gives you a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of new enemies, among which are even xenomorphs!
You think that combat maps repeat too often? Just install the mod that gives you 1000+ new maps for ground combat!
You wish for aliens to have more ships you can fight on and you want to have more weapons for your soldiers? There are mods for that too!
Xenonauts are really awesome game and if you want a game you can spend 50+ hours with, you want to shoot aliens, but you want that experience to be challenging and every mistake of yours to bite you right in your♥♥♥♥♥(there's even ironman option!), then this game is for you!

I waited almost 6 years before finally playing this. I figure by now the game would be a) properly finished and b) mods would have filled in any missing pieces.
Instead its a frustrating and weak copy of the original X-Com. Initially I found this game to be favorable, but even with the community mods its lacking in so many places that its hard in the long term to recommend this game. The primary problem is that the devs havent learned what most have over the last few decades: difference between difficult and punishing. Being unnecessarily punishing accomplishes nothing but forcing the player to reload the save and try again, or exit in frustration and play something else. Only those willing to put up with the games nonsense should bother playing this. Everyone else should steer clear and play Xcom 2 instead.

Frustrating, and at times even ridiculous, RNG combat copy pasted straight from XCOM:EU/EW, but FAR more engrossing and immersive. Even with its plain 2D graphics that might put off some, it doesn't really detract from enjoying such a great title. This is a straight retro, old-school type strategy game, more in tune with the older, and superior, XCOM titles.
Less pretentious than EU/EW too in its overall presentation, and with interesting enemies rather than those stereotypical, Mars Attacks!/Halo(Grunts)-esque dumb looking ones. And you will not spend ridiculous amounts of time customizing the armour, looks and fashion of a soldier that might not survive till the end, and that you might lose in the next mission. Which is what most people always seem to do in the newer XCOMs, spending more time customizing their units than playing the actual game. This ain't a dress-up, pimp your gang, fashionista title, it doesn't have any cosmetic DLCs to begin with.
It is recommended, even by the devs, to move to the Community Edition branch on the BETAS tab, by right-clicking on the game in the Steam library, and on properties. It's an updated version of the game, it improves upon it, fixing some bugs and balancing some other issues. So I suggest to do that before installing the game for the first time.

I like this game. I feel like playing it right now as I write this. I still can't decide if I want to give it a thumbs up or down. Chances are you're on the fence about this game; tempted by the unique PvP experience, but wary of the bugs, crashes, hackers, etc.
The short answer is: this game has apparently come a long way, and it still has a long way to go as well. But whether it'll get 'there' is a complete mystery.
The game is fun to play.... for awhile. Servers vary greatly. Some of them wipe frequently, others may never wipe unless an update forces them to. (The blueprint system further complicates this, but being relatively new, I don't know any better) This means that a full wipe (blueprints and map) is like the gunshot at the start of a race; everyone has a level playing field and servers will definitely be full.... for awhile. If the server didn't wipe their blueprints, then that's when you get players running around with guns on day 2, because they played on the server previously. Choose servers wisely.
Unless you can commit a lot of time to a server, chances are your progress won't be there when you return. You'll get home from work one day and everything you have will be gone. You never got a chance to raid anyone else because, from what I can tell, the blueprint system sucks, and hinders progression and fun. Unless you can find a gun, or someone gives you one (which is awesome when it happens, and again, there's an amazing social element of this game, make it what you will), you're going to be vulnerable. You're going to be vulnerable for a long time. But it's not to say that you won't get some decent spear battles, some bow warfare, because you will. The game holds up in a lot of ways. There's a lot of fun to be had here.
But ultimately, this is a game for people who either have no job, or have a lot of friends. From what I can tell, this game has gone through periods of great success, being fun at one point. But because things continue to change drastically, they haven't figured it out yet. The weekly updates are a good thing, it does appear like they're working on the game. Even though mine crashes at least once a session.
This game is going somewhere but nobody really knows where. Don't pay full price. Prepare for long load times.

There are five languages to choose from when you load the game, but thereafter, there are no options.  There is a faint button in the top right corner that will give you the option to return to the main menu, but it won't even pause the game.
Use the arrow keys to move left, right, and jump, and the space bar to creep and/or interact with objects.  If you want to pick something up, the down button is more reliable than the space bar.  Movement feels clunky, as the keys are not as responsive as I'd like.
The graphics are lovely and environmental, and the music is nice.  We have occasional thought bubbles that pop up, and there are intermittent voiceovers, as well.
Gameplay is standard platforming with some simple puzzles and interactions.  You will die -- a lot -- and that's not a bad thing, except when it happens because of poor controls.  Still, the game got a lot more interesting when I hit episode 2, so I persevered.
It's worth playing if you happen to have it in your library.  While I enjoyed the game, I'm afraid that I cannot recommend it unless you got it either deeply discounted or bundled.  It is very short (three episodes), and the ending is both abrupt and unsatisfying.
Sorry devs.  I believe that your work here shows promise, and I hope that you'll come out with an awesome game that I can give a great review to!

First of all I don´t know why it says 8 hours... I had played this for at least 50...

I really enjoyed this game from beggining to end, it´s a challenge,
The only other good games (at leas for me) are X-Com Enemy Within and X-com 2... but those are like completely new reboots, whilst this feels like the old X-com.
So... if you loved the first X-Com UFO Defense from 1994 go an buy this one out now...
Why are you reading this?  Go.  Buy the game.  Now.

Before I get jumped on by the fanboys out there I should point out that the only real reason I'm down-voting this is because I don't feel it does enough to differentiate itself from the original. So with that said, anyone who wants a slightly improved version of XCom will likely be very happy with this game because the original was a good game and this improves on it slightly. But only slightly. And for MY money it just isn't enough to warrant not simply going off and playing the original which is vastly cheaper if not free.
Xenonauts, even with all its community mods, improved graphics, and better flavour text also has several other issues. Getting around takes practice, it is either not possible or (since if there is a way I couldn't find it) not intuitive to rotate the map - and this often makes certain things hard to make out and makes deadly mistakes more a case of accident than design. Moving between levels, such as climbing a staircase, means that unless you have risked someone outside where you are being sniped from to use up the AI overwatch, is certain death on anything but the easiest level. The controllable interceptor scenes seem to be a bit of a non-entity as the controls are not very responsive and nine times out of ten you will simply hit the autoresolve. Throwing a grenade has such a cost that you can barely move and throw in the same turn. The same can be said for the heavy machine gun. The shotgun seems to work almost as well as the assault rifle at the mid range and, again due to the AI tactic of sitting and waiting, is otherwise all but useless since you can't get close until the overwatch is used. You can't sit and wait around like the AI does because either the AI just wont move or they will kill all the civilians.
Now I'm sure that mid game some of these problems disappear as your guys get stronger and more capable at their roles but for me it's just all a bit tedious compared to the new breed of XCom games. So my feeling on this is that it is worth having if you preferred playing the original but only if you also find playing the original itself so retro that a slight improvement in graphics and flavour would make a big difference. For me it doesn't.

SMB is a brutally tough platformer wherein you control a small cube of sentient meat in his quest to rescue his girlfriend bandage girl from the clutches of the evil Dr fetus. The game features hundreds of levels throughout a series of worlds which are just choc full of meat shredding obstacles. The game controls very nicely with fast and precise movement, and the levels are designed very well, with the difficulty slowly ramping up to the games famously crushing levels. One very nice twist is the replay function, when you beat a stage you get a replay of EVERY attempt you had taken at the stage. So if you can't beat a stage and you keep trying and failing, you know that all of those hundreds of deaths are going to be an absolutely amazing replay and it really helps avoiding the frustration that builds up in this situation.
-Tight, fast and precise. Movement feels good and there are multiple different characters with interesting moment options
-lots of content, the campaign and "dark mode" campaign are huge and there is also a user made level browser that sometimes has some cool stages
-the replays are very entertaining
-cool boss fights
-I like the music and sound design
-can get frustrating sometimes. I stalled out on the second boss for ages before I finally beat him
SMB is a classic in the genre and is very well put together indeed. Platformer fans will get a kick out of meatboy's adventures, non-fans probably won't get as much out of this but for a couple of bucks on sale you really can't go wrong. Seminal platformer

The third installment in the Souls series brings more of what you know and love, nothing more and nothing less.
Staying true to the formula created by its predecessors, it adds subtle but important changes to the combat system, like the stamina regeneration delay and improvements to strength and dual wield builds with guard break and power stance respectively. Most importantly, death now removes a portion of your health, until it reaches 50% of your initial HP but is reversible via the use of human effigies, the new version of humanity.
The way stats work has been altered as well, with stats now raising several secondary attributes along with the primary, while luck has been removed completely and is now adjustable only through specific items and equipment. The description of some primary stats might mislead you as well, so you better use the tooltips that describe exactly what they do, for example vitality does not raise HP but equip load.
Finally, keep in mind that adaptability is a very important stat for every build because it shortens your healing animation and generally hastens some basic actions like the roll, the time it takes to raise your shield e.t.c.
Moving forward to the level design, a staple of the series, unfortunately it’s not up to the standards of previous releases. Lending the branching design of the first game, while giving a more consistent feel to the world akin to the second game, it fails to touch any of those, due to uninspiring design and the absence of the intricate area connections. There is no Tower of Latria, Anor Londo or Sen’s fortress here, nor the feel that everything is connected via an ingenious shortcut system. This factor takes a toll on the general immersion of the game and gives the impression it lacks the heart, or the soul if you prefer, of the older games, sticking only to combat for an improved experience.
Regarding the difficulty and boss fights, I would say that, despite initial fears, the game easily lives up to the reputation of the series while being more fair and consistent that Dark Souls. If you  are coming into this game after an in depth playthrough of Dark Souls, naturally you will face less problems when progressing, but to the average new player the game will seem as unsettling as a bed of nails.
The difficulty pattern of the bosses is again same as it was previously, with mostly easy fights, disrupted by a few really hard ones. There’s no skill wall like Smough and Ornstein but there are several bosses that will excite you as well as many more that will be a face roll. Sadly, a few of the bosses are recycled from the previous game, which I can only address to laziness and unfortunately, this is a trend that is followed by items too, to a larger extent than I would like.
There’s also two ways to increase the difficulty, by joining a certain covenant at the start of the game or through the use of a rare item called the Bonfire ascetic. New game + has seen many changes as well, now not only limited to increased damage and life of enemies, but also by adding new behaviors, attack patterns and ambushing red phantoms in areas you thought previously safe. Some boss fights are also affected, getting tremendously more difficult if you play solo.
Last but not least, the enemies stop respawing after 15 consequent kills. This is a double edged sword, because on one hand it allows for easier progression, but on the other hand it removes the ability to grind infinitely, making mistakes and soul losses much more important. It is countered by the use of a Bonfire ascetic.
A few things I would like to note separately, would be that the characters this time around, apart to a few exceptions, are not so cryptic or tragic, again removing from the immersion.
Communication and interaction with other players has been made a lot more stable, PVP has been improved and the crafting system has been simplified to a large degree.
Hexes are now a separate thing which combines intellect and faith to great effect and are advisable for more of a sophisticated play, while covenants have been given more depth.
There is also less variation to enemies than before with some of them being reskined on later levels, but keeping the same attack patterns.
All in all, it is a masterful crafted game, which might lack in level design, heart and innovation compared to the insanely high standards of its predecessors, but on the other hand, is a great amalgamation of the mechanics you appreciated in the previous games, polished and improved to a mirror shine.
PC version is the definitive with higher resolutions, framerates and loadtimes in comparison to the console versions. Must buy.

is a decent little love letter to Limbo that suffers from a stunted playtime and some over-simplified puzzles.
A girl has no name as she crash-lands on a strange alien world, nor does a girl have much in the way of a defence from its many hostile inhabitants except for cowering in the shadows until danger has passed. There's some great set-pieces here, the best of which involves being captured by the terrifying resident Neanderthal tribe and your subsequent escape from their cave but while much of the art direction and atmospherics are on point, the entire experience sometimes feels overly derivative. There's no real reason for your character to be a copy of the glowing-eyed silhouette boy from Limbo. His anonymity was a major point of that game's story; here, you see the girl's face and hear her voice several times.
A lot of work has gone into
over the past couple of years from its original sole chapter and it arrives on Steam with another two in tow. It's not enough really; there doesn't feel like there's any real resolution at the end of the game which, for an experience that relies heavily on its plot to balance its plain platforming and puzzles, will leave some players feeling a bit short-changed.
Still, I can't really not give this a recommendation based on the complaint that I really wanted to play more of it, can I?

Dark Souls II is a hardcore JRPG. The game is challenging, and you learn from your mistakes from the punishments death give you. The more you die, the more you get hollowed, to the point where you only have half of your health. To get back the other half of your health you will need a human effigy, which isn't a common item at all.
The game is definitely better on PC, especially for the 60 FPS and faster loading screens over the 30 FPS lock and 20-30 second loading screens that the consoles offer. The game is playable with mouse and keyboard, but I still recommend getting a controller to play this game.
The gameplay is great, the fighting system is really fun. You have a HUGE choice of weapons, and you fight against many different types of enemies, and most bossfights are pretty fun, except for the ones that are complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (won't mention them because spoilers). You can also fight against people online, which I think, is one of the greatest selling points of this game, the PvP.
Speaking of the greatest selling points, I think the lore is very interesting as well. Each item has a description which tells a story, even though unlike the first game there is some missing lore. But as time passes, people make up theories about the lore which are very interesting as well (make sure to end the game before watching any lore videos though).
In conclusion, I really can't say which game is better: Dark Souls I or Dark Souls II. Both games are worth playing, no matter how much you rage, or how much controllers you throw to your monitor, these two games are probably the best RPGs i've played (maybe its because I dont play RPGs much but oh well). If you're new to the Souls series, I highly recommend Dark Souls I first. Still, a great game.

OddPlanet is a 2d platformer. It’s inspired by Limbo and Oddworld games. You play as a girl who has crash landed on an alien planet. Just like Limbo you only see a black silhouette of the girl character and only her eyes are visible. The whole theme however is not all black/white/grey like Limbo. You can see yellow color of what appears to be the sun in the background, and other colored creatures like a bee etc.
The graphics are similar to Limbo but not exactly, this game has color instead of all black and white. It’s very atmospheric and you get that same feeling of loneliness you got from Limbo, except it’s even creepier as you’re on another planet with aliens lurking about. There is no option for adjusting resolution and for me the game started in 720p, this could be a problem. I was getting 50-60 FPS the whole time I played.
Just like the graphics are, sounds are incredibly atmospheric as well. The slow music, the creepy wind and crows in the background really gives the chills.
Gameplay is very similar to Limbo, the movement, the jumping is very similar to how Limbo handles. Not that it’s a bad thing, in my opinion Limbo had really good gameplay. You can run around, jump, climb ledges etc. You have to solve puzzles and sneak around. You are always hiding from enemies in this game. Pressing space makes you interact with the objects or you can walk on toes also by pressing space key. This sneaky walk on toes is required to avoid enemies hearing you. It is a sort of survival game where basically everything is trying to kill you but it’s linear so you must keep progressing through episodes.
Fun little game which is heavily inspired from Limbo. I quite enjoyed it. There are a few bugs and problems but nothing too major. There is also no option to select resolution and bind keys. Other than these the game is fun to play and will remind you of Limbo a lot.

Plastiland is a very nice lemmings-like logic game. The goal is to help little cute round characters with eyes to go safely from start to finish. They are able to change shapes into various helpful objects, but they are unable to jump from height or swim in a lava.
I found levels of this game look like made more from candies, rather than from plasticine. Either way they look nice. Backgroung music fits right giving the game sweet atmosphere.
At first glance it might doesn't look so, but the game is challenging. It's rather easy go get 1-star ratings, but the majority of levels need some deeper thinking to get all 3 stars.
There are 2 main words and a bonus one, which levels unlock after collecting a proper amount of stars. Actually I found the bonus ones more entertaining since they give the player more freedom.
There are 2 issues I found that I would improve. First one - putting requirements for stars on the playing screen instead of having them in a pause menu. Or, at least, showing them right after getting to a new level. It's annoying when you go to a next level and right after that you have to pause to check the requirements.
The second one is getting an error after clicking the exit door. But it also might be my computer issue, anyway.
As I read comments, there were some issues with port in the past, but now I found none of them.
Summarizing, Plastiland might look childish and easy, but it's actually not that simple. If you like casual and logic games with no rush, this one is for you.

This is one of those times I would love to give a game a "no thumbs either way" review.
Xenonauts is basically a faithful recreation of the original X-Com UFO Defense from Microprose. That's a great starting point because the original is widely considered one of the best games of all time. I'm not going to compare and contrast it against the newer re-imagining of XCOM (well, not much) because there are enough people out there who have done that already. The old version, and this one, are tense turn-based titles of small squad combat against a more powerful alien force.
The core of the game takes place on small battlefields (a couple of city blocks, a farm, etc.) where you do battle against the aliens in good ole' tense turn based combat. These battles are often gripping and engaging as you slowly work your way through the terrain, using overlapping fire to kill the enemy and exterminate them from the map. When you're not fighting the ground war, you're back at your base researching the alien tech, improve your soldiers/weapons, keep your group financial stable and shooting down incoming UFOs. Like the original, it's a blend of tactics and strategy that is rarely found in any title. The original is one of the few older games that - as a complete system - can hold up against today's standards. It was that good.
This version adds a couple of new wrinkles, improved graphics and that's about it. As I said, it's a faithful recreation of the original game which remains an all-time favorite for me. So why the mixed review? Well, Xenonauts has a couple of massive flaws in it that any prospective buyer should be aware.
1. It always seems to me that the "to hit" numbers in this game are significantly lower than the original. My guys spend a lot of time missing and as such I feel like I'm at the mercy of the RNG. Even well thought-out tactics aren't rewarded very well - something the newer version of XCOM does much better.
2. Balance. The original game knew enough that with psionics a lighter touch is better. No one likes seeing their best troops open fire on their buddies because they lost a saving throw. These devs never seemed to learn that and so you'll find yourself constantly reloading not due to your mistakes but because they didn't properly balance some of the more annoying alien abilities.
3. Bugs. Bugs. More bugs. This is the reason for my mixed reveiw. This game has always had a reputation of being buggy and sadly it never got really stable. You'll read about people having crashes. Believe it - they do and somewhat frequently. What's worse is that my entire career was ruined because the enemy turn wouldn't end on a particular map. This is with no mods either - something on that map on that turn just froze the game and there was no recovering it. Since I didn't have a quicksave prior to that mission, it was game over. I even went so far as to open up an account on the devs forums to put in a case but heard nothing. There's not really any good excuse for that. This was two years ago - and so I loaded up the game today just to see if the bug was still there. It sadly was.
I'd like to give Xenonauts a thumb's up. X-Com UFO Defense remians one of my favorites. But when there's a show-stopping bug that ruins all progress in a game and the devs don't want to fix it, that's an auto thumbs-down from me.

There are a few problems in this game that make it so that I cannot recommend this game.
This is obviously a port of a mobile game, where it is only 2.99 USD, and has the same features and levels.
The title says "Touch to Start", obviously showing lack of detail in the port.
Gameplay is slow, and, even if it is thoughtful, it is more of a time consumer, more fit for a train ride or bus commute.
The asthetic is nice-ish, but looks choppy (which could just be a stop-motion esque look), but there are also bugs in the tutorial, softlocking the game.
This is better as a mobile game than a good PC game, with no extra features or levels to justify the 5 dollar mark-up.

Now, I haven't played this game much, but as I continue to play, I will update my review.
Based on the tutorial and first level alone, this game is clearly a mobile port. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but this game is not worth the $7.99 price tag. The game is quite clearly inspired by both Cut the Rope and Worms, both of which are highly entertaining games. There is not much depth to this game, however. It's a great way to pass the time, and can be entertaining at times, but I can't justify this game's price tag.
It's a very interesting concept, and if the developers were to go and add in more mechanics and more developed gameplay, this game would be a must-have at the price tag, but with a lack of multiplayer or a lack of complex game mechanics in general, I simply can not recommend this game. It's a great concept, I just wish the developers would do more with it.
If you're a fan of Cut the Rope or Worms, pick this game up on sale. It's a great homage to both of these titles, but it just feels... unfinished.
I received this product for free, in order to give my opinion of the game to the developers. I want them to know that I do enjoy playing the game, but it feels very mobile-oriented, with the mouse controlling most of the game, leaving no room for the keyboard to be used. A lack of controller support also prevents me from giving this product a reccommendation, as this game would be so much more playable when i'm lying around using my controller to play this game on  my TV. I'm including a link to a YouTube video to showcase some of the gameplay for this game.
Apologies for my voice in the video. It's hard to hear anything over this game's music.

A nice flashback to the puzzle games of old, especially Lemmings. Here, you turn rolling blobs into other...things to help him and the rest get to the exit. Artwork is really nice as well.

Plastiland is a lot of fun.  I played every Lemmings game ever made - Plastiland is a lot like Lemmings but without the downside.  Too many of the Lemmings games had levels where timing was critical and clicking at just the right place at just the right time made for something that went from fun to frustration.
Plastiland isn't like that, the frustration part isn't there.  It can certainly be challenging - many of the levels need some thought.  That's not just to get through, but to increase the number of your buddies that get to make it.
The slower pace at first seems a bit placid, but I soon found that it gave me time to think about what to do next without having to pause.  And you can always use the Fast Forward to speed things up.
I don't think you can go wrong with this game.  It's like a breath of fresh air.  You don't have to kill anybody or anything, you just have to put on your thinking cap.

This game is a neat start.  I like it's cartoon-y graphics, crafting system and the exploration of the unknown.  It's unengaging after about 5 hours because you've literally discovered every game mechanic available, built a spiderweb of a base that just doesn't look cool no matter what... you've built your space ship, loaded it will the basics and flew off to another planet.
THEN: You get out on the new world and discover that almost nothing of what you need to build another base is anywhere to be found.  Sure, it's there but where?  It's very difficult to find.. So you'll spend 10 hours this time building a new base... only to discover that you found everything worth finding on your starter planet.  No new items to make or build.  Nothing new to discover.  You'll have tons of the available elements and every buildable option and then what?
Explore.  All that's left is to walk around planets and look at things.  Sure you can go to different planets but you'll just rinse and repeat this formula.  I should have stopped at 5 hours.  The 20+ hours I have in is simply me hoping to find something that doesn't exist.. anything.  An alien civilization?  Any life form at all?  Sure there are crashed ships but no people.  No animal.  Just plants blowing in the breeze.. but with no water how is that even possible?
Bugs.  It's pre-alpha so I'm not dinging it on bugs.  They are ineveitible at this stage.  I'm just pointing out a couple.  There are many.  Build 2 vehicle ports and build a shuttle at one and a spaceship at the other.  The shuttle is non-removable unlike building a truck or rover.  The game has no problem landing your spaceship right on top of your shuttle even though there's an empty vehicle bay.  Simply remembering which it took off from and landing back there could sove this.
Shuttles can get turned upside down with terraforming...then you can get in.  This results in getting out below the terrain and "swimming" around in the scenery.  Taking off results in blasting THROUGH the planet. Physics. They are horrible.  My truck bounces and flips  on the smallet rock and floats like it's near zero gravity but my toon can't jump more than 1 foot or 2.
Finally there's a disconnect between the tech is gives you and the tech it doesn't.  I've flown trillions of miles to land on these planets but my computer didn't store a single blue print for creating a truck or a solar panel?  I literally have to discover that on a planet that harbors no life, no water... why would it have a solar panel plan on this planet??  No one lives here... and I could have just brought one along.  I'm advanced man but I can't have an airhose more than about 30 feet long? or an air tank with more than 2 minutes of air?  Oh, but if I link tethers I can have unlimited 30 feet sections.  Seriously.  Just give us 100+ feet sections so we can spend more time playing over placing tethers everywhere we go until we build a truck.  Why does the ship not have a number of buildable items right off the bat?  Logical things a space traveller would bring?  And make the formulas more comples.  Seriously, 2 copper to build a complex item?  Why not 2 copper, 1 aluminum, 1 lithium?  And if you take away the silly factor that I found plans for a solar panel on a barren planet why not let me experiement with formulas that may or may not make something.. and depending on how close I get to the complete formula.. maybe that affects it's efficiency or service life?
For the cost I cannot recommend the pre-alpha unless you really have expectations that it gets HUGE updates... which so far have not occurred.  You'll do everything in 5 hours making this a very high $ per hour game.  I hope that it does receive the updates and it adds base building, not just station adding, alien life, more reason to travel between planets; I'm hoping for advanced and cool tech that requires items found only on other planets...  this could be so much but for now it's seems like a demo.

Not worth the 99¢ it costs to purchase, or the space it’ll take up on your hard drive.
So, you've just downloaded Bitcoin Clicker and you're greeted with the unity splash screen. Cool, unity games can be fun. Suddenly there's a giant spinning background, a huge bitcoin logo in the middle of your screen, and one of the most sorry excuses for a GUI I’ve ever seen. From the very get-go, the music is the best part of Bitcoin Clicker, and I’m pretty sure it’s just non-copyright music if we’re being honest.
Ahh clicker games. One of my very favorite kinds of game. Usually so peaceful and relaxing, not much to do but click a couple of time and soon it’s doing it on its own. This is where Bitcoin Clicker is different, and not for the better in my opinion. You start making $1 a click with a $10 cap. Hit 10 and start over at 20, hit 20, start over at 40, etc., etc., etc.. The first autoclicker upgrade doesn’t even come in until you reach $160. Sure that doesn’t sound like a lot, but when you realize you have to click
times just to get to a measly 1 click per second auto, you see where it gets troubling.  So right off the bat I recommend an auto-clicker.
Once  you get going the game does pick up a bit. Before you know it you’re spending thousands upon thousands on new graphics cards and overclocks. You’ve been playing for a while now and decide to take a break. So you turn off the game and go do whatever. Come back a few hours later to boot it back up, when you realize none of your progress was saved! That’s right, the games doesn’t even local save your progress. That shows the the whole intent of this game is for you to open it for 95 minutes, get all the achievements, then close it forever.
And yet, none of the achievements work. You read that right, this 99¢ game that has over 5000 achievements doesn’t even give you achievements. As of writing this review (November 28th, 2017) the game is somehow broken. Around Halloween the dev released an update saying...
Well apparently this update broke the achievements. The one function this game actually serves, broken by an update. Well played dev.
Okay, honestly the music for this game isn’t terrible. As I said, the music is probably the best part of the whole mess. Besides the generic royalty-free music, there’s no sound in this game that I can find. There’s a music toggle and a sound toggle, but I can’t find any sound. So. Music, not great, but bearable (for a few minutes. It’s just one song on a loop).
So, if you made it this far I applaud you. Really I can’t say much that I haven’t already. It’s really not worth your money unless you’re an achievement hunter. Even then, right now there’s no point in getting it until the lone bug in this game is fixed. If the dev ever patches it I’ll update my review, but until then I can’t see a single reason to buy this game.

Review in a minute:
It’s a 4 player co-op dino horde survival shooter with one of the most ambitious developers backing it to create a great universe that expands from where the game currently is to everything they’ve ever wanted from a game, all for the low low price of a buck.  With solid gameplay today, it’s well worth the purchase while you wait for the rest.  It’s easily a few hours of content now for a casual game hopper, and a hundred or more for a dedicated fan.
It's a top down shooter...  No, it's a third person shooter...  No, it's a first person shooter!  You've got a range of shooting options, full controller support for all three perspectives, and a lot of variety for dinosaurs to slaughter.  It's missing a small bit of polish in some minor areas, but the devs have great ambition and have proven with past titles that they definitely won't give up until it's to their liking.
Currently it’s got “protect the harvester” and “survival” game modes, but they have more coming within the next couple months and a campaign mode coming by 2017.  For those of you who don’t like slaughtering dinosaurs, we’re getting robot enemies too.
But that’s not what you care about today, ‘cause every game promises big.  So here’s what you get for a dollar today (MSRP as of writing):
Dino horde survival co-op in top down/third person/first person perspectives.
Solid character progression through loot and levels.
Free currency to gamble with for chances at getting loot outside of missions.
Daily/weekly “quests” to earn premium currency, leaving nothing behind a paywall, not even cosmetics.
Solid controls with tight response times, resulting in great feeling gameplay.
A visually appealing unreal 4 game, beautiful from all perspectives.
Creative character customization in both serious and silly ways.
Access to all future ‘games’ within The Orion Project. -  An insane amount of content.

I originally thought "Guardians of Orion" as it was first called, was a nifty idea. A sci-fi top-down, multiplayer, horde mode shooter - if they added some more characters, differing armor/colour schemes, more maps, team death match, it could be something cool. But then came the third person view, and suddenly the floodgates opened for this weird lobby thing, incomprehensible item-crafting, dumb hats, and you name it.
I think a lot of what I said comes from how ambitious the devs are. They don't want to do what I had hoped for, which is strange since that's what it looked like it would've ended up as if not for all the people complaining that it was "merely" a top-down shooter. So now we're getting mechs, an open world, first person point of view, and all kinds of stuff in addition to the poorly done and meaningless additions I already mentioned. Trek is shoving so much stuff into the game in order to please as many as possible, that it drags the whole experience down into a mish-mash of half-baked ideas overcrowding what little good there is. "The Orion Project" is hardly anything alike what I had hoped it would become... So for me, this is my lesson in early access.
Also, animation quality is really bad.
Also, had I been aware of Trek's reputation I would've never bought this game to begin with, but thinking like that is hardly helpful, so being vigilant in the future and not an idiot is all one can do.

OMG! It’s modern Lemmings!: When I graduated primary school (elementary school for those of you in North America) my Christmas gift that year (school year runs Jan-Dec due to the  seasons being changed in the southern hemisphere) one of the very first games that I became addicted to was Lemmings. I loved that game. The entire premise around Lemmings and the cute way in which it was represented was everything that a near-teen could want in a puzzle game. You could play it properly and beat it or you could be sadistic and watch them die mercilessly. Plastiland brings much of the charm that I had in Lemmings back in spades and does it well.
Beautiful art work: There is absolutely no doubting the quality of the handmade art work in Plastiland. It took the artists
twelve months to produce the high quality artwork that you see in the game and it absolutely delivers. Plastiland is very pleasing on the eyes and is a joy to play as a direct result.
Nice soundtrack: It would have been a great pity had the soundtrack behind the game failed given how beautiful the artwork is. However, it’s catchy and never feels as though it becomes too repetitive or boring. In fact, I’d like to see Zillion Whales add the soundtrack to the Steam store preferably for free but if they even asked for a dollar or two more for it it’d be worth the added price.
It’s not as easy as it looks: Plastiland offers players greater challenge than what one would initially appear. The tutorial is brilliant as it teaches you all of the basics that you need to successfully play the game. However, from that point on there isn’t a lot of hand holding and the solutions are often not as simple as they look. This is a really good thing because it means that everything else that is great about the game doesn’t go to waste.
Please add achievements: Puzzle games without Steam achievements have quickly become one of my gaming pet peeves. There is no reason whatsoever that your game should lack them and every possible reason to gain from having them – especially when you factor in global achievements. They allow you to know what your player base has done in your game and that in turn will give you ideas on what you need to improve in that game and what things you can do for your future games.
Plastiland isn’t the greatest puzzle game ever made and it doesn’t pretend to be. It is, however, a beautiful game that will appeal to people of all ages and offers something for everyone. Don’t be surprised when your six year old finds the solution to a puzzle before you.
