Having played Dark Souls 2 on Xbox 360 and PS3, I can say that the PC version now is definitely an improvement graphically, running at 60FPS opposed to 30. The textures are a bit more crisp and the game feels a lot smoother. I strongly recommend using a controller though as the game still doesn't feel very keyboard/mouse friendly.
It also seems like some people are unable to start the game and have been experiencing crashes. I haven't encountered either of these problems. If it helps, I'm running an I5 3570K, 16GB ram, and a GTX 560TI at 1920 x 1200 resolution.
Now here's my original review of Dark Souls 2, if it's too long to read, I've made a video version for your convenience:
While the narrative still unfolds in the nuanced manner that characterized past Souls tales, players will notice Dark Souls 2 features a more refined story. There is still much to be left up to player's interpretations with many details to be found in item descriptions and conversations with the various denizens of Drangleic. Series veterans will find allusions to the first Dark Souls with many subtle tie-ins. As is customary in the Souls series, cut scenes are limited, mainly used to introduce the lethal bosses that players will encounter, thereby never interrupting the pace and flow of the game.
Dark Souls 2 attempts to make itself a bit more accessible by offering an early tutorial section that walks players through its combat and mechanics. While this easy tutorial feels out of place, it is wholly optional allowing veterans to skip it. After a brief introduction, players are left to explore the world where they will encounter an old woman who enables them to utilize an in-depth character creator to customize their avatar and select a class. Like Dark Souls, class determines the players starting attributes, items and spells but has little influence in the long run since the flexible leveling system allows players to specialize however they wish.
While Dark Souls 2 does try to draw players in by being a bit more accessible, it would be foolish to think that the series has gone soft in an effort to sell more copies. Drangleic is quite a bit more difficult and unforgiving than Lordran or Boletaria from Demon's Souls and those looking for a challenge will be more than satisfied. As someone who has personally beaten both Dark Souls and Demon's Souls numerous times, I'm not ashamed to say that I died on more than one occasion in Dark Souls 2. Deaths can feel a bit cheaper and sometimes unavoidable; but the game manages to get away with it by offering an unmatched sense of reward, compelling players to continue even after the most egregious deaths occur.
Upon reaching Majula, which serves as the game's hub area, (similar to Demon's Souls Nexus) players are given minimal guidelines and are left to their own devices; being simply told to seek the king and gather four powerful souls. The NPCs you encounter in your travels will congregate in Majula offering goods and services for sale as well as other means of upgrading your character. You're also forced to level up in Majula, as the option to level at bonfires has been removed. On one hand, this might feel a bit tedious as you're faced with an extra load screen every time you want to level, on the other hand, this makes the game feel more structured, and having a constant safezone to visit allows for a much needed reprieve from the harsh world.
Once players decide to leave Majula, they can tackle the available areas in any order they wish, though clever design choices ensure that players are on the intended path without feeling as though they’re sheep to be corralled by the game's level design. Unfortunately, while the world in Dark Souls 2 is larger than its predecessor, it suffers from a sprawling design that leaves it feeling less interconnected and forces players to be more reliant on the fast-travel system.  You won't find as many of the clever short cuts as there were in Lordran and as such, Dark Souls 2 provides players with the ability to fast travel from the onset. There are some positives that come from this design choice however, the larger world makes exploration more exhilarating and there is much greater variety in the game's areas. The secret areas and items are more obscure than ever and require plenty of searching to find.
The combat is fundamentally unchanged but is far more refined. Changes to various weapons and equipment provide more viable play styles than ever before. Shields are far less powerful than they were in previous games making dodging and rolling more important as well as making the temptation to dual wield or two-hand a weapon all the more appealing. These changes wouldn't mean much without a cast of dangerous and disgusting enemies to test your sword and board or casting skills against. Fighting even the lowliest enemy involves a bit of strategy and care, while groups of enemies provide the greatest challenge. Torches have also been added which are held in your left hand in place of a shield. They can be lit by any bonfire helping illuminate your way through dangerous areas.  Lamps lit by your torch stay lit for the duration of the game, and certain enemies will react differently to light as well. The boss fights are more intense than ever. While a lot of the bosses felt similar in past games, each of them feels unique and different from one another in this installment. The optional bosses add another degree of difficulty as they’re quite a bit harder than the final boss of the game.
New Game + has also been changed, typically in the other Souls titles, once you complete the game, you’re given the option to start all over where all of the enemies health and damage have been adjusted to provide a greater challenge. New Game + in Dark Souls 2 has all of this but also includes new enemies that cannot even be seen on the first playthrough. The inclusion of additional items and souls means that you’ll be playing Dark Souls 2 for a very long time. That combined with the fact that the world and game in general is quite a bit longer than the first, makes this all the more welcomed.  The average playthrough will run you around 60 hours, without including pvp and leveling the various covenants.
The innovative multiplayer makes a return as well. You can once again leave and read messages, allowing you to interact with other players. You’re also able to summon players to aid you in difficult situations, as well as be invaded by enemy players. This is no longer limited to being a human, as you can be invaded by hostile players at anytime with the only safe spot being Majula.
The art direction has been improved from the other Souls games, relying less on the gloomy interiors we're accustomed to as the environments offer greater variety and feel more distinct from one another. Some areas are absolutely stunning though the tech powering Dark Souls 2 is still rather disappointing. Textures can have horrendously low resolutions in some areas and some really poor tiling is noticeable on certain structures. We don't play Dark Souls for the graphics though.
By improving on the near-flawless combat system, adding new playing styles, more variety, and tons of content Dark Souls 2 manages to improve the legacy of its predecessors despite its quirks. It manages to be even more difficult than its forbearers and the changes to New Game+ as well as the covenants add more re-playability than ever before. Dark Souls 2 is one of the best games I’ve played in years, and one that I strongly recommend.
Pros
+ Incredible Combat
+ Caters to different playing styles
+ Challenging Gameplay
+ Tons of Content & Re-playability
+ Unique Multiplayer Component
+ Great Art Direction & Soundtrack
Cons
- Graphics aren't on-par with 2014
- Minor Bugs
- Latency Issues can ruin PvP
- World lacks the clever interconnected feel of Dark Souls 1

My first impression on launch day:
Let me start out by saying that this is another great installment in the souls series and I am loving the game thus far. HOWEVER there are some minor issues with the current PC port, namely the lack of native controller support (neither my ps3 or xbox controller were recognized by the game), and awkward-at-best standard keyboard/mouse controls. This is launch day so some issues should be anticipated but all in all I'm very pleased with how well the game runs, even more so considering how frustrating DKS was to set up on steam/GFWL. I was able to get into co-op easily and often and the lag wasn't bad at all. The graphics were stunning at first glance. I ran everything on high settings and 1080p. There's even more of the beautiful vistas, breath taking scale, bosses impressively grotesque, and attention to detail in the environments that we've come expect from FROM. You need this game.
Combat and the keybindings I use:
The combat is... well it's just awkard without a controller, I ended up rebinding almost every key (several times) and eventually settled into a layout similiar to how I keybind my WoW character. 1,2,3,4 bound as strong/weak on Lh/Rh weapons and 5,6 as swap Lh/Rh, unbound nearly all the strange mouse bindings except for scroll wheel press. I decided on R to lock on to a target and T + Y to swap left and right between locked targets. Z for jump, X for X on the controller (Function 7 I think), C for function 8. F for use item, G for 2h weapon, H for menu and J for gestures.
It's not perfect but I thought I'd share for anyone else struggling to find comfortable keybinds.

I find this game alot more interesting than American Truck Simulator (ATS), its newer little brother. So this review will have a comparison approach.
#1: This game has MANY places to go, beating ATS's small 3 (soon to be 4) states (California, Nevada, Arizona, and soon to be New Mexico).
#2: This game comes with DOUBLE the trucks that ATS has.
#3: TruckersMP (the multiplayer mod for both ETS2 and ATS) has more servers and players on ETS2 than ATS
#4: Driving on the left side of the road is a challenging experience for an American like me. Also having the choice of having your steering wheel be on either the left or right side of your truck is nice. You do have to get to the KPH dashboards and speed limits but you can have your route advisor read MPH if it bothers you (it will even change the signs on the device to show MPH speed limits).
#5: The DLC.....holy cow.....Theres a TON of dlc for ETS2. Granted 90% of it is paintjobs but there is also 3 map expansions. I don't have them yet but I will when I can.
#6: Not sure if I was imagining things or not but I think I saw FedEx somewhere in one of the cities, which if true means that this game has licensing to use real life company names....unlike ATS where Walmart is Walbert (bleh).
#7: Textures in this game look more real to me. Not as bright as ATS, and a little more gritty. Roads look like they have character to them (which is wierd to say about an inanimate object).
I understand ATS is still getting on its feet and if you can buy it when its on sale, do it, but I think for right now ETS2 is still the better of the 2. I'm still new to this game, as you can see by my low amount of hours (At this time of writing its 1.3 hours) but I love this game so far and will enjoy it more when I get the map dlcs.
Buy and play this game. Its really great to play when you want to burn some time, maybe while you are wanting to get to sleep or you are stoned xD.

If, in 1994 you were already old enough to play computer games and were lucky enough to get smitten by the charms of XCOM or UFO (depending on which edition you purchased), then you probably would love to play Xenonauts. It is a very faithful recreation of XCOM, more so than Firaxis' X-COM, which is more of a re-imagining. The game mechanics are almost identical, offering a mix of engrossing strategic and tactical layers. Xenonauts is not simply a clone or a remake, though. There are enough differences that can either make it better or more frustrating depending on your point of view. The setting is different, for example, placing the invasion in the middle of the Cold War. Which kind of make the limited technology available at the beginning slightly more understandable. It also, on the other hand, may make some people question whether we were advanced enough in the early 80's to do research and manufacture of alien technology. The air interception is now a fun real-time mini-game, unlike the abstracted view of the original. A change that may annoy purists is the elimination of psy-capable soldiers. The alien retains this ability, though, so be prepared to get smacked by your own alien-possessed soldiers. Ouch. In all, Xenonauts more than live up to old fans' expectations. An excellent strategy game that has an ability to warp time: what you think is a few minutes of alien-hunting exercise might actually be a couple of hours of wasted productivity. No, it's not safe for work.
Oh, yeah... what about you young ones that were still in your cribs when the original XCOM was released? Listen to us old folks, kids. We were not in love with the original for no reason. And now, you can have a new incarnation, in all its high-res glory, if you can't stand the original XCOM's graphics. Give it a try, you are not going to regret it.

SteamWorld Dig is pretty much a perfect 6 hour video game. It has intuitive gameplay, charming atmosphere, whimsical character design, beautiful 1080p environments, fun abilities, and great pacing. It takes the joy of digging, adds in leveling and upgrades, and packages it in a wonderful homage to the spaghetti westerns of yore with a steampunk/robot vibe.
The story is mysterious enough to keep you digging until the end to discover what lies beneath. The music and sound effects fit perfectly as well. It also is forgiving regarding death and provides quick teleporting to avoid backtracking.
Basically, this is the perfect game: simple, fun, and charming.
Quibbles: you can’t rebind all the KB/M controls or the 360 controller buttons. Some of the Achievements are a tad annoying. The first hour is the weakest since you have no cool abilities.
Note: I used a 360 controller and highly recommend you do so as well.

If you've played the great flash game Motherlode, then this game is very similar! While the length of the game leaves something to be desired, the 'dungeons' scattered throughout make for a nice detour from just digging down. If you can get this on sale, then do so for a great few hours of fun.

This game is great. It's like steampunk Terraria with a more Metroidvania twist to it. You have to be careful with digging early on, though. It's easy to get yourself trapped. The only complaint is that the game isn't long enough. It needs more content, and a better end game.

SteamWorld Dig is a simple premise. Dig up gems, Buy upgrades, Use upgrades to dig deeper and find better gems. While it has some Metroidvania elements, it's important to understand from the outset that this is a short game: ~5 hours for your first playthrough, maybe a couple more than that to grab every achievement.
The puzzle rooms, where you unleash pickaxe, drill, dynamite and other essential mining tools are the star of this game to me - they are just suitably challenging that when you succeed, you feel pleased with yourself, but they are unlikely for you to get stuck on for any length of time.
While overall I recommend the game, It's lack of depth (An irony for a hole digging simulator) means that I'd certainly wait for a sale before you pick it up.

I do not always write reviews on steam (in fact in all these years I haven't done a single one), but when I do it has to be about Guilty Gear.
Seriously though, this game is so great I literally feel obligated to do so.
I always loved fighting games even though I wasn't particularly good at anyone. I still played quite a few but none hooked me up like this one.
I only knew Arcsys from previous titles like Blazblue, a game I also liked but despite the huge tutorial with loads of info, I couldn't fully dedicate myself to the game and get good at it.
This changed with the recent GG: Revelator title.
I immediately fell in love with the art style and character design which looks REALLY polished. Each character  has really some "character", meaning personality, and all play vastly different, offering various gimmicks and approaches in combat.
Additionally GG offers an awesome tutorial which -unlike in BlazBlue- doesn't slam all the info in your face, but instead gives you a mild approach to the very basics. If you want to dive further into the matter you can learn some basic combos for your character and even train for various match-ups you might have problems with.
You can clearly see that Arcsys really cares about bringing in new players which also include total fighting game newbies and they've done a great job with that. In fact the best one I have seen in my life so far.
I even bought the all-in-one package which is about 55 bucks but is worth every single penny and I don't regret anything about it and never will.
It is my most precious purchase I have ever made as a gamer on par with Overwatch (maybe even better). This may sound a bit overwhelmingly positive and you may think: "Is this guy getting paid for that?..." or whatever. But trust me when I say that I'm not and I'm not a person who praised any game company until now but the devs did a great job and earned my respect.
SO THANK YOU FOR MAKING SUCH A GREAT GAME! KEEP UP THE GREAT WORK!

I'm mainly writing this review for people like myself who may be put off by the anime-style and the (mostly) weebish fanbase. I myself am not really a fan of anime stuff and I have a general dislike for 'weebish' stuff and its ilk, but such is the quality of GUILTY GEAR Xrd -REVELATOR- that it has won me over completely.
To put it quite simply this game is amazing, not just as a fighting game, but as a video game period. The fact that it has compelled my lazy self to actually type out a full review says a  lot.
At first I didn't believe the hype around this game and I didn't really get why everyone was always singing it's praises, but my biggest regret now is that I didn't buy this game sooner.
Just some points about what makes this game so good:
Buy this game you honestly won't regret it, I know I don't.

I cannot reccomend this game enough.
Guilty Gear is one of my early fighters so I'm slightly biased in that regard, but even without that bias this game has a lot of what I want: a training mode that will get you through all the game concepts before you ever fight someone, a quick and easy way to figure out combos that work and specials so that you can pull them off yourself, a straight arcade mode with exactly enough story that is still wonderfully animated.
And, ohmigod, it's all done in unreal? And is technically 3D? The game reminds you without getting annoying about it that, oh yeah, you're fighting with 3D models that can show off your specials and victories from a bunch of different angles. SteamWorld Dig is a game trimmed of fat, an experience in pure gameplay. It feels like a flash-based browser game or a Starcraft/Warcraft custom game.
This isn't a bad thing.
Gameplay rules in SteamWorld Dig. Your job is to dig further and further down. As you dig, you find money and trade it to dig better. Thats it. That's the whole game.
The digging is made challenging by limiting the reach of your implements and making backwards travel difficult. This is enough to keep your mind occupied with what would otherwise an exercise in "hold down and press dig for several hours."
As for atmosphere, the characters you meet are colourful, the world and its critters are engaging, and the music is twangy as all get-out. It sells the steampunk-robot-wildwest setting well.
All told, SteamWorld Dig is pure gameplay that doesn't get stale over the modest length of the game.
Note to achievement hunters: two of SteamWorld Dig's achievements are speed runs. Ew.

It's a stronger sequel to XCOM:UFO Defense than anything that came out until XCOM Enemy Unknown. In some regards it's even better than Enemy Unknown. The ambient soundtrack is awesome, and makes for an uneasy feeling throughout the missions. I felt the same sweaty-palmed nervousness that the first game gave me every time I entered a terror mission. I think I let out a long groan and a quiet "damnit, I hate those things" when the chrysalis equivalent (the reaper) walked on the screen. Definitely had the nostalgia points going.
It's obvious that this game was put together with love and care. The reports and xenopedia entries have a certain authenticity and wittiness to them that surpasses the original XCOM. I also thought the bitmap-esque style drawings had a certain charm to them. Overall quite polished and professional.
But it also has fairly tight gameplay with a surprisingly good storyline. I've noticed that recent kickstarted/indie games tend to do one or the other well. Everything feels as fleshed out as a good 80s action flick (Rocky IV or Red Dawn, in keeping with the Cold War theme). Just enough good bits to keep you playing. Which is necessary because this game is unforgiving. Expect to restart missions often, unless you're fine with all your best troops dying. It's nice to have to earn the win, but it did border on frustrating. Especially when the difficulty would seemingly spike at random times.
It's not without flaws though. Probably a 3rd of the way through the game all of my crack troops all forgot how to shoot their weapons. It's annoying to go from nailing targets repeatedly across the battlefield to missing the alien standing right next to you multiple times in a row. I also found the funding to be difficult to manage, I seemed to spend a few million dollars in less than 24 hours without explanation. Only to then spend the remainder of the month limping by on a budget of $1000. There didn't seem to be any connection to what projects or buildings I authorized and how much money was spent. I also found the base screens to be surprisingly flat, for a game with this much care put into it; it was irksome to see the same quotes each time I clicked into the screen. At least randomize the ways my lead researcher would show his disdain for me interrupting him!
The one major flaw I found in the game though was the handling of alien technology. It was either sold off or destroyed. Which would be find except it was made clear that humans couldn't use the technology. This lead to the question "Then who was buying it?" It also meant that I was constantly playing catch up in the engineering game. Not enough money, not enough resources, not enough fun. I agree that in the late stages of XCOM it was ridiculous to have 500+ heavy plasma weapons in storage, but it is equally ridiculous to throw that entire concept away.
All of these are minor inconveniences that do nothing to detract from the game. Even if it wasn't on sale, this is worth a buy.

Overall a solid experience. The only thing that annoyed me was some questionable mechanics in the ground combat mode. Ex
* No melee weapons except the stun baton?
* Experienced solders going berserk without any apparent reason killing your squad with a bazooka or other weapon of choice. And apparently when berserk they have hugely increased accuracy?
* Soldiers missing shots at point blank range (95% hit)
* Soldiers that cant throw grenades over flowers/bushes killing them self in the process (same with bazookas).

I solved this by doing 2 saves each turn (At the beginning and at the end of each turn) and reloading if any of the soldiers messed up. Would be fun to know how many times I did a quicksave but i'm sure its 2000+ times.

Xenonauts developed by Gamethunks, Goldhawk Interactive & released on 17 Jun 2014 for PC. According to Metacritic
it has:

I'll dare say that Xenoaunts is a great remake of the original XCOM title. If you've played Firaxis's XCOM, you should give this title a try. Both titles differ in many aspect of the game however both are notable titles for the remake of XCOM. Xenoauts on the other hand could do with a little more love and attention for what it's worth.
The Story:
To keep it short, alien invasion on earth seems immanent and a multi-nationality milatary organization known as XCOM is task to defend our beloved earth from these invaders. Take command of this organization. Build bases across the world, research, manufacture and battle these invaders. One things for sure, soldiers will die. Period.
User Interface,Controls, Visuals:
The UI on a whole; on battle/soldier/weapon stats window were designed in blocks (nothing fancy), clean and organized unlike the original XCOM where there were tons/clusters of buttons on the  screen.
The information are presented in a simple, clean & organized fashion. This also includes research result/aircraft/vehicle capabilities/alien autopsy. This is important because you may need to look them up after some time or after a break.
To be real honest, controls are easy. It's quite standard for me really but for some who are new to turn base RTS, they may feel overwhelm on what's being shown on the screen. With the options and bars and what not & freak out far too soon. Or when they see the list of key bindings, the fall off from their chair. Lol. In actual scenario, all you need is the tab key and your mouse. That's it.
Visuals:
Xeno is a 2d, top-down looking game. It looks good for me. Nothing fancy  if compared to Fira's XCOM. The entire art style looks like hand drawn. Don't get me wrong, it is not a negative point. Everything in here has been designed/colored cleanly with details and a whole lot of effort has been put into the images as you progress with more technology getting unlocked.
Unlike Firaxis's XCOM, where its design lean closer for sci-fi futuristic looking gears@soldiers. (those shiny & glowing things) Xeno takes place in cold-war era. Ballistic weapons, bazookas, grenades, tanks and jet fighters. You might feel unimpressed as you are in plain clothing with a standard machine gun/shot gun.
Due to word count limit, I'll just summarize that the human world art concept and the aliens art concept are totally different. Units, ships, weapons are all designed differently but with “realism” still the main point of design. Kudo's on the graphic department.
Mechanics:
I've said this and I will say this again, beautiful games without substance is no fun. What Xeno (may) lack in visuals, shine in it's mechanics & game play experience. Xeno resembles closer to the original XCOM with greater emphasis on micro managements. It takes a while to understand the weapon handling and on the TU points. Once you do, your gameplay are much more direct. In Xeno, there is no nonsense of that shot missing a 75% or 80% chance. Xeno shooting mechanic is more realistic and is largely affected by the  distance.
The good news, there is base building and the aliens can invade your base. They can even build base across the world and you have to disable it. Similar to Fira's XCOM, once you lost majority of the world continent@support, you lose the game.
Xeno has better air battles than Fira's XCOM. Air Battles are tricky when you don't have uber jets to fight for you. Some air battles require micro mgt to win.
The ground battle is always tedious but rewarding. You need to understand the aliens capabilities and your weapon capabilities to have a decent chance against them. Failing to understand your weapon capabilities will only make you waste turns. Grenades are the highlight of xeno. They are an important asset to storming into room, provide cover and the best way to deal with aliens. Which is why Fira's XCOM later introduce enemy within with more grenade design.
Game difficulty
To be honest, I feel xeno is generally harder than Fira's XCOM in the early days until Firaxis released XCOM Enemy within a major bump in game difficulty.
I dont feel that the aliens are hard to beat or that this game is hard rather I feel that the game is annoying. Because the aliens capitalize on their advantage and with the constant nuisance from the praetor messing up my squad. But I guess, that’s challenge for you.
There's day and night mission as well. Yes, Night missions are harder due to the vision disadvantage. To aid night missions, your entire squad is presented with unlimited amount of flares. It helps in a certain way but not effective enough because the aliens have higher stats then the humans and can shoot further. Oh and their weapon hurt more too. Many have mentioned this and I am going to say this too. Please re-tweak the reapers. They can see players out of the visibility range – they can move in and kill your squad with ease. It is rather an unfair design decision because the reaper only has to poke your unit and say goodbye to whatever Armour/weapon your unit has – or how utterly useless your squad reaction fire is. =(
The final mission was really tricky, interesting and freaky suspense. As you try to make it out alive from the endless wave of repears. lol. On a whole, the game felt paced right. You are constantly battling against time for research/manufacture something to give you a slight advantage over the aliens.
I use the term "slight" because no matter what tech-tree you research unlike in Fira's XCOM, xeno's aliens will always have the upper hand whether its in stats, numbers, weapons. I can share with you the moment I researched tank/super heavy suite/uber 1 blast kill weapon, I thought to myself: "this it man! this is the game changer!" but no matter what, if I am careless/I don't plan properly, the aliens will whop my sorry <bottom>.
My Summary
Xenoauts is a solid product. Thank you Gamethunks, Goldhawk Interactive for this product. While trying to stay true to the original XCOM title, many of the retro/feel/game mechanics have been adopted into this product. You did a great job with Xenoauts.
Many might not have heard of xenoauts - unlike Firaxi's XCOM due to marketing approach maybe? But the gameplay experience is on par for both titles. It's not sci-fi and it tries to remain grounded on many of its design choices. Xeno does offer slightly more option for ground battle, where you are able to bring in a whole lot of soldiers (more than 6), the choice of soldier weapons and Tanks. Xeno gives you the option to train your soldier however you want and allows you to equip whatever weapon you so desire. The retro feel is there. Xeno's air battle@base planning will always keep on the edge as you try to cover a part of country/continent and prepare air crafts. All of the micro mgt aspect will allow players to feel more engaged unless you don't fancy that.
I am a little disappointed on the ending. Upon completion and saving humanity from the alien invaders, players are presented with a screen of "hey congrats! you won!" After all that battle, terror missions, blowing up alien HQs, XX soldiers dead. My reward was 1 screen. Hmph. lol. I love the game, please don't repeat this in future titles. This game draws you in, it is insidious, it is subtle. I thought I was playing responsibly but then hours passed and I've forgotten my name. I've forgotten who I am and how to shower. All I know is that I'm supposed to farm slimes and grow crops and feed the slimes to appease them. There is nothing in my life now. All that remains is slimes.
Anyway, this game is really cute and fun!! You're equipped with the Vacpack resembling a Portal Gun and you're able to suck up slimes, crops, chickens, water, and other cool stuff. You then corral your slimes onto your ranch and start feeding them food, growing crops, and collecting the slimes' poop to sell for money. Think the agriculture and independent time-flow of Harvest Moon, the collection and variety of Neko Atsume, plus exploration of a game involving exploration. There's so much to do and the game is still in its early access stage. I think this is a smart move because releasing everything that the developers are planning to at once would be really overwhelming; introducing more lands and slimes bit by bit lets us get used to the game and take it slow.
The graphics are incredibly saccharine and colorful. Slimes come in pink, blue, tabby cat, lava, and they're all weirdly endearing even though they're just viscous little mounds. You can also indirectly combine slimes to form bigger ones!! The music is quite relaxing and has that banjo-ranch-cowboy kinda feel to it. This game is still in its early stages but I'm definitely excited for what's to come!!

Dishonored 2 so far has some of the best world-building I've seen in any game. The sheer attention to detail to how large the levels are is insane. The fourth stage alone consists of 3 huge areas, with the last being one of the most unusual and puzzling areas I've ever had the joy of working out how to get around in general, let alone undetected.
The levels themselves are so full of content that the first time I played, I thought the game had no loading screens between levels. It does, but the levels are just that huge by comparison to most other stealth games it's genuinely stunning.
There's so many things you can learn by listening in to the AI chatter, or by paying attention to the world around you. For example, at one point, a homeless man is speaking to himself. If you approach him he's tell you of whale oil and people below. Sounds like utter madness, until you find your way down below and find two people with two whale oil tanks against a wall speaking or breaking into a store. You can take them out, and bring a third whale oil tank to break down the wall and rob the store, if you like. And that's not even the best example of the side content.
From the small notes hidden about that build up backstory to certain characters, to the things you can find adoring walls that you can't pickup but can still read that offer a great amount of insight into where you are, ongoing events, characters. It's all there and it really comes together to build up a magnificent lore that expands on the first games more than the first ever did.

AI is as reactive as ever. I don't think I've ever played a stealth game that had AI that reacted to such small details. If you take a painting or something as small as a coin or food, a guard that patrolled that area will remark on it, and some find it more suspicious than others. AI also reacts to doors not being left as they last were seen, and will react accordingly, looking for an intruder and changing their patrol route. Guards and even civilians notice when a guard is missing from their post and will look around for them, and sometimes alert other guards that one of them is missing.
Guard banter is typically not as repetitive as before and tends to be FAR more reactive than the first games banter. while this (sadly) means no more "Shall we gather for whiskey and cigars" moments, it means it pays off to listen to guard banter more closely as they may be speaking of noticing signs of an intruder and the sort, or a hidden stash, or where they plan to patrol next.

Gameplay is as solid as ever. certain things don't work as they did before, but honestly I think this is for the better. For example, sleep darts no longer take effect instantly, instead taking a few seconds to knock someone out, unless you get a headshot. knocking someone out seems to take longer than before. You can drop down on someone from above and choose to knock them out instead of killing them outright like what was the first games only option. Traversal is as enjoyable as ever, being able to link vaults and slides together, and for the most part, the game plays like the first but more polished in every area.
Up front combat is more viable than the first, it's entirely possible to do a high combat based non-lethal run. The gun can get a full auto, no reload firing mode unlock, basically turning the thing into a burst action rifle. Springrazors are better than before, and can be upgraded. And every ability in the game so far can be used to give an edge in combat, which is a good thing.

Powers are something I've yet to fully explore. As I've said, I'm only just up to the 6th stage this game has to offer. But so far, Emily's powers are extremely fun to use.
Her traversal ability, Far Reach, while it may seem like Blink, has so many changes and traits different that it really does feel like a completely different skill over time. Far Reach has the obey gravity, and so can't go super far, and seems to lose range the more vertical your movement. Unlike Blink, however, you can use it to reach the ground faster without taking damage, and you can use it to bring items, bodies and even enemies toward you.
Her Shadow Walk renders you almost undetectable, but you can only move against the floor while in this form and seem to also take more damage. You can kill a single enemy or knock out a single enemy before returning to normal, if you don't first run out of time.
Domino is an ability that ties the fate of one person to others, so long as you first link them with the ability. For example, if you kill one, everyone connected by the ability will die. Same goes for knocking people out, and blinding enemies.
You can also craft bonecharms as an ability now. This is actually a great thing. That bonecharm you don't use or want? Recycle it to learn its trait and make a bonecharm with 4 traits so you're not wasting a slot to have it anymore. You can also stack the same bonecharm trait up to 4 times with crafting. I have stealth mode movespeed a little faster than normal walk speed thanks to this.

In terms of player variety, Dishonored 2 certainly has it in spades.
Bonecharms come in 3 varieties now. Normal, Corrupted, and Black. Normal have a base buff trait and nothing more. Corrupted have a stronger base trait that has a minor effect on how you'll play, but come at the cost of having a heavy downside. And Black charms give only one effect with no downside, but effect playstyle greatly. It's not a straight buff they give. It's a perk almost. Like not being able to be smelled by hounds, or doing an AOE blast when you drop from high enough.
Skill variety is still here, but moreso than ever before, witht he game providing two characters to play as with vastly different skills and with characters speaking to you differently depending on who you are.
Map layout is well done, with every level I've encountered so far having many paths to get to where you need to go, and with different paths being available to different characters depending on their skillset.
As of writing this review, however, on the 10th of November, 2016, the game runs like a hot pile of garbage on a summer's day. It's really that bad. I wasn't expecting much as it's day one and I have an SLI laptop (2 860m GPUs, 16 gigs ram, core i7-4860 clocked at 3.40ghz) and it runs worse than I would've expected. It would be better if the frame rate didn't dip so hard when looking at certain scenes with no difference in graphic quality. I expected poor performance for the first day, not no performance.
Forums are abuzz with the same issues around, though, people with even 1070s are having huge FPS drops out of nowhere in some spots. hopefully they add a performance patch soon.


The game is amazing, and I feel as if they last however many levels could be awful and this game would STILL be worth getting seeing as the first 5 stages alone are so great and large. The first 5 stages legitimately contain more content than all of Dishonored 1 base game experience.
The performance issues set off a HUGE red flag, though. So don't buy it now unless you have a space age rig that can actually handle the game.

I find this game alot more interesting than American Truck Simulator (ATS), its newer little brother. So this review will have a comparison approach.
#1: This game has MANY places to go, beating ATS's small 3 (soon to be 4) states (California, Nevada, Arizona, and soon to be New Mexico).
#2: This game comes with DOUBLE the trucks that ATS has.
#3: TruckersMP (the multiplayer mod for both ETS2 and ATS) has more servers and players on ETS2 than ATS
#4: Driving on the left side of the road is a challenging experience for an American like me. Also having the choice of having your steering wheel be on either the left or right side of your truck is nice. You do have to get to the KPH dashboards and speed limits but you can have your route advisor read MPH if it bothers you (it will even change the signs on the device to show MPH speed limits).
#5: The DLC.....holy cow.....Theres a TON of dlc for ETS2. Granted 90% of it is paintjobs but there is also 3 map expansions. I don't have them yet but I will when I can.
#6: Not sure if I was imagining things or not but I think I saw FedEx somewhere in one of the cities, which if true means that this game has licensing to use real life company names....unlike ATS where Walmart is Walbert (bleh).
#7: Textures in this game look more real to me. Not as bright as ATS, and a little more gritty. Roads look like they have character to them (which is wierd to say about an inanimate object).
I understand ATS is still getting on its feet and if you can buy it when its on sale, do it, but I think for right now ETS2 is still the better of the 2. I'm still new to this game, as you can see by my low amount of hours (At this time of writing its 1.3 hours) but I love this game so far and will enjoy it more when I get the map dlcs.
Buy and play this game. Its really great to play when you want to burn some time, maybe while you are wanting to get to sleep or you are stoned xD.

You'd think a game about just driving a truck around for hours would be pretty boring, but actually, there's something strangely soothing about ETS2 that I can't put my finger on. The sound of your rig cruising along the European countryside, the vistas, the salaries from shipping goods on time, and the general freedom of the game are very nice. I would suggest give this game a try when on sale. It may not be foreveryone, but hey, they won a Steam award so I guess these people are on to something.

I found the game to be long, definitely your money's worth, although if you were to play it again in the near future I feel you would remember the order of events and solutions to puzzles. I cannot reccomend this game enough.
Guilty Gear is one of my early fighters so I'm slightly biased in that regard, but even without that bias this game has a lot of what I want: a training mode that will get you through all the game concepts before you ever fight someone, a quick and easy way to figure out combos that work and specials so that you can pull them off yourself, a straight arcade mode with exactly enough story that is still wonderfully animated.
And, ohmigod, it's all done in unreal? And is technically 3D? The game reminds you without getting annoying about it that, oh yeah, you're fighting with 3D models that can show off your specials and victories from a bunch of different angles. You get the magic and tight 2D combat that comes with GG and then amazing cell shaded 3D shots of your combo or dust strike finishing off enemies.
Don't get me wrong, some of the systems in this game are COMPLEX. There's a number of different ways to block and cancel straight through moves and combos to keep pressure high on your opponent and an instant kill incase you feel confident that you're skilled enough to land with it and insult your opponent with a cutscene to end your round immediately. But, the tutorials and mission modes will show you how to do it assuming you're willing to.
It's amazing. A capstone game I would have hoped for.

This is my favorite 2D fighting game, i know i don't have alot of time in it but i feel like i'm ready for my review.
Story: It is actually a anime movie in which they break down into chapters. I've only seen the first few, but as a fan of anime i must say they've kept me interested and i like the characters. And apparently the story is continued from previous games in the guilty gear series.
Online: I've only had the chance to play with a friend of mine, but we literally sat and played through 48 matches straight. It got quite competative and it felt like we both had a fair chance in every match. I also love the lobbies i think that was a clever idea.
Arcade: This has Episode which i havent played yet but supposed to contain your actual story matches i'm assuming similiar to other 2d fighting game standard arcade mode.
Versus: Your standard free battle mode.
M.O.M: I've literally barely delved into this mode but it looks like an rpg character building mode. Where you fight waves of foes and collect gear and treasure, in which you can use the year to make your guy stronger and make it through more waves later. I already started liking it but as i said barely played it.
Dojo: This is the training mode which really made me comtorable with the combos not leaving me feeling stranded and confused like alot of other similiar fighting games.

Also surprised to see that the game records every replay of every match you do, so you can go back at anytime an see exactly what your thumbsticks and buttons were doing through the entire match, so you can see exactly where your combos are lacking and what ones your opponent was doing.
This is without a doubt a hidden gem in the fighting game world, I do plan on buying the rest of the games in the series to catchup on all the story. But from what i've played so far I would give this game a 9.2 out of 10.

SteamWorld Dig is a game trimmed of fat, an experience in pure gameplay. It feels like a flash-based browser game or a Starcraft/Warcraft custom game.
This isn't a bad thing.
Gameplay rules in SteamWorld Dig. Your job is to dig further and further down. As you dig, you find money and trade it to dig better. Thats it. That's the whole game.
The digging is made challenging by limiting the reach of your implements and making backwards travel difficult. This is enough to keep your mind occupied with what would otherwise an exercise in "hold down and press dig for several hours."
As for atmosphere, the characters you meet are colourful, the world and its critters are engaging, and the music is twangy as all get-out. It sells the steampunk-robot-wildwest setting well.
All told, SteamWorld Dig is pure gameplay that doesn't get stale over the modest length of the game.
Note to achievement hunters: two of SteamWorld Dig's achievements are speed runs. Ew.

While very simple, Steamworld Dig is a short but very enjoyable experience. Glad they put a boss fight at the end. While it describes itself as a MetroidVania, it lacks alot of the combat options most of these title have. It's mostly about digging down, but the exploration and puzzles are all very adequate. If it's on sale, you might want to jump on it if you are starved out on metroidvanias like I was.

Forget the new Motherload, THIS is the Motherload that you know and love.
Three different areas, split into differing 'levels', with both secret and mandatory 'caves'; More ore types than you'll remember; Enough upgrades to fill three different shops; A consistent stream of new abilities that keep the levels fresh; Long enough to be enjoyable, short enough to not get boring (My game came to 6:30 hours). There is one boss battle to end the game, which while a little bland, works well with the mechanics and offers a high note to end your adventure on.
This IS Motherload. But what's wrong with it?
Well, my biggest gripe, albeit cosmetic, is that none of the upgrades change your character. Visually you'll finish the game the same way you started (minus the three weapons). One of the biggest pulls to the old Motherload game was how each upgrade made a visually significant impact/improvement, which was sorely missed from the characterisation of this game. The townsfolk even mention how much your character has apparently changed.
Also, as other reviewers have mentioned, this game can be seen as short, and there isn't much replay value. You get ranked based on deaths, money earned, etc., so if you really feel like playing again to get gold (and acheivements), then you'll get at least one more run for your money. If you know Motherload, you know exactly what you're getting, and you'll be pleasently surprised with the innovations this game brings to the table, but you might want to wait until a sale to buy it.
In short:
I enjoyed this game very much. It is a golden example of its genre and I would highly recommend it tothose who know what that is. To those looking for Terraria, Dwarf Fortress, a 'Metroidvania' or whatever other games you think this is like, this is not like that. There is no crafting, no building, and you only attack to survive. This is a game about digging down, mining for money, and buying upgrades to survive digging further. Good luck, 'pardner.

I wanted to like this game so bad, I tried so hard to like it... but after about 15 hours vanilla and 15 hours modded, I just can't recommend it. I can break this game down into a few components and I'll review them individually - let's start with the good:
I absolutely adore the air battles in this game. The geoscape is a flat map, UFOs pop up, and you send out your aircraft. When you hit them, you get to know exactly what they are and can choose to retreat, tail them to get a better engagement positiion, or just go in for the kill. What follows is a fast-pased "real-time" (though pausible) battle between your jets and the enemy aircraft. Depending on your armement and the foe, these can be breeze or a complete nightmare. Shooting down UFOs over land gives you the option to simply annihilate the remains for money, or go in to attempt to capture resources.
Base management is also great! You do the thing, build the rooms. Manage the number of people your base can provide for, the ratio of scientists to engineers to soldiers. Keep enough medbays for sick fellows, hangars for your planes, garages for your vehicles. If aliens get to your base (and they will), the battle will take place in your base, as you designed it.
But that's not the end of it, because you don't get just one base, you get as many as you please! Each one with it's own radar range, vehicles, squads, researchers.
And here we go. I know this may be vein, but I think it's important - Xenonauts lacks absolutely any semblence of luster. It is the most God-damn dreary, drab, boring, plain graphics I have seen. The original X-Com was more colorful, Gameboy games used better palettes, and it can't dare to compete to anything with a budget (ala XCom 2012). I feel absolutely fine playing old games with crappy graphics, but there's no life in Xenonauts. Everything but fire and smoke are perfectly still when you're thinking. There are no idle animations, in fact there are almost no animations at all! Shooting isn't satisfying - just lift the gun and a gentle "pew pew". Threw a grenade? "Poof" and it's over. This game feels like it was drawn up by an insurance salesman. It's completely lifeless and boring, it feels like a placeholder.
This complaint isn't even superficial, it actually impacts gameplay. Handling the different vertical layers is painful at best, you'll lose enemies because their colors are exactly the same as the environment they're standing in!
But it gets worse. The ground combat is just
. Watch as you:
* Throw a grenade and have it fall to the feet of your soldier, killing him and perhaps another squady.
* Struggle to work with the LoS cover mechanics - the enemy shoots you, you can't shoot back, you move out from cover, they take a reaction shot (we'll get to that later), you shoot (and miss), and then step back into cover. There's no peek mechanic. The awkward camera and bad visuals just make this even worse. There's so little feedback ever given to you on what you can expect and the feedback you do get straight-up
. And don't forget, and I'm not joking, the aliens can shoot through the hulls of their ships. You read that correctly, they shoot through the hulls that you can't so much as see through because the engine can't handle their circular shape.
* Not take reaction shots, - seriously, who thought of this? In the original X-Com, units would consistently take reaction shots if they had enough TU. In the new XCOM, overwatch just
. Reaction fire in this game is a delve into madness! A team with 100% TU will just completely ignore an enemy reaper walk up and murder them.  It's completely RNG, yet the aliens take them almost every time you move!
* Have soldiers panicking or unnerve every turn, losing half or more of their TU. Fine. Workable. But then you get worthless mechanics like "berserk" - which have your unit turn to their nearest ally and blow out their brains. This isn't a psi attack, it's a game mechanic. Fans of the game counter this by, and I kid you not, always holding their weapons in the backpack - taking them out each individual use.
* Just die. Not because you made a bad decision, not because your weren't equipped, not because of clever AI, and not in a way you can learn from, but just because. They shoot through their ship walls, they shoot through cover you can't even see around, they toss grenades before they get any form of LoS. Your soldiers kill each other, your soldiers kill themselves. Opened a door, eat shrapnel. No one takes reactions shots, reaper squad kills them all. Rockets and grenades blow up at you or the flanking squad's feet. Dying is good, it makes you learn and gives your decisions meaning and consequence. But you don't die in this game, you just stop living for no reason at all.
Despite all this, though, I still want to love it. I'll come back to it from time to time; and I'll update my review as I see fit.

The environment, audio logs, lore, documentns all end up enhancing the gameplay more. The side missions fully tie in to the story. The game looks superb, is a lot more polished and the tools and mechanics at your disposal are just so much fun.
Third: If you stopped playing due to technical issues at the 1st/2nd Mission, the FPS rates only get better in later phases. Doesnt mean no FPS drops,
(for me, the FPS loterally stabled out from 4th Mission onwards. Dropped a bit on 6th again but then stabled out again.
Fourth:
'nuff said.

Do not get this game now.
This game is VERY poorly optimized for the PC, its almost as if this is a last minute port.
On medium preset settings, everything seems fine at first, and although the menus are super laggy, the intro cutscene and tutorial runs pretty well.
The problem starts when you get into the first room.
Simply by turning 180 degrees in that small room, I get frame drops to 50.
It got far worse when I left the room and the environment expanded, the frames dropped to 40, making me physically sick to even play it.
Then I got to the throne room from the cutscene, and it was literally a constant 30 frames.
At this point I swallowed my anger and lowered all my graphical settings to very low.
Everything went pretty alright at first, constant-ish 60 frames.
That is, until I got outside into the open world.
Simply by looking at a marginally wide region my frames fell to 30 again.
This is ridiculous.
Its not even an isolated incident, many users who have preordered this game have been complaining about the optimization, i've heard of someone with a GTX 1060 strugging to maintain 60 on medium, and he even drops to 35 frames upon peeking into a keyhole from the first room.
What's even more insulting is that very low settings looks pretty much the same as medium, and medium looks nearly identical to Dishonored 1's graphics.
Please don't purchase the game as of now, I cannot comment on the gameplay as I cannot play without feeling queasy as of this moment, but I still hold out a lot of hope for the game, and what i've seen so far has kept me hooked, so I really hope this gets fixed ASAP...
Update:
I have found one temporary fix for the game's issue here for both Nvidia and AMD cards:
I applied this fix as well as reinstalled by graphics drivers and now I have a playable 60 frames most of the time, however, there is still microstuttering and even though Steam tells me I have 90 fps sometimes, it seriously feels like its far less.
I've completed the first mission and am in the midst of the second, the level design is phenomenal, very open with various completely optional areas that you could avoid entirely if you're not careful.
The gameplay so far is pretty similar to Dishonored 1, and from what I could see of the power upgrades, its also pretty similar for Corvo, nothing too revolutionary. Basically, the gameplay is still superb, and they've made several improvements to non-lethal gameplay, such as non-lethal drop attacks.
However, the performance is still utter trash, the FPS drops drastically when you look at certain panes of breakable glass, which is really inexplicable.
In addition, myself and many people have found it extremely nauseating to play this for extended periods of time due to mouse lag, stuttering and fps drops altogether.
Reportedly, Arkane has taken note of this issue so we can hope for a fix soon, will update review then.

I'm surprised they didn't add a record book to keep track of your times, because beating your own score (or worldwide scores) would add tons of replay value. Following the Princess is a time management game characterised by great pacing, comfortable mechanics, terrific level design, and a metric load of easy Steam achievements.
While Following the Princess is a direct sequel of the previous, fourth game of the Weather Lord series (which also was the starting point of a new storyline), it is so much more polished and fun that I’d say you can safely start with this one.
This game knows its place among the time/resource managers: it offers its full content in casual (no time limit) mode, but it can also provide adequate challenge if someone wants to race against a clock.
Just like in the previous game, there are tons of enemies on most of the levels. They add a new layer to the gameplay style, since you need to use one of the weather powers to dispatch them—the same powers that can replenish productions buildings. This gives the game more of a tactical feeling, especially since it is focused more on stockpile management rather than planning routes on when to gather what.
The game only lacks in one area, the amount of levels. There are only 30 of them, with all but one offering an optional replay for different goals. Compared to the 40-60 levels we are used to in other games, it is a bit thin, but at least the level design is superb enough to warrant those replays.

Weather Lord is a series of casual time management games, with Victor as a young hero able to manipulate the weather. However, Victor wasn't always the hero there as previous games were showing more humans and less cute animals.
Anyway, Victor managed to defeat his evil uncle but it seems that a princess needs his help as she's a prisonner of an ancient evil. Besides, her kingdom needs some restoration, as it's devastated.
I'm beginning to be used of the hero being helped by servants/workers and it's also the case here: your loyal friends will be the ones to build workshops or grainmills or anything else that will help to increase ressources (food - you can find them on the paths or you can harvest crops -, wood - same as for food apart that you can cut down trees -, gold - but you'll need your wind power to get some - or crystals - same as for the others). However, your weather skills will be very interesting and needed: you have always three skills. They can be useful against enemies but also for ressources: wind can make the gold mine work, sun can resplenish the crystal pit and rain will resplenish fields and trees. These same skills can also reveal new places or new paths.
However, you can also have super powers thanks to altars (but they're limited in their use and will need crystals to be reactivated): tornadoes, lightning and rainbow. They're useful against more powerful enemies or to clear the paths.
Anyway, you have assigned goals and you just need to reach them to score a three stars - well at least in casual mode, because I didn't try higher difficulties and didn't check if there was a timer.
You have also bonus to help you: some may vary in the levels (work faster, more ressources, etc...) but others can be chosen by you! Indeed, you can find artifacts and choose three of them to help you (skills available quickly, three uses of the super powers instead of 2, more ressources, etc...). These artifacts can be found in normal levels and alternative ones, that are unlocked after finishing a "land".
As you can see, Weather Lord is really nice in terms of mechanics and gameplay. However, my little complaint is that achievements on Steam are only unlocked when exiting the game - on some sites, you could be accused of using an achievement unlocker because of the timestamps, when it's not the case.
However, while I'm not really in love with the graphics, they're still good and the soundtrack is also nice to hear.
Weather Lord is a good purchase and is even better than Gnomes Garden and as good as 12 Labours of Hercules. For the price, you're not robbed, though I suppose that you should wait for a bundle or a discount to purchase it.

Anyone describing this as a "Metroidvania" game doesn't know what the term means.  Yes, your character finds upgrades throughout the game, but there's no exploration aside from "dig down, then dig down some more".  If you want a good feel for what the game's like, go look up the flash game "Motherload".  Steamworld Dig is pretty much just a prettier version of Motherload.
You dig until you can't dig any more (lack of resources or full inventory), you go back up, sell what you've found, go back down, dig more, and repeat until the game's done.  There are some puzzle caves along the way, but they never really present a huge challenge, and I ended up spending the entire game waiting for things to start getting interesting, and then the credits rolled.

Darksouls 2 manages to capture and enhance the classic RPG feeling of old, with a western European theme created from an Asian point of view. Darksouls 2 doesn't seek to wow you with explosions, or wildly impractical cutscenes. It instead provides a semi-open world sandbox of old school customization & deadly enemies. Just when you think you've mastered the combat and get cocky, the game will take unexpected turns to defeat you often succeeding. Death is now something to be feared & avoided instead of a lane bumper used by modern "hollywooded" video games. Those worried about the quality of the PC port can be at ease, as Darksouls 2 embraces full remappable keyboard & mouse controls. Besides improved texture quality, sunshafts, expanded graphics options & the ability to run the game smoothly at 60fps, there are no noticeable "pc exclusive" features. However, the PC port gets it right in all the areas most important to any competant gaming enthusiast.

Ah, good old Xenonauts, personally I find it to be as good of a game as xcom:eu and xcom 2, it does have it's flaws here and there, and it doesn't have the 3D of the modern xcom series but I find it to be a really cool experience nonetheless.
Pros:
-Really good strategy game
-Has a Time Units system rather than the double move system from xcom:eu
-A whole variety of UFOs to shoot down
-A more in-depth soldier equipment screen than xcom:eu
-Amazing artwork
-Ability to research 2 or more projects at once
-A pretty sweet modding community
-Nice base building system
Cons
-2D map view rather then the 3D of xcom:eu
-Game tends to get tedious as time goes on
-Slighty buggy at times (luckily nothing unfixable)
-Animations can be jerky at times
-Graphics in ground combat mode aren't that pretty.
The game really does has it's moments and it's pitfalls but after all I've said I still recommend it because it's still a good game and most of the bugs you can work around.

Gameplay
Pretty basic shooter, but either top down or third person. This is changable with the click of a button, which is pretty cool situational awareness. Dodge rolls and blink dodges are also big factors in keeping an advantage over enemies. Each class also has a specific special ability that can fit just about anyone's playstyle, and just seems to add that little something extra.
Each class also has a skill tree of its own with a leveling system for different kinds of specialization or talents, which is just about as good as any skill system you'd see in a AAA shooter. This doesn't mean the game has no shortcomings or room for improvement. It is, after all, still in Early Access. Nonetheless I'd find it important to mention how lousy the crafting system feels in this game. It seems like what you can build now is currently limited to upgrades, consumables, and worst of all, other materials. I've nearly all of my crafting in the game so far on building better materials out of worse ones so I can build specific upgrades. This isn't unavoidable though, I find armor and upgrades all the time in the field, and  consumables are always pretty simple to craft with common items.
All in all, the game's sure not done, but it's very nice for a 99¢ Early Access, and hands down the best Early Access title I've subscribed to yet. Not to mention the rewards for helping the dev's by playing, it's pretty damn nice. :steamsalty:

I'm not quite sure how I ended up with this game, or when I bought/received it, but decided to take some time to see what it had to offer.
To summarize the whole game in one sentence, it's basically a poor imitation of the old Shinobi games. It's a game created using Game Maker, which in and of itself isn't a sin, but does nothing to hide the fact that it was created using this software. It looks, sounds, and plays "like a Game Maker game". Interpret that however you wish. Originally, ♥♥♥♥♥daria was offered for $4.99, which I believe was excessive for the quality and content of the game, though its current price of $2.99 is closer to being reasonable. (Especially if it is on sale for less.)
Before getting into the negatives I'll share what I enjoyed about the game. The levels, while simple, are not linear. The second stage has a shortcut to the fourth one, for example, and the desert stage has an alternate route for you to find. The bosses are also simplistic but have patterns like a classic console game which are fun to figure out. Once you figure out their patterns though, what little challenge the game had disappears. The unlockable second character offers an alternate way to play the game; it's not necessarily a great experience but it makes you look at each level with a new perspective.
The music in the game is not that great, it sounds like MIDI music. For a game that's supposed to be an homage to retro classics the music doesn't fit at all. Additionally, the visuals don't match any particular "era" or invoke a nostalgic feeling of any particular system. Pixel art does not automatically equate to "the 90's". The humor/plot of the game is also severely dated and belongs in early 00's era "random" Web humor. The power-ups are neat but the shield is so broken that you can literally defeat every single boss with it by standing in a certain area and jumping repeatedly. The unlockable character is also a nice touch, but his ability to double jump breaks the levels; you can tell the stages were not originally designed to be played in this manner.
There are some other gripes I have about the game but they are more nebulous like the bounce trampolines seemingly not working all the time. Sometimes you'll bounce when you land on one, sometimes you'll fall right through it. The shield power-up also fails to work if you are moving at speed and run into a fast enemy (such as a bird or elf) moving in the opposite direction. Those issues are circumstantial and uncommon however, and aren't really major complaints.
Overall, when it comes down to a yes or no answer, ♥♥♥♥♥daria Upgrade is not a game that I can recommend. If it's in a bundle or on sale or something maybe it's worth checking out as a novelty, but as a standalone game there's a lot left to be desired.

This game is a throwback to an older era. Seriously, it uses DOS. While it is an RTS with turn-based movement, it... is tricky for the modern sensibility.
Now, the backstory of the game does make a few changes to history. In 1268, the English king was Henry III, but he was... having issues with the barons of the realm. In fact, the year prior had seen the end of the Second Barons' War. So unrest does bubble beneath the surface. Frankly, his staying on the throne was more due to the efforts of his son than his own prowess. Now, the throne DOES end up empty for over a year in 1272-1274... but this was due to his son taking his time returning from Crusade. Steno Arcade is a great project: it's a suite of games meant to practice typing on stenotype machines (i.e. not your regular laptop keyboard, but some pretty specialized devices that let you type much faster - once you've learned how to use them).
When I played it in Early Access, there was only one game out of the four planned (Steno Hero), which lets you type the lyrics of some nice songs karaoke-style. With a normal keyboard, only the very easy and easy songs are playable, higher levels of difficulty may prove quite frustrating - but it can be an incentive to discover stenotyping ;)
The game is provided with its source code for the open source Godot game engine, so you can actually check how it is designed and tweak it for fun. The community also provided a nice tool to let you create your own song templates, so there's potential for a lot of community-made content.

The Orion Project is a survival/objective based game. If you have played games such as Killing Floor, ORION: Dino Prelude and other titles similar to those, then this game shouldn't be
strange to you. As of now there are two game modes currently availiable and seven classes.
Don't think that just because the game is priced at a single U.S. dollar that it's of low quality. This game is very unique title worth well over one dollar even in it's current early acess state. If this game was completley polished and full of content I would be willing to spend upwards around $40.
But let's talk in detail about the game in it's current state.
Protect your collector machine as it mines "blue gold" veins from the planet. Ten waves of fighting dino's and alien creatures as this machines mines money from the ground. While doing this at certain waves a secondary objective will appear rewarding you will crafting materials, items, and currency.
Right now survival is the exact same as harvest except it never ends, you protect the collector untill it gets destroyed or everyone dies in a single wave. The devs have future plans to make survival a lot different by removing the collecter so you only have to worry about self and team.
Think of each playable class in the game as a different hero or champion you can select to use, and each of them level up on their own; and have their own inventory; and their own unique skills; and their own weapons types yaddha yaddah.
Well anyways the skill tree is essentially your classic skill tree found in the game Borderlands, or like Masteries in LoL. There's 3 catagorys and every time you level up you get a points to allot in each catagory. You can reset all alloted points at anytime, free of charge, so don't worry too much if you missclick. <I beleive the current level cap is 50>
The only thing there is to tell about items is that you can gear them towards a specific type of build prety well. My only problem is equipting different items doesn't change any visuals on the player.
Seven different classes and many more in the making.. You will find one you like I promise.
