I played Sign for 6 months, and when I mean by play, I mean grind combos in the training room and doing nothing else as Millia. So, when revelator came out, I was super excited. Unlike Street fighter V's launch (Sorry Capcom fans please don't hate me) Revelator's launch went exteremly smoothly for me.
So, let's take a look at what the game does well:
+Netcode- HOLY MOTHER OF GOD THE NETCODE IS AMAZING. On average, I get 2-4 frames of delay and it feels like I'm playing on a console offline. Granted, this assuming you have anti-aliasing and post-effects off, but even with everything on, you'll get 5 frames at the max. The only netcode that can top Guilty Gear's is Killer Instinct.
+Accessibility - Revelator has a wonderful tutorial minigame that teaches you basic mechanics such as roman canceling, bursting, Faultless def, air dashing etc. If you are wanting to learn a specific character, there is a combo mode that teaches their special moves and practical combos both easy and advanced. Lastly, Mission mode spoonfeeds you fighting game fundamentals, advanced mechanics of Guilty Gear, EVEN CHARACTER MATCH-UPS. They give you all the tools to be successful, it's up to you to put in the work.
+Casual Appeal- Take notes Capcom, because this is why Guilty Gear and other fighters are on the rise. Revelator introduces a new control scheme called "Stylish mode", If you played UMvC3, it is same as playing on simple. While in stylish mode, you can press random buttons to automatically perform (unoptimized) combos with your character. I love this mode because It gives casuals a taste of what a character can do. If they want more, they can hit the combo dojo and play on technical. M.O.M. and acrade modes also help to appeal to casuals.
+Balancing- By Far, Revelator is one the most balanced fighting games I've played. Yes, there is a tier list but the power level of all the characters is exteremly high and they have at least one glaring weakness. Everybody is viable. Case in point: A Player won Anime Ascension, a fighting game major, using Slayer who is considered low tier. Additionally, Every character is unique in terms of mechanics and playstyle. Meaning, there will be a character that you enjoy. Guranteed.
+Visuals - THIS GAME LOOKS ♥♥♥♥ING AMAZING. That's it.
As good as Revelator is, it is not a perfect game. Here are some cons:
- Information Overload - Despite having a good tutorial and Mission mode, There a lot of mechanics in Guilty Gear and remembering the universial mechanics in addition to your character's mechanics is overwhelming. Although it's better now, the tutorial still does throw a lot of information at you once and some parts of it needed to be sectioned out.
-No incentive for Ranked Play - I personally don't bother with Ranked play to much, but for some people, the lack of people doing ranked matches is a turnoff. This is mostly because there is no incentive for improving your rank. Maybe have seasons and offer a color for your character if you reach a certain rank? I dunno, just throwing out ideas.
-Not being able to specatate mid match- I know they are fixing it in rev2 but it is annoying that If I don't start specating before players start a match, I have to stare at tiny health bars and round markers.
-Forced Character picks for most Missions- Although the missions teach you fundamentals, most of the time you will be playing as Sol or Ky which is kind of annoying if you don't play either of them. The mission mode would be perfect if you were able to chose your character for each mission to help the player learn what options the character has for different situations.
Conclusion:
If this is your first fighting game, I actually DO NOT recommend this game to get into fighters. The reason why is the information overload stated in the negatives part of the review. Street Fighter V may not be as flashy and fast as Guilty Gear, but fundamentals are apparent and eases you into the FGC the best.
However, If you are an eager young newbie that is willing to put the work into this game, or FGC veteran looking for a game, or a Street Fighter V refugee or if you're just a fan of the Guilty Gear series, THIS GAME IS A MUST BUY.
Thanks for reading and happy grinding!
~TeddyTreebark

As you may have heard, Super Meat Boy is a very difficult 2D platformer game. It’s very famous for its difficulty, in fact. However, difficulty doesn’t make a game, and Super Meat Boy is no exception to this rule. It’s also very fun..even if it may not seem like it if you die on a level enough.
The levels in this game are short, mostly fitting on one or two screens. With 6 worlds and 20 levels each (not counting the 8 in a 7th world or the secret exit levels or the bosses), the game has quite a bit of content even if someone were to run through the game and only die a reasonable number of times. The thing is, all of these levels become hours and hours of playtime per playthrough when you get stuck on them. The story isn’t much, but it really doesn’t need to be. For what it is, it’s just a funny little diversion in-between worlds. World 1 is pretty easy and helps ease you into how the game plays and what levels are going to be like, but starting in World 2, the difficulty curve starts to get steep (yet consistent) throughout the game. And each world adds a multitude of their own mechanics that are implemented very well. Collectibles and secret exits are craftily hidden or placed in certain levels (which, unfortunately, you can’t see in-game) and provide a slightly different way to tackle levels in order to get them if you want to.
The gameplay is extremely satisfying. The controls are tight, as you may have heard many times before. There are plenty of characters in the game, but Meat Boy himself not only can make it through every level himself…but personally I prefer him the most. The way he walljumps is just so dang fun. Practicing levels to be able to fly through them is extremely worthwhile when you finally make that perfect run of inputs and execution.
I can completely see people getting turned off by the difficulty in certain parts of the game. World 5 and the retro levels (that life system is so bad) usually feel like unenjoyable difficulty compared to the final world’s extreme difficulty still feeling worth going through. But that’s about it on my negativity for this game. If it looks up your alley, I say get it. As said before, the game occurs in 1992 in the West Coast-themed state of San Andreas, which is heavily based on California and Nevada. San Andreas is an island containing three cities. You'll begin the game in the city of Los Santos, which is based roughly on Los Angeles and consists of a mixture of ritzy downtown areas and the gangland ghettos of South Central. San Fierro is based on San Francisco, reproducing the real city's hilly terrain and ever-present fog. The game's third city is Las Venturas, which is a great take on early-'90s Las Vegas, complete with a strip full of casinos and the surrounding desert. San Andreas is definitely a much larger place than Vice City, and the growth of the player is handled intelligently. There are plenty of things to do both in and out of the cities, and the missions are especially well done and with a nice difficulty level.
San Andreas draws its inspiration from the ghetto and gangsta struggle films of the early '90s. And it is the stage for the arrival of the main character of the game, the eternal "CJ" - aka Carl Johnson. In San Andreas, you play your role. The game opens with Carl returning to Los Santos after spending the last five years in GTA III's Liberty City. But his homecoming isn't a happy one. He's returning home because his mother has been killed. Carl isn't on the ground for more than an hour before he's picked up by a pair of crooked cops and thrown right back into the middle of the street life he left Los Santos to avoid.
____
As soon as you reach to Los Santos, you have the priority to reestablish the reputation of your gang, the Grove Street Families. The objective is to put your set back on the map. GSF has fallen into disarray over the last five years, and their influence is minimal at best. So you, along with the three other leaders of the gang, the long-winded Big Smoke, the dust-smoking Ryder, and your stubborn brother, Sweet, set out to take back the streets from your rivals, the Ballas, who have turned to dealing crack to earn money and gain influence in the hood. You established a set of missions to take back your territory, starting small with things like spray-painting over other gangs' tags (which is one of the many new types of actions that replace previous GTA games' more-generic hidden package collecting here), but quickly moving up to drive-bys and other acts of extreme gangsterism. First off, it's inevitable that XCOM will be mentioned at some point, so lets start there. Yes, you're likely to enjoy this if you enjoyed the original XCOM games. Xenonauts began as a passion project on Kickstarter for those wanting to relive the original XCOM experience. It stays mostly true to XCOM without replicating it, even expanding on originally lacking features like interceptor combat, which is now much more involved.
Some elements of this game work in real-time (aerial combat, although you can pause), but the majority of your time (~85%) will be spent in grounded, turn-based missions. I should mention that both ground and aerial combat missions are skip-able, but of course you'll miss out on a lot of resources if you decide to pass on them. There
workshop (cheat) mods out there that allow you to essentially skip areas of gameplay you might not enjoy, so if you find yourself wanting to focus on the ground-based missions for example and ignore the Geoscape, you can pretty much do that.
About aerial combat: it is, in my opinion, not that great. It's not particularly bad, but it doesn't feel fleshed out beyond the dodge and missile mechanics. I tend to think of it more like an optional mini-game that gives you a break from other points of strategy every now and then. On a normal run I found myself skipping most aerial combat scenarios with little to no penalty for doing so, and apparently that's fine. Although I didn't enjoy it personally, I'm glad I was given the option to skip as it seems a more experimental point of gameplay compared to everything else.
Ground combat is brilliant, and most things in the Geoscape are brilliant. You'll need patience and time to plan out your approach to the alien invasion, particularly since this game is a multifaceted strategy. By the end, you'll probably be managing several bases and many troops/employers/vehicles at the same time. For those reasons, this might be a game you need to stick to before moving on, and certainly not play if you're an amnesiac. That would leave you with an overwhelming amount of management to do and no memory on how to do it. Also, if you like your micro/macro organisation, you'll fall in love with this. In the micro sense for example, each soldier can be personalized by name and load-out (there's a pretty huge arsenal if you research weapons), with class-specific types you can set as defaults. One thing that's lacking which affects both ground combat and the Geoscape, is vehicles. Only one vehicle variant exists in this game and it requires a hefty amount of resources to get up and running. But... is it worth it? No. Even when you acquire it, you sacrifice two soldiers in exchange for having it on the ground. Unfortunately it isn't even worth two soldiers. In short, vehicles are pretty underdeveloped in this game and almost not worth bothering about. You can upgrade it into pure bad-assery way later on, but the climb to get there isn't economically efficient.
Another flaw: monsters and civilians sometimes have stupid AI. Aliens tend to be at their deadliest when they're throwing grenades at you non-stop and the AI still has issues with pathing and awareness, as it tends to know where you are half the time without a good reason as to why. I was able to ignore these issues as the experience was mostly fluid.
Oh, as a side note; pretty much everything in ground combat is destructible.
My lord, the writing. It is monstrously good, and might honestly be the best experience with reading I've ever had in a game ever. And normally I
taking time to read in games. Hell, Xenonauts even comes with it's own novella, yes, a freaking
hidden away in the extra features. Now, I don't think it compares to the in-game text you get for completing research projects, but it's still kind of impressive that they actually hired an author to do it. One of the major things keeping me coming back to this game was the thought of completing a research project and being handed a bit more information of the alien invasion.
SO, I recommend this game. It's worth the price, but most of all it's a lot of fun. A lot of issues posted in top reviews have been fixed/have fixes for download or are already within the game but need to be enabled. I suggest that upon starting the game you click the mod manager and enable the mod already downloaded which adds a ton of map variety.
I'll close out saying Xenonauts has a lot of really awesome mods in the Steam workshop section, so at the very least give it a glance over before or after playing for your first time. The community is regularly patching this with updates even after the devs recently stopped, so there's also a community build if you switch over to beta.

I love the X-COM concept. I didnt discover the PDS genre until I stumbled upon XCOM:EU and dug into its history. I bought the OG X-COM, and i loved what it had to offer. However, its more degrading issues kept me from fulling enjoying it, and i never finished.
Fast forward to about two summers ago, and BAM Xenonauts shows up. It completely flew under my radar during its early access stint, but I was devouring EU at that point and was looking for something new. God damn, it was love at first sight.
By no means am I good at this game, i'm only writing this review several years later because moments ago I just beat the game for the first time. After that experience, I feel like I have a decent grasp of the good and bad sides of the game, which I will now outline.
THE GOOD, a few notable things
-INTERCEPTOR GAMEPLAY: The typical RNG cutscene-esque UFO interceptions are replaced with a 2D real-time combat simulation. This can be simulated, thankfully, but taking direct control can result in you winning dogfights the game said you had zero chance of surviving.
-BASE DEFENSE: Yep, just like X-COM if you cant maintain air-superiority in the late-game, prepare to have your door kicked in. Xenonauts improves the experience by giving it a bit more realism, a preperation period. Aliens will spawn not in your hangars, but from breach pods that can be seen in the fog-of-war. This allows you to actually counter-assualt the invaders. You also start with your secuirity team in the central command room, which is nice.
-AUTO-UPGRADES: By far my favorite change is researching tech that effects aircraft and vehicle weaponry is applied without the need to construct new equipment. This is awesome, because it makes getting these tech milestones feel immediatly rewarding, notable the air-game which can be quite brutal if you fall behind.
THE BAD, a couple notable things
-ALIEN AI: The aliens in this game are annoying, especially during base assualt missions. As another reviewer states, they seem to have the advantage of always knowing where you are, meaning assualting a control room is a frusturating process indeed. Bunch your guys up and stack the door? Three grenades up your♥♥♥♥♥ guaranteed. Send a few guys at a time? Grenades. Two? Grenades. Its not tactical, its cheap. This leads to more "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥et" moments than I ever experienced in XCOM or X-COM.
-MEMORIAL: There is none. Simple.
Still, this game is well made and I highly recomend it.

If you enjoyed the 1990s XCOM games, you will probably enjoy playing Xenonauts.
You have to manage a base and use your radar to track UFO, deploying aircraft to down them like in the XCOM games, only this game takes place in the late 1970s (with the Soviet Union still in power).
Unlike the XCOM games, you can have up to three aircraft in a squadron attack a UFO or a squadron of UFOs.  The air combat is unique in that if you know how you want to manuever your aircraft to attack the UFO(s), you may down them with taking little to no damage to any of your aircraft.  You also do not lose your aircraft if they are downed by a UFO or run out of fuel, but you will have to wait for some time to pass to wait for it to be repaired.
When engaging the aliens on the ground, you will need to decide which weapons will be ideal to use.  Shotguns are bad for long range attacks but excel up close, so they may be best for use in urban areas or when entering a UFO.  Rifles are ideal for general use, like at range shot or up close.  Sniper rifles are useful for taking a shot at an alien whenever it is spotted far away.  Rocket launchers are useful for distant but powerful area attacks.  New to this type of game is the shield.  It can be used to absorb attacks so your other troops may move in behind and provide support.
As you capture and research the alien technology, new versions of firearms will become available to produce (you do not use the alien weaponry to equip your troops before engaging the aliens on the ground).  These weapons will also be based on the shotgun, rifle, sniper, and rocket launcher use.  You will also be able to create new aircraft and weapon ground vehicles for use against the aliens.
The aliens in this game are primarily focused on attacking the locals, which you will see often in ground encounters.  You may need to use caution to not harm the locals.  While the locals will most likely either get in the way or run in terror, some may also be equiped with firearms of their own and shoot at the aliens.  Keeping the locals alive helps boost ratings in the territory and help keep the supporting country there happy and thus continue providing funds to the Xenonaut organization, along with successfully downing an alien craft in the ocean.
As the game progresses, you will uncover the insidious plot the aliens have for arriving on earth.  While I enjoyed uncovering this story and the need to stop the alien threat, the ending felt very limited and more could have been done.
Although I did encounter a few bugs, like my troops occassional ability to spot an alien on the second/third floor of their UFO but have no way to shoot them because the UFO wall apparently is see-through but not shoot-through and blasting a staircase away can strand a soldier on the second/third floor of a building unless he/she is using some kind of flying armor.
My final, minor, issue with this game is the female doll pictures used when showing them equiped with armor and firearm.  Except for the head, the torso is the same as the male.  I would prefer if the women had a more feminine torso used instead.
Overall, I enjoyed playing this game quite a bit and would recommend it for those who like squadron-based tactical games, especially fans of XCOM.

I played this one through just out of boredom. First I tried playing it on ironman, but soon noticed that the whole game is riddled with oneshot ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t through walls and other cool stuff like that which you have zero control over in any way and absolutely no way to counter them, in any way. Your guys will constantly get oneshot, even in the best armor, out of the blue, or sometimes, through walls.
I especially love the grenade mechanics in this game. You see that comforting animation of something flying and you're like: "yay! grenades!". Sadly, the reality is cold: they thought it's too much hassle to actually code grenades to have their own mechanics, like flying path which would allow them to fly OVER the obstacles. Instead, they fly in a straight line like bullets hitting every possible obstacle on the screen and in addition to that they have ridiculously low hit % and the scatter is random to the max. Of course this doesn't prevent the aliens from throwing grenades THROUGH EVERYTHING, including walls, and hitting with them 100%. More ofthen than not that results in the death of everyone in the blast radius, even with best armor and 100hp. Mass oneshots, yay. If you ever happen to hit with your own grenade, you can feel happy if it makes a scratch on the alien. Also you can't even blow up covers effectively with grenades thanks to the... "interesting" explosion mechanics they use. And in addition generally you need 2-4 grenades to destroy any envinroment block. So yeah, grenades, why are they in the game?
Also your hit % with most weaponry is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly low unless you go into melee and the cover mechanics are iffy at best. If there's a pebble anywhere in the path between you and your enemy, your shot will lose hit %. And I mean literally a pebble. A pebble will lower your aim by 10% and anything fist sized will lower it by 25% and so on. And... I don't even want to get started about the % based action costs. Basically your virgin rookie who hasn't drawn first blood will shoot his/her gun as just as many times as your battle-hardened commander who's looked death and slaughter into eyes and laughed. Your highest rank soldier will move a few squares further and that's it. He'll still get oneshot anyways.
The combat is extremely simplistic, exactly like it was over 20 years ago in the original X-COM games. That's all nice and cool, but if I want to play a game with 20 years old technology I'll play those games, which actually have functioning grenades as well in addition to some other cool stuff. Additionaly they have the great excuse of actually being over 20 years old, so you can forgive their flaws more easily.
From the newer X-COM games I really missed the classes and how they affected the game play in various different ways. It added spices to the old mix, making missions different and changing your approach. Also another thing I missed was the "trinket" items of the newer games. Like S.C.O.P.E.S. and stuff. The lack of player usable psionics is also a con.
But is there anything good in this game at all...? Well, I liked the base buildling and how you had to manage more than one base to save the Earth. Also the air combat mechanics, even though simple, were a nice thing. Both of these could've been improved on, massively. The base structures could've had more variation in different ways and so on. But still, it's an indie game and at least they tried.
And why do you have storerooms in the game at all if they are basically not used? You store what? 2 items in those? Alien alloy and energy things. Why do you destoy the alien corpses after the missions? I'm sure there would be a market for alien skull decor for housing if you have no other use for the corpses. Super Meat Boy will make you a man.

As you may have heard, Super Meat Boy is a very difficult 2D platformer game. It’s very famous for its difficulty, in fact. However, difficulty doesn’t make a game, and Super Meat Boy is no exception to this rule. It’s also very fun..even if it may not seem like it if you die on a level enough.
The levels in this game are short, mostly fitting on one or two screens. With 6 worlds and 20 levels each (not counting the 8 in a 7th world or the secret exit levels or the bosses), the game has quite a bit of content even if someone were to run through the game and only die a reasonable number of times. The thing is, all of these levels become hours and hours of playtime per playthrough when you get stuck on them. The story isn’t much, but it really doesn’t need to be. For what it is, it’s just a funny little diversion in-between worlds. World 1 is pretty easy and helps ease you into how the game plays and what levels are going to be like, but starting in World 2, the difficulty curve starts to get steep (yet consistent) throughout the game. And each world adds a multitude of their own mechanics that are implemented very well. Collectibles and secret exits are craftily hidden or placed in certain levels (which, unfortunately, you can’t see in-game) and provide a slightly different way to tackle levels in order to get them if you want to.
The gameplay is extremely satisfying. The controls are tight, as you may have heard many times before. There are plenty of characters in the game, but Meat Boy himself not only can make it through every level himself…but personally I prefer him the most. The way he walljumps is just so dang fun. Practicing levels to be able to fly through them is extremely worthwhile when you finally make that perfect run of inputs and execution.
I can completely see people getting turned off by the difficulty in certain parts of the game. World 5 and the retro levels (that life system is so bad) usually feel like unenjoyable difficulty compared to the final world’s extreme difficulty still feeling worth going through. But that’s about it on my negativity for this game. If it looks up your alley, I say get it. If you’re afraid you might give up on it a ways in, I’d wait for a sale (which this game has plenty of) so you feel less bad about it. Regardless, I still think it’s worth trying out…and not only just to see what makes it so famous.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

Over the years we have seen Traveler's Tales take several iconic film properties and give them the LEGO makeover. This strategy has proven to be incredibly successful for both Traveler's Tales and publisher Warner Bros. with LEGO games consistently outselling numerous other big name properties and franchises on the consoles and now to coincide with the release of Jurassic World we get the LEGO version which also happens to contain condensed LEGO versions of the first three movies including, of course, the biggest blockbuster of 2015 so far (until the new Star Wars movie arrives) - Jurassic World
These people obviously never watched Alfred Hitchcock's The Birds.
A Screenshot of LEGO® Jurassic World
By: Sir Faulty
If you are not a fan of this kid-friendly branding exercise, the humor or the simplistic puzzles then I suggest you stop reading now and move along. However, if you happen to enjoy a bit of LEGO mayhem in-between playing your other games, enjoy the sly parodies on display or just happen to be a massive fan of the film franchise then LEGO Jurassic World pays just enough lip service to the originals that should have fans chomping at the bit.
Once again you will find yourself exploring various film scenes from all four of the movies smashing everything in sight to bits while piles of unbuilt LEGO will bounce up and down around you indicating that you can build some sort of device or structure that will enable story progression. While LEGO Jurassic World does incredibly little to tinker with what makes these games so addictive and well loved amongst many, the game mechanics have been slightly overhauled indicating that Traveler's Tales seems to be getting a better handle on the LEGO engine than its previous iterations but like any film licensed product LEGO Jurassic World has the air about it of something that was rushed to the market in order to meet the deadlines determined by the release of the film. Characters repeatedly get stuck in the environment causing the player to have to reboot out of the level and restart it. This can sometimes get incredibly frustrating especially when you are near the end of a level only for this to occur forcing you right back to the beginning. Traveler's Tales have implemented a save feature at certain mid-points in the levels but they very sporadic with some not having any save feature mid-way at all.
LEGO Jurassic World_Jurassic Park 3-5
A Video of LEGO® Jurassic World
By: Sir Faulty
Part 3-5 of Jurassic Park in LEGO Jurassic World playing story mode. Played on PC through Steam. Game can be purchased at the following link:-
While I did not experience many bugs throughout my first playthrough, perusing the forums reveals a host of issues that are preventing people from completing the game. While from a production stand point LEGO Jurassic World looks fantastic and is a very strikingly good looking LEGO game; the game does tend to feel a bit more rushed than its predecessors but I suppose that boils down to the fact that most of the scenes in LEGO Jurassic Park mimic the fight and flight scenes from the original movies which does require the action to fly thick and fast. With that being said there is hardly a lull in any of the games 20 chapters (5 across each film) as they move at a breakneck pace. As a huge fan of the franchise I really enjoyed the LEGO treatment given to the films so much so that LEGO Jurassic Park has emerged as my favorite LEGO game to come from TT Games thus far.
Where the game does tend to falter is in the use of its voice overs. Certain scenes are mixed in with the original dialogue from the movies but the movie dialogue sounds tinny and it becomes quite jarring to hear famous lines from the movie sound like they being beamed in from the inside of a soda can compared to the clarity of voice work composed specifically for the game.
Now I am sure we can settle this amicably
A Screenshot of LEGO® Jurassic World
By: Sir Faulty
LEGO Jurassic World is not going to win over any new fans but for those who enjoy these kinds of games it's a fun and wild romp through all four films and is the perfect game for families playing some couch co-op over the weekend. The humor is as sharp as ever and should have most adults that play it giggling away like children. LEGO Jurassic World gets the all clear in my books. You are free to enter the park.

I would definitely recomend this game to any people who love an amazing RPG and the old unique action RPG experience. This game is packed with hundreds of hours of lore and content. "You will die alot" isn't exaggerated either, dying in this game is very common and anyone who's played a souls game will know about that. This has got to be one of my favourite RPG's ever, the combat is both challenging and satisfying just knowing how good it feels to kill that one boss you've been trying to kill for the past hour. The main story can take around 60-100 hours to complete depending on how experienced you are with a Souls game, there is also a new game plus mode which can go up to around 10 times i think and in new game plus the enemies are alot harder and have different reactions and every time you go through the game it feels different. There is lots of different things you can do within the game that includes, CO-OP with up to 2 of your friends and PVP which insists of fighting each other to the death and either loosing or gaining rewards. There is also alot of customisation involved, that includes up to hundreds of different armor sets, weapons, spells and items, a deep customisation on making your character its like the posibilites are endless. Also coming from a Console version of the game to the PC version of the game at 1080P with higher frame rates is such a treat, it makes the game more enjoyable to play with the 60 frames per second and the lush and stunning visuals of the game. Also i must point out that the game runs VERY VERY smooth even on top settings, i don't think i dropped from 60 at all, because when Dark Souls 1 was ported over to PC it was horrendous and you was unable to even play over 30 frames per second and the ability to play with mouse and keyboard or even change the graphics settings, but with Dark Souls 2 FromSoftware did a fantastic job on making an excellent PC port with custom key binds, custom graphics settings and even 60 frames right off the get go, even the mouse and keyboard is useable but still not perfect. Only one complaint about this is when you use a keyboard and mouse, the action buttons are Xbox button prompts so it makes it feel a bit confusing on what button does what, but i think most people will use a controller anyway. Overall Dark Souls 2 is an amazing experience that any fan of the RPG genre should enjoy and shouldn't be put off to get into it because of the first game and how hard it was to delve into the storyline, lore and the difficulty, Dark Souls 2 definitely irons out all of these problems, but without making the game too easy or rediculously hard like Dark Souls 1 did.
Overall Score 9.5/10 I would definitely recomend this to any RPG fan that needs a great RPG experience without the loss of difficulty or story.

Tactical turn-based squad combat within spitting distance of its finest.
The upsides:
The time unit system, inspired by the original X-COM. If your soldiers are fast, they can shoot their weapon several times, then run. Or shoot and move and shoot again.
The overwatch system. You just point your soldiers in the right direction and leave them some time units, and they'll shoot reactively when they see something.
Research. This could be better integrated, but the basic idea is that you need to acquire specific alien technology to study and thereby improve your equipment.
Difficulty levels. I'm playing on easy right now, and it is in fact easy. A small challenge in places, but if I'm a bit careful, I don't lose soldiers. Higher difficulty levels are progressively harder and require more care to get through.
The midsides:
Enemy variety is okay. You've got normal mooks, regenerating enemies, androids, reavers (scary), fliers, and psions (also scary). Enough to keep you on your toes, but I rarely see much difference between androids and baseline Caesians.
Weapon variety is a strict progression on one axis, with different purposes on another. Shotgun to scatter laser, for instance; rifle to laser rifle to plasma rifle. Armor progression is similar at first, but branches out a bit later, letting you choose between medium armor, flying scout armor, and walking tanks. The variety is just sufficient, no more.
The controls are mostly intuitive -- but who thinks about controls unless they're bad?
There's a decent number of maps, but you'll start recognizing them after a bit. For standard missions, I think there's like industrial, city, arctic, farmland, and desert, with about three maps each. That means you've got good odds of seeing a duplicate after just a few missions. And terror missions always take place in a city. Enemy bases have more variety, but you're not likely to see that many alien bases. I would have liked to see procedurally generated terrain, but that's difficult and time-consuming to create.
The downsides:
The UI is a little clunky for switching between levels (upstairs/downstairs).
There are occasional bugs -- the other day, I encountered a ghost Caesian. It wasn't aligned on tile boundaries, my soldiers could overlap it, and I couldn't shoot it. I had to run away. There are occasional crashes, too. Not quite stable enough for me to recommend ironman mode.
It's somewhat expected in this kind of game, but losses can snowball. You spent a lot of time building up your forces, then got a full team wipe and lost half your equipment in a bad mission. At that point, you should maybe scrub the campaign and start over. You research things in the wrong order and things get a lot more difficult than they would otherwise be.

The game starts relativerly boring and basic and I based my passed judgement on that, but the game gets a lot better and strategic when you progress further in the game and when you have unlocked a lot of the technology.
The ground combat in the beginning is fairly easy and you only have traditional weapons to work with, but as you progress and get better equipment you encounter interesting tactical situations with new opposition where every move counts and any mistake can be a brutal punishment that has a long term effect on your gameplay.
What I especially like from this game is the scientific lore. Every new technology you recover and reseach has a very detailed background. And even though fictional the way it is explained sounds credible and makes sense. The devs have really thought about the underlying details of the technology and thats pretty cool.
Overall the game has a lot more strategic depth than I originally thought (first few hours of gameplay). And the game mechanics and the AI is a lot better than I originally expected. This is clearly not a game made for the $, but made with passion and devotion... and it shows.

Slime Rancher is easily the most adorable game I've played on Steam yet. The premise of the game is quite simple. You use your handy vac pack to suck up various slimes, deposit them in purchasable slime corrals, feed & care for them, and harvest their plorts(poop) for money. It's a simple concept yet extremely addicting. I played it for 4 hours on the first day I purchased it.
For an early-access game in its alpha stage, there's surprisingly a lot to do. In addition to the actual ranching of slimes, you can build a chicken coop and raise roosters and hens, farm for fruit and veggies, feed giant "gordo" slimes for big rewards, and fight off evil "Tarr" monsters.
There are moments where the game can be quite buggy, mainly that you can access parts of the game you aren't supposed to access yet, but they're so minor and the game is in its alpha stage, so they're completely forgiveable and barely affect your gameplay whatsoever.
Even in the early access stage, I say Slime Rancher is very much worth its $20 price and I definitely recommend it. I can't wait to see what else is added to the game. Keep up the good work, devs!

Honestly, a Steam game has to be really appealing to me for me to spend more than £10 on it nowadays, and it took me a while to buy Slime Rancher, but damn I'm glad I did.
I've only bought into a few early access games/sites/etc in my time, and usually I find myself with money lost and no reward, but here is a happy exception.
As of this review I've had 6 hours gameplay and I feel I've done everything the game has to offer. I have every paddock unlocked in exactly the way I want it with every single upgrade unlocked. If the game was completely finished, £15 for 6 hours gameplay would be bad, but considering the game is still in Alpha? I'm super excited for every update, I've already seen the rise and fall of bugs and can't wait for extra features to be added.

Would be great if slime mortality was added in the future as a difficulty setting? Maybe sickness too? (I know Rad Slimes used to exist so sickness is possible in-game already)
I'd thorougly recommend this game to anyone who likes management or casual games

A well-made, faithful remake of the classic X-COM. Has its quirks (vanilla AI, cover system), but will be very enjoyable for any turn-based strategy fan.

Review:
An almost perfect game, especially if your looking for a game like the classic XCOM.  Unfortunatly there are not really any others these days so this game definitely fills the void.  Yeah it has some problems and a few glitches here and there such as an alien, rarely, being able to get that shot off through a wall killing a guy but with the same line of sight back you cant shoot them.  It is rare but it does happen.
The main difference between this game and the classic XCOM is that Xenonauts uses a 2D system rather than the 3D one XCOM: Ufo Defense had.  This has its limitations and is probably the biggest gripe I have with this game because it makes the line of sight issues, among other things.  It calculates the chance of hit, does the math, and then either hits or misses the target while cover dramatically reduces that chance.  This is opposed to XCOM's 3D engine where it instead used a complex calculation with the accuracy taken into account and calculated a trajectory of the bullet and whatever it hit it hit, whether it be a guy way off the side of the target, hitting the guy behind the target, or just flying off the map.  It was much more fun that way, with this game their system is ok but definitely a step back.  On the bright side I hear Goldhawk is using a 3D engine for their sequel so hopefully the next game is going to be the true successor to this genre.
Pros:
+Great Graphics (for the style they are going for)
+Air battles are intense
+Streamlined management (you still have to manufacture all the weapons besides the base ones, armour, planes, ect. except the ammo)
+Loadouts. You still have to account for how much ammo you bring, grenades, and everything of that nature with penalties if you bring too much.
+Soldiers are now much easier to track (very powerful feature, something XCOM lacked in and you'll understand why when you play it)
+Tons of tech
+Cover mechanics are great but again I just wish it was a 3D engine
+Has room for alot of strategy and different methods of play
+Great community and many mods to change your experience
Cons:
-2D engine which accounts for most of the issues people have with line of sight and accuracy.  It isn't bad but the 3D engine would have been 100x better.  This is my biggest gripe with the game and is mainly the reason I feel the game isn't perfect (otherwise it would have been!)
-Most other negative issues relate to the 2D issue such as not being able to through granades over walls, shoot someone in the air if their is a wall in the way, and other annoying little things like that.
-Usually each map will have only 1 race of alien, sometimes 2 if they are similar, such as both being robotic for instance.  Theres a mod that changes that but thought it was worth mentioning.
Last Thoughts:
Personally I did not mind that my dudes would usually get 1-2 shotted as it adds to the difficulty, and for me the realism.  I can't immagine someone would take a few shots from a plasma gun, especially at close range, and keep chugging through like nothing happened.  It is manageable though, and if played right usually the casaulties can stay pretty low.
Also the game is pretty brutal and challenging, you always feel behind.  This game is all about trade offs.  Overall a great foundation for the sequel, but still alot of fun.  Great job Goldhawk amigos!
If it had a 3D engine would be 9.5, but alas

This game is interesting despite its shortfalls which I'll discuss later in this review.
First, I'd like to point out how early we're getting this game.  There are basic, core features promised in the description which are not present in the current build of the game.  Early access is almost an understatement.  However, do not let that deter you from buying the game.
Second, I'd like to point out that the game is currently on sale for $0.99 and is worth all ninety nine pennies.  Buy it if you're thinking about it.
Now, the review:
I'm not going to give a list of pros and cons because this game is expected to change drastically, and hopefully my review along with it.  I will simply mention the things in this game that make it worth playing and things that make it not worth playing, just things that I happened to note throughout my experience.
As a top-down shooter, it succeeds.  The controls are intuitive and feel familiar, yet they're refined to work in both third-person and top-down mode.  I would recommend remapping the blink key (default 'c' I believe) to something that your right hand can hit quickly; preferably on your mouse.  Blink often, this is a feature of the game that will make it much easier and will probably be nerfed at some point.
Let's talk about the third-person shooter aspect.  Press F1 to toggle between top-down and third-person.  I was excited for this feature, but quickly realized that I'm at a slight disadvantage because I can't see the miniature dinosaurs through the grass, whereas in top-down you can see them coming from quite far away.  There is one advantage though, which is that you can easily take down the flying dinosaurs before they can even attack you.  That's really about it, though.  And the flying dinosaurs aren't even that big of an issue unless they're in large numbers, which they rarely are.  The mouse feels funky.  Aiming does not feel good in third-person.  I've removed mouse acceleration (or whatever the setting is called ingame) and it still feels like there's some latency between when I move the mouse and when my character looks around.  It's very difficult to aim in this game, but luckily, aiming isn't important.  Your stock weapons can kill mostly anything on your level within 1-2 hits depending on your class.  Shotguns are 1-hit kill on all lower level mobs.  I recommend using the support class if you're new to top-down shooters.  It is very intuitive.
The graphics are really not impressive, but I'm not complaining about them either.  There is some customization, but not a whole lot.  I turn them down because it seems to reduce the foliage which makes it easier to kill the tiny little dinos.
Crafting appears to be fully implemented and from my limited experience with it, it seems very well-done.  The menus work, I haven't experienced any bugs with it, and it seems to be easy to teach yourself how the crafting system works without much (if any?) guidance.  Your inventory has an intuitive sorting function which I love.  Makes things very easy to read.
Features missing from the game...major.  This is major.  But, luckily, I know for a fact that they're coming, so I'm not upset that my $0.99 game is missing a few major, core features.  Open world?  No sir.  Travel the galaxy?  Not even a little bit.  Persistent universe?  Where?  Living, breathing?  Let's call it...not living, or breathing.  The game isn't finished, guys.  I can't comment on these aspects of the game because it simply lacks these features entirely.
So, that's pretty much my review.  If you're curious, and reading this later in time and now have the fully fleshed out game, then let me explain what it's like now.  You spawn in, and there's (I think?) a tutorial to show you how to do some basic stuff.  There might not be, I really don't remember.  But you enter this unknown space station in an unknown location, with zero identifying features, and you're told...nothing.  Nothing about how to start games or what you're even supposed to do.  Through asking people, I discovered that there is a strategy table where I can start a matchmade game, or another table nearby where I can craft, although crafting is all done through your inventory anyways so these hubs are utterly pointless.  So, the only thing you can do is start a game right now.  You can control the map, the difficulty, the item level requirement, and a few other things as well.  There are two game types to choose from at the moment, survival and harvest.  Survival is classic wave survival, dinos just keep attacking you until you can't hold out anymore.  Harvest is a bit different, but same-ish concept.  A harvester travels around the map harvesting an unknown material, and you must defend it from waves of attackers.  Occasionally a chest will appear, guarded by more powerful mobs.  All drops are personal, meaning no one can just steal a chest from you and get all the items while you get none.  Everybody gets their own randomized drops.  There are also powerups in the game, giving you things like running speed, shooting speed, etc.
Anyways, as it stands, this game is hard to play consistently.  It's very grindy, but there are multiple maps to choose from.  Around 4-5 maps iirc.  Far from open-world, far from living/breathing, and far from completion, but a promising game worth $0.99 nonetheless.  In this state, I'd give the game a 5/10.  Enough to buy it, not enough to play it for over 100 hours yet.  If it had all the promised features, I predict an easy 8/10, and if they fix the mouse latency issue, 9/10.  Implement PvP = 10/10.

Recommending because the problems are the type that can be fixed in early access, and they aren't large enough that it's unplayable.  Well, mostly.  For example, the crafting, while playable, is effectively unplayable because of how tedious it is.  But crafting itself doesn't seem necessary so the game at large is playable in a practical way even if the crafting isn't playable.  What needs addressed:
- Game crashes easily on launch (above spec computer)
- If your objective is located gruading a "harvester", then enemies should not run away from you OR you should have a teleport to harvester option.  This happens on timed missions to kill things.  But they seem to sometimes run away and sometimes meander.  Though once you are in range they start chasing you.  It doesn't feel like the challenge is to catch them in time, it feels like wonky AI that takes you out of the immersion.  The larger problem is how tedious it is to run back to the harvester.
- Crafting menu needs LOTS of work.  It seems to be oversaturated with refinements over end results.  Categories could use work.  But probably the biggest thing is when you mouse over components, it should give you info or at least let you cross link to them by clicking on them.  It should go both ways, such that when you are on a craftable thing, it should show you what is needed to make it, and what it can be used for to make other things.  This is just information and organization.
- It's far too cnsole centric.  From minor things like a useless splash screen if you are mouse/keyboard (showing you gamepad controls on PC even if you don't have a gamepad plugged in... lots of small development games make an assumption of what control type you are using based on what you have plugged in).  To larger things like not being able to type your name into a new save game field (you click on letters with mouse / gamepad).  This larger issue makes the game feel like PC was an afterthought.  Fortunately the gameplay feels fine.  But the tedious nature of these other things is a big negative to me personally as I feel this is representative of a build philosophy that isn't in line with my play philosophy.  It's fine that these games exist, but it makes me favor those in line with my play style (and who wouldn't look for games of their play style).
- Inventory menu could use work.  Just the basic thing of highlighting the slot something you are dragging goes into.  This has been a stable of UI for a long time, and there's no advantage to removing it.

Valve decided to jump on the Terra- oh wait thats not right, let me try again.
Rusty just inherited his old man's mine upon him going missing.  Not a miner himself, he decides to take a pick-ax for himself and go tunnel down to see what happened.
There are some mystery elements for sure while traversing the underground, but ultimately the ending of this game could've done loads better with an expansion DLC or something as it feels incomplete.  The characters you meet in the Uptown are cute in their own western way, and overall just has alot of charm to it.
The character designs are great, though sadly you'll be looking at wads of dirt 90% of the game.  That isn't to say the hazards in the dirt aren't animated competently, as the textures and so on are there, but not pushed to the limit.  Given there are only 4 different zones (Uptown being one of them) there isn't alot of variety in what appears, but the enemies, or what appears of them are all different for the most part in design.
This is definitely not a stressful game by far, as you'll most likely just be digging around, collecting types of ore, heading back up and purchasing upgrades for yourself such as longer lamp lights or better pick axes.  Because of this, the action element is somewhat lacking a bit, and I felt I was going to get hit regardless when having to attack an enemy in my way due to your short range (until later abilities are acquired).  So your enjoyment of this game depends on how much of a collector/completionist you are, and how well your observation skills can be.  My honest to god main qualm about the game is the final boss being ridiculously easy compared to the rest of the game, and coupled with a lackluster ending kinda put a dampening spirit on my exploration mood.
Keyboard wise, the only awkward mechanism is having to switch between items and abilities, as I've accidentally used an item when I meant to switch it.  With that said, the controller just overall feels smoother, and gets the victory based solely on non-awkwardness but the game is completely playable on kayboard nontheless.
There is only one two main song themes while underground sadly, the rest are playing in Uptown or in finding items in a victory melody.  Otherwise you will be hearing yourself dig through dirt, and more dirt and maybe hear something shriek offscreen.  The sound is admittedly barebones for what it could've been for sure.
This is the lazy man's casual Spelunky.  The game is great for relaxation and so on, and even appeasing to the completionist in us, but it could've done with more content.  If you want a challenge, the achievements are indeed a pain in the butt and will force you to beat the game in under 3 hours which is incredible given the game is around 4-5 hours or so playing normally.

Games becoming easier over the years is an interesting discussion. Were games too hard? Were they legitimatly hard on the nes? Snes? But difficult games are not gone completely. Games like dark souls and blood bourne show people still enjoy testing their limits. If those games names make you shutter at the thought of playing them due to the difficulty then this isn't a game for you. But to me? I love this game. It's a challanging platformer and yet...I almost never felt frustrated. But to start off, here we go.
Graphics 10/10-They're very pleasing to look at. Very minimalistic and not taxing on your hardware. I enjoy the little touches like blood trails on where you walk or climb. Don't expect ground breaking, but I don't think that was the intent.
Sound 10/10- Sound tracks are good. And never really repetitive. And the death sounds are gross in the best way possible.
controls 10/10-Perfect. Period. And it needs to be. If the controls were even a little bit off, it would be unplayable due to the pin point accuracy you need to get through the game. Ironicly the controls are so perfect you will need to get used to them. There is NO delay and that may throw you off for a little bit. But I never felt like the controls messed me up.
Gameplay 9/10-I love it. But it's really hard. I cannot say this enough. You need so much practice and such great reflexes, that you may not be able to beat the game. My point is that this game isn't for everyone. But this game does make it less frustrating by respawning you when you die at once. And the levels are not long either meaning you can get back to where you died quickly. Unlimited lives as well. My only problem is the hidden levels that have lives. It seems counter intuitive to the idea of the game and doesn't seem like a good idea.But it's so rewarding when you beat a level, it just feels unmatched.
replay 10/10- Yes, this will last you a while. unlockable characters with their own abilities,hidden levels and a harder dark world to complete...you get the bang for your buck.
overall 10/10-This isn't for everyone. But with it's perfect controls, great level design, and dark sense of humor, I always had fun even when I died, a lot.

Core loop:
Go underground.
Dig through rocks/dirt.
Pick up ores that fall out.
Kill/avoid monsters.
When backpack is full, teleport back to surface.
Sell ore for money.
Immediately spend all money on equipment upgrades.
Go back underground.
Repeat 30 or 40 more times.
End game.
It's not a complex game, but it's fun and has enough going for it to keep you chugging along. A fair number of secrets to uncover. Also the underground caves that shift the gameplay focus away from digging and briefly toward segments of platforming/combat/problem-solving go a long way toward staving off mining fatigue.

Spiral Games Studios started off with a hell of a launch. They released Orion: Dino Beatdown to steam and it was recieved with a TON of negative feedback. I bought it and honestly could entirely understand why, though I still had fun with it. It eventually became Orion: Dino Horde, which was a slightly better version of beatdown. Awhile after that it became Orion: Prelude. By this point the game improved a lot. It gained a lot more content, polish, and became a really enjoyable game, as well as hit the low price of $1. The Orion Project is their next game and wow, I'm blown away. One thing, however, they do tend to market their game as what it will be, rather than what it is.
The Orion Project is a massive step up in quality. There's much more in depth mechanics, incredibly improved visuals, better animations, much better models, and impressive world design. The roadmap for this game is impressive, but I think totally believable. According to SteamDB, Orion: Prelude now has 2,000,000 owners. That's a good amount of income. They also are about to hit 100,000 with The Orion Project. Assuming David Presson and his team stay true to their promises, this game will be one hell of a thing. It's on its way to being a Destiny Esque RPG Shooter Exploration game with space travel, dogfights, dinosaurs, and more.
-----
On to the game. It plays pretty well. there's a good amount of maps, 7 classes/Guardians, 3 skill trees with varying skills depending on the class, a ton of items, a interesting and well built crafting system, and a wide variety of enemies ranging from Dinosaurs to Android robots. Each Guardian has a 50 level cap and each a unique set of weapons. It's very enjoyable to play and supports a Third Person over the shoulder view point or a Top Down Twinstick style view point. First Person View will be released in May 2016 as well as quests and I'm sure a lot of other content. The game is planned to be supported with monthly updates and so far they have delivered. My first time playing I ended up playing for 8 hours straight and I've been addicted to the game since. It has a social aspect, where players are placed on an orbital command station in a lobby with a bunch of other players. Here you can check the leaderboards, stats, access the store, and party up with players.
Currently there are two gameplay modes, Harvest and Survival. Harvest is a 10 wave survival-like mode where you follow and defend a harvester collection Ion crystals, the main currency. Every few waves there is a side objective consisting of harder enemies and bosses with loot chests as a reward. Survival is similar to Harvest, except the harvester is in a static location and the waves are endless. Survival has a lower Augment (equipment) drop rate and no loot chests, but is great for experience, testing skill, and competing in the leaderboards.
The Orion Project does have some short comings, though. A great example is the never failing sequence of freezes when you first get the game. To play online, you are required to make an account which is very easy to set up and requires no activation. However, during the first launch you will end up in a infinite loading screen which you must close. The second launch, when you attempt to sign in it will infinitely attempt to sign in and must close. The third launch works 90% of the time, though, and you'll be able to play.
Some players report having massive stuttering during game and freezes. For some, this has just gone away, others cannot find a fix and so far have not recieved any attention from the developers. This bug seems to be for a minority, though.
Occasionally after signing in you will get kicked to the menu, sometimes multiple times, sometimes enough to not be able to play. Most of the time this will go away on its own and I assume it's issues with their servers. There is also a chance of being kicked to the menu when you try and launch the game.
----
Do I recommend this game? Short answer, Yes. The game in its current state is buggy, could use optimization, and may require some patience. However, it is fun as hell. It has enough content to keep you going for awhile and is a great game for coop with friends or even randoms. I usually don't enjoy being paired with random players in coop games but this one is an exception. I highly recommend this game if you are fine with experiencing some bugs and setbacks and want a really enjoyable shooter with in depth loot and crafting mechanics and/or want to support development and see this game grow. I don't reccomend this game in its current state if you have a low end machine (needs optimization), don't like dealing with any bugs (which is common in many Early Access games), or don't enjoy cooperative shooters.

Review:
An almost perfect game, especially if your looking for a game like the classic XCOM.  Unfortunatly there are not really any others these days so this game definitely fills the void.  Yeah it has some problems and a few glitches here and there such as an alien, rarely, being able to get that shot off through a wall killing a guy but with the same line of sight back you cant shoot them.  It is rare but it does happen.
The main difference between this game and the classic XCOM is that Xenonauts uses a 2D system rather than the 3D one XCOM: Ufo Defense had.  This has its limitations and is probably the biggest gripe I have with this game because it makes the line of sight issues, among other things.  It calculates the chance of hit, does the math, and then either hits or misses the target while cover dramatically reduces that chance.  This is opposed to XCOM's 3D engine where it instead used a complex calculation with the accuracy taken into account and calculated a trajectory of the bullet and whatever it hit it hit, whether it be a guy way off the side of the target, hitting the guy behind the target, or just flying off the map.  It was much more fun that way, with this game their system is ok but definitely a step back.  On the bright side I hear Goldhawk is using a 3D engine for their sequel so hopefully the next game is going to be the true successor to this genre.
Pros:
+Great Graphics (for the style they are going for)
+Air battles are intense
+Streamlined management (you still have to manufacture all the weapons besides the base ones, armour, planes, ect. except the ammo)
+Loadouts. You still have to account for how much ammo you bring, grenades, and everything of that nature with penalties if you bring too much.
+Soldiers are now much easier to track (very powerful feature, something XCOM lacked in and you'll understand why when you play it)
+Tons of tech
+Cover mechanics are great but again I just wish it was a 3D engine
+Has room for alot of strategy and different methods of play
+Great community and many mods to change your experience
Cons:
-2D engine which accounts for most of the issues people have with line of sight and accuracy.  It isn't bad but the 3D engine would have been 100x better.  This is my biggest gripe with the game and is mainly the reason I feel the game isn't perfect (otherwise it would have been!)
-Most other negative issues relate to the 2D issue such as not being able to through granades over walls, shoot someone in the air if their is a wall in the way, and other annoying little things like that.
-Usually each map will have only 1 race of alien, sometimes 2 if they are similar, such as both being robotic for instance.  Theres a mod that changes that but thought it was worth mentioning.
Last Thoughts:
Personally I did not mind that my dudes would usually get 1-2 shotted as it adds to the difficulty, and for me the realism.  I can't immagine someone would take a few shots from a plasma gun, especially at close range, and keep chugging through like nothing happened. I want to start by saying that I recommend this game because of one of my favorite sayings, "No harm, no foul". It's free and it works, so at least give it a try...
Having said that, let's get down to the real discussion.
If you are looking for something new but familiar to play, get this!
If you want something fun to play with friends, get this!
If you need something sort of laid back and not too dificult to pick up and learn (which is kind of a negative when it comes to a survival game...), get this!
It has a familiar feel to it, especially if you have played any sort of survival game before.
As far as I can tell, it is still being developed and worked on, so it has not been abandoned (yet).
Additionally, it feels as though there is a lot that has not been implemented yet, so there is room for new and interesting additions in future patches and updates.
With a large map and persistant worlds, you can spend countless, fun hours exploring, liberating, looting, and building.
I must say, it has definitely satisfied my pre-Fallout4 looting addiction! Especially since everything you pick up is useful!
However,
If you are looking for a well done zombie survival game, this is not it...
If you are looking for a new masterpiece of a game to play, this is not it...
This game is shoddy at best. It appears as though they did not put a terrible amount of concern and effort into the basics of the game.
The zombies are not very threatening, either visually or physically (unless you are swarmed or in a tight spot).
They do not roam, they do not move in groups, and they rarely exhibit idle animations (really...?).
The source code must be far from optimal, as I have had it crash several times from massive resource consumption...
When you first play, you really should only be concerned for food, drink, and blueprints, as you cannot do anything useful with other resources until you have blueprints, which are rather difficult to find.
Combat with zombies is a joke. You can melee a zombie from a safe distance, without worrying about getting hit.
All in all, the game can be enjoyable and is worth the download, but if you were looking to have a challenging zombie survival game, you will be let down.

LEGO Batman 2 was originally supposed to bring together the two most popular and successful DC superheroes in a spectacular team-up. Unfortunately Scooby-Doo was unavailable due to legal complications and was replaced by Superman. The odd couple of the DC Universe, Batman-Superman is one of the most oxymoronic superhero team-ups ever, after all, one of them is powerful, smart, and amazing, a veritable god amongst men, and the other one's Superman.
The reason this team-up works is because Batman makes up for all the weaknesses of Superman. For example, Superman has a fatal allergy to Kryptonite, an ultra-rare substance that can only be found in supervillain gift shops and sometimes on eBay. Superman is also hyper gluten-intolerant and can be killed by a well thrown muffin. Fortunately, none of the supervillains know this. Batman of course has no weaknesses. He's only slightly vulnerable to guns and knives. And sharp sticks and heavy rocks.
Everyone thinks Batman wears Kryptonite underpants because Superman is a dirty alien and Batman doesn't trust him. This isn't true. He does it to protect the self-esteem of his friend. If Superman was foolish enough to use his X-Ray vision to check out the size of Batman's package he would be totally embarrassed by his own inadequacy and probably fly off into the Phantom Zone in shame, never to return.
The reason why recalcitrant loner Batman is so awesome, is because of his tragic past. Born as Bruce Wayne, his parents were wealthy billionaire philanthropists who made regular fully tax-deductible donations to charity via their anonymous Panama trust fund. As founders of the "Wayne Foundation for Kids Who Can't Read Good And Wanna Do Other Stuff Good Too," they were also extremely humble and modest. They even built the tallest skyscraper in Gotham and named it Wayne Towers to remind everyone how humble and modest they were. Sadly they were murdered in a botched robbery when Bruce was very young. As to why two wealthy individuals would want to rob a homeless peripatetic hobo remains a mystery to this day.
Instead of wallowing in self-pity and turning to hookers and cocaine, young Bruce became obsessed with vigilantism and justice. However he had a strict credo against killing and felt that all criminals could be reformed, even the hardened psychotic ones. A policy he no doubt stole from the Greens. One day after attending PAX, he had an epiphany. Perhaps he could reform criminals by scaring them straight. He also realised that what really terrified people to the core of their souls was bad cosplay. However, becoming obese and dressing as Lara Croft was not a realistic option. Dressing as a bat was the next best thing.
Because Superman wants to be more like Batman, he also conveniently has a tragic past. His real name is Kal-Fail and although raised by humans, he is really an alien from the planet Krapton. The Kraptonians were a highly intelligent and advanced race that somehow managed to blow up their own planet in an event known as the "Great Fuster Cluck". Superman named his alter-ego Cluck Fuster Kent in memory of this event. Superman's real dad Kal-Zone tried to warn everyone but nobody trusted him because he looked like choleric phone-throwing New Zealander Russell Crowe. Superman only survived the catastrophe because his parents were ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. They really hated him and sent him on a one-way trip to Earth, one of the worst places in the universe. Even episodes of Hanna Montana didn't deter them from this lunacy.
Coincidentally Kraptonians look identical to humans which was fortuitous for Superman and the budget of every Superman movie ever made. Growing up in Kansas, Superman fights for Truth, Justice and The American Way. Enigmatically, Superman doesn't explain what The American Way means except perhaps hinting that it's orthogonal to Truth and Justice, but it probably involves eating copious amounts of
. Fortunately for Superman, he derives all his sustenance from sunlight which is not only fat free but gluten-free and approved by the Heart Foundation.
Naturally Batman and Superman don't always work alone, but are part of a crime-fighting bowling club named the Justice League. All members of the Justice League have wonderful powers that rival even those of Superman (but not Batman). Fortunately for fans, some of the more notable members of the Justice League like Flash, Wonder Woman, Green Lantern, Cyborg and Martian Manhater become playable characters towards the end of the game.
Flash, also known as "The Fastest Man Alive," gets his superpowers and reputation from being very fast. Testimonials from his numerous disgruntled ex-girlfriends confirm that he's entirely deserving of his unflattering sobriquet. Nobody is sure exactly how he uses this talent for crime-fighting, and nobody really wants to know, but it works.
Wonder Woman is named after the enchanted Wonder Bra that she wears. It has the uncanny power to hypnotise men sending them into a vacuous drooling stupor. Also voted the "#1 Superhero I want to be caught by" in
five years running.
Green Lantern derives his power from bad poetry. Before he fights, he recites a poem about the brightest day and the darkest night, the birds and the bees, and what not. While his opponent is trying to work out whether it's some kind of magic haiku or maybe a clever pickup line, he runs up and kicks them in the bread basket. It's a technique so effective it's been used by the Guardians of the Universe to keep the peace for thousands of years.
Cyborg as his name implies, is half-man and half-machine, deriving his superpowers from an accident involving superglue and a washing machine. Now all he wants to do is clean up crime. Just don't ask him where his USB port is.
Martian Manhater is possibly the most controversial member of the Justice League. A feminist alien cougar from Mars, also sometimes known as Left-Wing Liberal Chick, she gets her superpowers from getting people all riled up over gender inequality.
LEGO Batman 2 is a vast improvement over LEGO Batman, with better visuals and dynamic split screen for co-op mode. The plot is your typical buddy superhero melodrama spiced with irreverent comedy. Humourous banter during cutscenes accentuate the friendly rivalry between Batman and Superman, playing the slightly dysfunctional but successful relationship to good effect. The addition of voice acting also greatly enhances the storytelling with Batman voiced competently by Troy Baker instead of the inimitable Kevin Conroy.
The most significant enhancement to gameplay is the open-world LEGO rendition of Gotham City that is impressive in both scope and detail. The entire city is quite large, even containing a zoo, and an amusement park with working rides. Although there are fast travel points to expedite travel, it's definitely more fun to walk, drive or fly. Unlike it's squeaky clean counterpart Metropolis, Gotham is a dark gritty city, ensnared in a preternatural perpetual twilight. Supervillain henchmen prowl the streets waiting for vigilante justice to be meted out upon them, and the city itself is replete with puzzles and challenges to complete.
As with the prequel, this game is better with a co-op partner than solo. I had the opportunity to test this with a 4-year old co-op partner whose favourite activity is flying around Gotham as Superman; even though I helpfully suggested many times that Batman is a far better character. Having completed the game to 100%, LEGO Batman 2 is definitely bigger, longer and better than it's predecessor, and gets another two thumbs up from Batman and jaywalking Robin.

Even though this game is technically unfinished right now, I'd say (having played 40 hours of NMS) it's already much better than No Man's Sky.
How is it like NMS? It's got a vibrant aesthetic and crafting and resource gathering across different worlds.
How is it different? Astroneer's art style and animations make for a more pleasing and charming visual experience than NMS. It also runs much better than NMS and the controls are more responsive. The crafting is not tedious and inventory management is, dare I say, fun? Which is a complete departure from No Man's Sky's resource gathering loop which became rote and monotonous and just no fun very quickly. Astroneer also has a good variety of vehicles and things you create with different resources you can find around the world, even now, while it is still in alpha (or is it pre-alpha?).
One thing that's very cool is the power and oxygen system. You might think limiting the player's oxygen supply and power supply (which supports terraforming and collecting resorces) would induce a sort of constant range anxiety. However, I think that making de facto roads with tethers (which supply you with oxygen) and making oxygen tanks out of very rare titanium is a core component of the game that I personally found very rewarding. The progression you can see in the paths you've taken, marked by tethers, and the oxygen tanks and power cells you carry with you on your pack was enough to keep me playing at least for the first 3 hours or so.
Beyond the novelty and awe of the first 3 hours though, building advanced parts for rovers and spaceships has kept me going so far, and I think I'll enjoy this game for at least another 5 or so hours (not that I'm only valuing my experinece with this game through the amount of time it kills). Also,  I have only really explored the first planet and a bit of the moon and one other planet, so there is much more for me to see and build.
The music of the game is pretty chill, it definitely adds to the soothing overall aesthetic.
I haven't played any multiplayer yet, but I anticipate it will only make the game more enjoyable.
As for bugs, I've gotten stuck momentarily a couple of times and I've fallen through the ground when a large object seemed to push me through it. I haven't encountered any actually significant or game-breaking bugs, however, and performance has been quite smooth on my admittedly powerful PC (i7-4790K, GTX 970).
If you're looking for a fun and relaxing game with a great art style to play alone or with friends, look no further.

However, here is a fantastic Deep Dark Chocolate Cake Recipe;
Ingredients:
2 cups granulated sugar (500 mL)
1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour (425 mL)
3/4 cup HERSHEY'S Cocoa (175 mL)
1 1/2 tsp baking powder (7 mL)
1 1/2 tsp baking soda (7 mL)
1 tsp salt (5 mL)
2 eggs (2)
1 cup milk (250 mL)
1/2 cup vegetable oil (125 mL)
2 tsp vanilla extract (10 mL)
1 cup boiling water (250 mL)
BUTTERCREAM FROSTING
6 tbsp butter or margarine, softened (90 mL)
2 2/3 cups icing sugar (650 mL)
1/2 cup HERSHEY'S Cocoa (125 mL)
1/3 cup milk (75 mL)
1 tsp vanilla extract (5 mL)
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 350°F (180°C). Grease and flour two 9-inch (1.5 L) round baking pans or one 9 x 13-inch (3.5 L) baking pan.
2. Stir sugar with flour, cocoa, baking powder, baking soda and salt in a large bowl. Add eggs, milk, oil and vanilla. Beat with an electric mixer, on medium speed, for 2 minutes. Stir in boiling water (batter will be thin). Divide batter evenly between prepared pans.
3. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes for the round pans (35 to 40 minutes for the large pan) or until a wooden pick inserted in the centre comes out clean. Cool for 10 minutes on a rack. Turn cakes out from pans; cool completely. (Sheet cake may be left in pan if desired.) Makes 8 to 10 servings.
4. Buttercream Frosting: Beat butter in medium bowl. Combine the icing sugar with the cocoa. Alternately add the icing sugar mixture and the milk to the butter, until a spreadable consistency is reached (additional milk may be required to reach preferred consistency). Stir in vanilla. Frost cooled cake.
Makes about 2 cups (500 mL) of frosting.
