This game feels a lot like XCOM: EU where all they did was remove the best parts of the game but this time they did it even worse. The only thing great about this game is the workshop, because the vanilla game is actually pretty bad.
You see, what made you invested in the tactical part of the game was the alien loot you could grab when you finished the mission. From there you could continue your research, or if you were low on funds, sell it to foreign powers. That was the best part of the game, manufacturing weapons, and then selling them to the governments of the world. It allowed you to continue funding science projects, and recruit staff had the odds swung against you. Sometimes you couldn't get enough missions or things didn't turn out right, and a few nations stop funding your project.
That was removed, and from what it seems, the political aspect as well. You aren't trying to convince the governments of the world that your project can work. You seem to just get a set amount of income each year, I don't know who funds us, or why, we just get money.
Well, I can take a good challenge, tough aliens, and the great level design the game throws at me. But the most disgusting part of the game is aiming. This game takes XCOM's difficulty over the top. While yes, enemies did cheat a bit, but there were few times when they could shoot through walls. But the game's difficulty doesn't come from enemy health, uniqueness, or powers or even intelligence. No. The game's difficulty comes from your soldier's ability to aim, alone. I find it hard to be invested at all in this game, with the ability to sell loot, manufacture items, or attempting to convince the UN that the xcom project works. I find it even harder to invest myself when soldiers shoot like idiots.
You can have 1 alien surrounded by four soldiers, and have ALL of them miss. You can have the odds in your favor, the perfect LOS, and miss. What? You don't think it's that bad? "It might not be that bad, I'll give it a go" Let me give an example of how BAD a soldier's aim is:
There was an alien in a ship, the door destroyed by my rocket launcher. I took my heavy weapons soldier, told her to fire at the alien inside of the ship. You know what she does? SHE TURNS AROUND AND SHOOTS THE SOLDIER NEXT TO HER. SHE UNLOADS ON THIS POOR ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LIKE SHE WAS INJECTED WITH ADAMANTIUM RAGE. KILLING HIM INSTANTLY.
This game has so much potential, but it's like the developers thought the only way to make aliens any kind of threat was to nerf your soldier's aim. Down to the point where they couldn't even shoot an alien that's in a square next to them. Stuff like this NEVER happened in xcom, in xcom YOU'D HIT! But you were never sure if you were going to KILL!
Also, the morale in this game feels so screwed up! Your soldiers would take one hit, and then immediately go beserk? The last time I played xcom, your soldiers would only go beserk if someone DIED. In fact, beserking soldiers were actually pretty rare if you kept everyone alive. And even if I'm wrong on this, they should fix it, soldiers should not beserk or panic after getting hit once.
This game is frustrating but I feel like the workshop fixes some of it's problems.

Additionally, if you hit 4000-5000 gold, money will no longer have value since you can buy pretty much everything.
I'm looking forward to further expansions of the world map, proper end-game content, and a use for all my hard-earned cash.

When 90% of your game is based on the strength of its controls, it's a shame when said controls are terrible.
I love the fact that I get to control a snake, and I love the fact that the stages are mostly simple skill-based obstacle courses, littered with collectibles that mean absolutely nothing other than "look at me I'm such a tryhard". The levels and obstacles are decently designed, and the graphics and music are sufficiently okay for a game of this kind.
And then, there are the controls. If you're wondering how on Earth you're supposed to control a snake in a 3D environment with keyboard and mouse, the developers almost got the right idea. You hold the left mouse button to slither forward and use WASD to control the direction. On paper, it seems good enough, but within thirty minutes of playing this, I was convinced that this game NEEDED tank controls. Within one hour, I was dying to quit the game and go play the original Alone in the Dark. Press left to turn left, press right to turn right. What could be more simple? But no, tank controls apparently are the Unholy Spawn of Satan and it should be avoided like the plague (especially where it would make the most sense)(. But I admit, having WASD controls wouldn't necessarily be a bad idea if the camera were good, and he camera is, by far, the worst aspect of this entire game. It gets blocked in places where it physically shouldn't (if there's a pillar between you and the camera, you can't spin the camera on the outside of the pillar to get a good view of the level; instead, the camera will suddenly zoom in and you can't see anything), your sight gets blocked by scenery, the camera moves on its own even though you control it with the mouse, it spazzes out when you're in tight places and forces you to make involuntary U-turns and go back to where you were coming from, and so on. Seriously, the camera is a mess, and the fact that your movement is entirely dependent on the camera angle makes the whole control scheme come crashing down. I'd press the directional button to move the snake in one direction, only to see it spinning like an idiot in the opposite direction and fall of the pole I'm trying to hold on to. And if your answer is "duh, just adjust the camera!", you obviously don't know the camera in this game.
Oh, and did I mention this game seriously lag? I'm sorry, but I can't admit sub-20FPS precarious in a game that can't possibly be more detailed and complex than Skyrim or Arkham City. The optimisation is terrible, and that makes the camera control even worse.
I suppose I could spend some more hours mastering the finely and precisely SCREWED UP camera control, but honestly, what's the point? It'd be more fun, not to mention easier, to physically transform myself into a snake and beat these levels in the real world, spikes and endless abysses and all. And if I want to struggle against a dysfunctional, uncooperative camera, I can always go back to Super Mario 64. At least the collectibles had a point in that game.
I can't recommend this at all. With controls as broken as these, any notion of fun completely vanishes. If that is your cup of tea, though, try something safer and less frustrating, such as driving a car without a steering wheel.

About as close as you will get to the original XCOM experience.  Although the graphics are lackluster, this game has all of the elements that made XCOM such a memorable game.  It also includes common sense improvements and minor embellishments that add to the theme without deviating too much.
Just like the original, you will find yourself gripping the arms of your chair as you find out whether that last shot you fired will kill the alien that is about to throw a grenade that will incapacitate half of your team. You will sacrifice squad members to capture alien leaders for interrogation.  You will make the hard decision to let a city or two be terrorized to better utilize your resources elsewhere.
The bottom line is that this is simply a much better game than the much praised official XCOM remake.  Fires, night missions, base invasions, terrain destruction, and most importantly:  a sense of dread as you barely hold off waves of alien infestation.  Highly recommended.

Sooo, I am currently limited to a weak tablet as only means of computing power and decided to give this game a try, seeing it's requirements were rather humane and the screenshots looked neat. Handdrawn graphics, classic turnbased action. Seemed nice enough.
What I got from that was absolutely amazing. This game managed to pull me in entirely and made me go through hours, making progress and playing to see what it might pull out next. The handdrawn nature made the absolute best out of this. Detailed depictions of the autopsies, backgrounds for the sections of your base that look like a masterpiece each and change over the time as you develop new technology. It really proves that great graphical experience has nothing to do with a powerful GPU.
The narrative style of the game and lots of lore that come with it only increase the experience and keeps you going on, wanting to see the next artwork and the self loving speech of your chief scientist as he tells in his eccentric way of mixing imperial and metric systems what he developed this time.
Gameplay wise there is nothing too revolutionary, the game relying on what had been proven good on the early XCOM games and making you wonder why so much was lost in Enemy Unknown. It's a good strategic experience that challenges your mind at times but doesnt frustrate you or make you desperate to a point that you toss away the game.
I definitely recommend this to fans of Xcom and the genre in general, a good experience for casual players and more experienced alike and a pleasure to look at.

For a supposedly tactical game, half your success on missions comes down to "not failing your save against psionic enemies with unlimited range and no line of sight required". I think that one of the best ways to define Xenonauts is as a "spiritual remake" of X-Com: UFO Defense. By that I mean that the developers attempted to recreate the original X-Com as faithfully as possible (while at the same time improving on the classic's flaws) but had to use a different setting, considering they don't own the rights to the X-Com franchise (hence the "spiritual" aspect). What is the result of said remake? Simply put, the best X-Com game that I have ever played. Xenonauts succeeds admirably at perfecting the formula that made the original game a timeless classic, and while it does have a few flaws, it is nonetheless a fantastic turn-based strategy game. It also brings forth a very nice artistic design, and streamlines the original's cumbersome UI, thus successfully bringing the original concept into the modern era of gaming.
In Xenonauts, you act as the commander of the titular organization tasked with defending the Earth against an alien invasion set in a Cold War-era setting. The game is divided into three separate components: a real-time administration simulation with 4X and sandbox elements where you manage the bases of your organization (assigning all kinds of tasks such as research, manufacturing of equipment, and building of annexes) and monitor for UFO activity in a map of Earth; a real-time with pause minigame where you engage UFOs with your interceptor aircraft; and a turn-based strategy component where the actual combat against the aliens happens. This last mode is where the meat of every X-Com game lays, and in the case of Xenonauts, I'm happy to state that said combat missions are every bit as challenging, tense and satisfactory as they were in X-Com: UFO Defense. Furthermore, the turn-based combat has been largely improved from the original, featuring more deep, complex mechanics, a wider array of weaponry and artifacts, and a healthy dose of streamlining where it was needed.
You have to keep in mind that this is a very challenging and difficult game. Every choice you make has consequences, and actions are irreversible. Furthermore, if you play on Ironman (a mode which I recommend activating from your very first playthrough, as these kind of games are clearly designed to work that way) you will not be able to reverse to a previous save state. You'll have to learn to go on with your choices, both good and bad, and I can't emphasize how fulfilling it is to achieve victory in these conditions. Remember though that if one of your soldiers dies, they're gone. Forever.
A rather notorious addition that Xenonauts made to the X-Com formula is the air combat. As I mentioned earlier, this is a real-time with pause minigame where you direct your aircraft against the UFOs in a radar-like interface, trying to maximize the damage you deal to them while avoiding their deadly attacks as much as possible. While I think this mode is far from perfect, as many times I felt it was a bit shallow, it is nonetheless a huge leap from UFO Defense's barebones interception system, and I think it succeeds in getting the job done.
The only real complaint I have with Xenonauts is with the way that psionic attacks works. This was a huge flaw in the original X-Com, as psionic abilities were hugely overpowered. In Xenonauts, they tried to fix this by making psionics unavailable to humans and making it a bit less powerful in aliens. Unfortunately, the result is that many times you feel completely powerless against psionic attacks, as there's no research that allows to counter it (something like the Mind Shields in XCOM: Enemy Unknown would have helped a lot in making it a fairer mechanic). Still, it's not a game breaking flaw, and the game it's still an excellent one even with the annoyance it poses.
At the end of the day, I don't see any reason not to recommend this game to everyone interested in a deep, complex, and tactical experience. For classic X-Com fans, this is a no-brainer, and for newcomers the lower difficulties are forgiving enough to make learning the basics of the game a smooth experience (keep Ironman mode activated though, that's the way to play this, in my opinion). Go for it.

Read if you want a fair review! (Remember at this time Aftermath is 3 days old, right out of the beta stage so you can still expect problems!)
First of all Steam needs to get rid of this "User Reviews" crap...Make it more professional, I see this with so many games not just Aftermath but if you look at the negative reviews of this game almost everyone is 1 hour or less. How can you even say yay or nay with that little time played! Also there are some people that don't read and the game cant be played due to requirements, OS, etc. Its completely ridiculous, it really is...But here is my review for Aftermath.
Brief Reviews for each Section OR Upfront Score (For those lazy people that dont read lol)
1.) Gameplay - 6.5/10
From the very beginning this game is very easy to get into. Main Menu is simple enough that theres no problems to be had. Once you spawn into the world your home free, the map/world itself is vast and different landscape throughout it (Desert, Urban Areas, Farms, Etc.). Using the UI is pretty straight forward also whether it's crafting items with different materials or selecting what melee weapon to use from your inventory. The AI (Zombies) unfortuately is lacking alittle bit of "juice" but for the most part it works and doesnt take away from the completely Aftermath experience. PVP is a big part of the game also, you can group up with others or go lone wolf and hope your good but each are just as fun as the other. To be honest there is a few things that could be improved such as something simple that when your weapon breaks it should tell you and your not wondering wtf is going on or trying to group up with others, only reason I know is Ive been in alpha and beta. The past few things listed is the only reason i dropped Gameplay from atleast a 8.5/9 to a 6.5
2.) Graphics and Sound - 7.5/10
So the graphics of this game is great. Ive read a few reviews saying graphics are bad or fps is bad, in my experience I think thats a load of crap (Ill explain later)... Like stated above the environment of this world is just amazing theres so much lush grass, weeds, flowers, and forest in some places or great looking deserts with tumbleweeds, rocks, etc. The layouts of different areas are setup really good also such as junk yards, oil plants, cities, and other places along with how they look (resolutions and textures) are great. I have not experienced any FPS (Framerate) issues while playing (NOTE: This is for alpha, beta, and Steam release), lowest Ive noticed was around 28 give or take and there was ALOT going on around me (PVP battles, zombies everywhere, and looting) and a maximium of around 60+ FPS. My PC specs are on my profile page if needed but for thoses that are having FPS problems its not always the game/Devs fault, accept your PC could be the problem. Even my PC has problems and I have thrown atleast 3k into it. Now onto the sounds of the game. Unfortuately this doesnt hold up as good as the graphics part. Now there are some just really good audio files and sounds throughout the game and some that are just weird or unnecessary. Good sounds - Birds, Wildlife, Environmental Sounds... Bad Sounds - Same Zombie sound imported from Infestation, Walking Sounds (Too Loud) But overall this section is the high point of the game even compared to H1Z1, Rust, and DayZ it looks really good and has its ups and downs with the Audio of the game.
3.) Challenge and Fun - 7/10
For the most part Aftermath is a fun and great game to play but it still lacks also... Throughout the gameplay of Aftermath main goal is to rebuild, survive, and loot. Simple Enough? eh yes and no. While the actual looting is easy and straight forward its not all that rewarding, not saying its bad just missing a little something. But as you obtain different loot you can craft TONS of diffferent items (Food, Survival Items, Guns and Ammo, Etc.) or on the other hand use the loot to build you (and your team) a base or shelter. From there you can even make it your "safezone" or use it as a new spawn point for you and your group/clan. This part is actually pretty badass compared to other base builders Aftermath is on point with constructing bases. Now the so called "Fun" of this game is both good and bad but its more of a bitter sweet thing, such as PVP. PVP in this game is just amazing if your blood doesnt start pumping your doing something wrong but you get that sweet, prideful feeling when you kill another player and even better when the loot bag is FULL of goodies or on the other hand your that guy that got killed and you say screw this game and get off lol its happened to me I know. But for the most part the fun and challenge of this game is pair not bad but not good.
OVERALL SCORE - 7/10 (GOOD)
PROS -
- Its FREE!
- Good Graphics
- Fun Co-op or Single Player Game
- Great Crafting System
CONS -
- Awkward or Unnecessary Sounds
- Zombies arent much of an enemy
- Its a newer game (Updates Will Follow)

This is a horror game that happens to be in the first-person. While the atmosphere and sounds are intense (if you turn off the god-awful music), I didn't find any story or narrative to draw me deeper into the game while I played. Also, it's not actually scary - and I'm a wimp when it comes to horror games.
Graphically, it's nothing impressive, but the lighting and environments get the job done.
As for the gameplay, I found it slow and clunky. Your character moves slowly, swings melee weapons slowly, and gets tired after 2-3 swings. Despite this, the game has no sense of urgency or danger because the zombies move at a snail's pace and are dispatched with ease.
Pros:
- Sounds and lighting create an atmosphere that can suck you into the game
Cons:
- Terrible music
- Slow gameplay
- Not actually scary
- No story to draw you in
Overall:
Not recommended. The gameplay isn't enjoyable and there are plenty of games with better atmosphere and gameplay.

Day 1 hour 2: Slightly disturbed by pink slimes hopping desperately to get chickens. Built walls higher. Ventured into the wilderness.
Day 2: Made a sizeable profit wandering about collecting slime poop. Admired the shiny golden hue of spontaneously appearing phosphor slimes. Admired how much their poop went for on the open market. Decided to take some home.
Day 3: Phosophor slimes spontaneously combust in broad daylight. Goal of raising free range phosophor slimes put on hold while I quarantine the next batch in my primary vacpack slot.
Day 4: Mildly annoyed by rock slimes spin-dashing me in the face like little blue Sonic-spawn. They ignore the copious amounts of fruit I'm throwing at them for some mildly disturbing displays of coprophilia. They swell into giant pink Amy the hedgehogs and beat my face into my own♥♥♥♥♥harder than Amy's hammer swing. Officially done with Sonic metaphors.
Day 4 hour 16: Run from killer pink/rock hybrids. Find a valley of adorable kitten slimes. Pick one up. Get booped in the face. Kind of cute. Watch in bemusement as they proceed to chase down and devour a family of chickens, leaving behind even more valuable droppings. Pink slimes, as they are wont to do, eat everything including kitten poop. Turn into giant pink kittens. Remain sweet and adorable... until night falls... phosphor slimes gather and I vacuum up several for safe-keeping. Pink/kitten hybrids proceed to eat the valuable phosphor poo before I can grab it, transform into swirling rainbows and muck. Eat everything in sight. Seem to prefer the taste of me.
...I run for my life ignoring the squeals of horror and ghosts of the dead...
Day 5: Notice a slight dip in the price of pink poop. Also find my chickens may be suffering from PTSD. I discard pink slimes and gather some purebred vegetarian rock slimes instead. The chickens seem happy. I persist only mildly bruised.
Day 6: Expand the farm and dump colony of phosphor slimes into it. They seem pretty happy, all things considered. I decide I may need to feather my nest egg and start stocking up on kitten poop. As usual, night ends battling a rapidly growing army of black tar trying to eat me. Could throw them into the ocean, but far more enjoyable to shoot them in the face like a ghostbuster.
Experiment with breeding slimes for higher production value. Settle on kitten/rock hybrids. Can't tell whether they want to boop me or kill me. Just in case, lock the first subject in a cage on auto-feeder/auto-poop-harvest and watch it make me money.
Day 8: Purchase expansion pre-loaded with native chickens and fill it with kitten slimes. Free range kitten poop dreams achieved. Quietly ignore the plaintive cries of free range chickens slaughtered by free-range gelatinous carnivores. Perhaps for this reason I have gone 8 in-game days without in-game sleep. I fear the in-game nightmares awaiting me.
Day 11: Learn to ignore the startled cries of dying chickens. Turn my face away just so from the bouncing kitten/rock hybrids rattling about in their plasma cage. Is this what I got into slime ranching for? What would Slime God think of my slime breeding ways? Gather up a new stock of fresh chickens to throw into the kitten slime pit. Try to talk myself into moral legitimacy by claiming it's just nature.
...And yet, nature creates tars...
Day 12: Race deep into the jungle to gather new breeds of slime. Valuable. Profitable. And yet, dangerous. Rebuild the farm to contain, capture, and control. Convince myself I'm preserving them for posterity... just like the chickens. Just like the chickens. I load an auto-feeder full of them into a box made of light and pain so I don't get blasted into gibs by the boom slimes.
It's for science, I think. It's for the good of humanity. The galaxy. It's to preserve them from the inevitable entropy of their own uncontrollable hungers, the endless cycle of slime, tar, death.
Oh, Slime God, if slimes even HAVE gods, what am I doing...?
Day 13: I empty all of my cages. Send the carnivores back into their homes. Let the free-range chickens be free. I WILL do better than this. Because I AM better than this. Also, honey poop is ridiculously valuable and those dudes eat fruit.
Day 14: My kitten slime friends have all hybridized into kitten/pink largos. They still try to boop me when they see me. I load a vac canister with water from a fresh spring, partly to feed the puddle slimes back home, partly for the inevitable entropy of a nighttime walk, a sudden surge of phosphor slimes, and their poop just waiting for my former kitten slime friends to nibble on.
It was them or the chickens. I can be a sanctuary of civilization in the Far Range, but I can't save the world. Not without selling a lot more poop.

Xenonauts is a quite fun turn-based strategy, closely similar to XCOM.
++The A.I. is very smart on higer difficulties.
++Nice 2.5D eye-pleasing graphics.
++Absolutely no P2W.
+Detailed air combat: Control your planes. Ability to disallow use of certain weapons, too.
+Excellent cover system, akin to XCOM.
+It's the Cold War: You won't have advanced weapons. This is true in Xenonauts, as you start with quite weak 1960's era weapons.
+Weapon technology: Once you get more advanced, you get better weapons.
+Amazing autopsy system: You can see the insides of every alien, robot and organic, and even study them.
+Amazing research trees. In-depth research trees with about 100 projects to research.
+True-to-the biome maps: Artic tileset on Artic biomes, Desert tileset on Desert biomes, etc.
+Cold War airplanes, and more: As you get more advanced, your planes get more advanced, too.
+/-The A.I. is quite dumb on Easy-Normal difficulty.
-Sometimes-dumb plane AI. I had a plane circle a Corvette, not firing its' torpedos.
-Crashes: The game will sometimes crash when you start a mission.
Conclusion: This is my first detailed review, and I hope it's good. I cannot give enough praise for this game: it is absolutely brilliant. In my opinion, it is DEFINENTALLY worth the 24.99$.
Final Rating: 9.8/10.

Be careful what you wish for. Xenonauts is a detailed re-invention of PC classic X-Com, which was difficult in the masochistic way gamers seem to love these days.
Xenonauts also dispenses with tutorials about core game functions and mechanics. It's a complex game, and unforgiving of the slightest mistake. If that sounds appealing to you, dig in. Personally, I found it similar to those "Tough Mudder" "fun" runs. I get why some people enjoy it, but I think it's ridiculous.
As a hardcore fan of the original X-com, and a fan of Firaxis' remake, I find Xenonauts tough to enjoy. Maybe I'm spoiled with "fun" gameplay, intuitive controls, and being able to play a game without reading a Wiki for hours first. But having a starting soldier equipped with "default" gear he lacked sufficient Time Units to fire, one of my jets shot down on the first UFO, and my first squad fully wiped on 3 starting playthroughs didn't make me say "wow, this is great". It made me want to do just about anything else.

A very faithful update of the original X-COM.  It is a perfect complement to Firaxis' offering, giving new gamers a glimpse of what so enamored us so long ago and inspired Firaxis' fine game.  It takes what was before and adds reasonable and intelligent decisions to improve the original design while keeping true to the original formula.  It is a tense, and quite difficult game, enjoy.

I'm fairly returning player to the fighting games genre, playing daily for an hour or 3. I've been told that Guilty Gear games have a great tutorial that makes everything pale in comparison.
They weren't joking.
Yes, I'm aware that this review for now is going to be me gushing over the tutorial mode, but I wasn't expecting to be that basic and engaging at the same time. For example, you navigate from the left side of the screen to the right as you dodge traps on the ground and floating flames. To learn combos you get monsters that have comic-book style clouds that have a letter inside that corresponds to the button you need to press next (Punch - Kick - Slash - Heavy Slash - Dust). And that's just scratching the surface, because I haven't even read the in-game FAQ to pick a character (the FAQ suggests Sol or Ky if you're new to the game so I'll go with one of them).
Can't believe that I've spent an hour learning the basics of the game in an effective and fun way.
I will be updating my review the more I dive into this game, but rest assured that it's a great fighting game to get into fighting games. My only fear is that Steam's online matchmaking will feel deserted in a week or two, because the game doesn't have cross-platform matchmaking. I hope that finding people through communities and chatrooms (Reddit, Discord) to practice with will suffice.

This game is really hardcore. This isn't L4D or Killing Floor where you run around killing zeds by the hundreds. It'll take a lot more effort to survive here.
How? Well for starters, ammo is much more difficult to find. You better make your shots count. Also, you have to complete objectives and scavenge for supplies. If i'm making that sound simple, then imagine a mob of zombies chasing you while you're doing that. A mob of zombies that shamble around like in a Romero zombie film, but never stop coming at you, can infect you with the zombie virus if you're not careful and like I said before, you've only got a handful of bullets (and also preferably a melee weapon) to fight them with.
If you can surmount the somewhat steep learning curve this game has and get a game up with a few friends, it's a ton of fun. It's cool to explore the vast maps, scouring the place with a flashlight looking for that jerry can/key/blowtorch you need to progress. There is no ingame tutorial or solo mode to teach you how to play though, but there are some helpful guides with everything you need to know.
Oh, just a word of advice, if you have friends who play this game (or can be convinced to try it out), set up a listen server and play it with them instead of playing on public servers. It's easier to co-ordinate your team that way and a lot better for your sanity.

Exactly what it says on the tin. Snake Pass harkens back to the early days of 3D platformers, where the entire game would be built around a few contrived movement mechanics. In case you couldn't figure it out, you're a snake in this one. It's great.

I never try to make "useful" reviews. Sometimes I make a joke, sometimes I debate other reviews, sometimes I share one thought or a stream of consciousness. This time I just want this game to have another positive review, because it deserves another thousant of those, but I can give only one. So you don't have to read it. Probably lots of better reviews had already been written ;) [a joke]
I'm actually blown away with Snake Pass. I always admire when devs have some genious and innovative idea. It is really hard to come up with something new when the game industry is already bigger than movies (which are 100 years older) and music (how much it is older, could be a topic of a long debate). But those guys made it. The experience of controlling the snake moves is beyond my expectations, if I ever had some - but I didn't, becasue this idea is so original and ingenious. [one thought]
Others write that controls are too hard. Yeah they maybe hard, but in a good way. That's the whole point. You have a small set of moves and actions (moving forward slow, slithering to sides to move faster, turning your head in all directions, gripping harder, and lifting tail) and by combining them you can come up with very large portion of evolutions like coiling around things, using them as lever, and overcome any fancy obstacle that was designed. Other others write that this is not a puzzle game, but I do not agree. The kinetic, physical, "manual" (yeah this word do not fit to snakes :P manos means hand) quests of how to climb an obstacle or get out of a trap are in fact puzzles, and they are also intelectual, becasue you need to think about how to do it, even if it is only analizing your errors and repeating. The difference is that those kinds of tasks use not only your brain, but also your body so they are different from "classic" puzzels, where phisical role is minimalised. Those are still puzzles. [debate other reviews]
Noodle and Doodle are cool and look great. Snake have cute face expressions and you can bond with him and his efforts, and feel bad when he fails. Music is insanely great, and even if the songs are few and repeat through the enire set of levels, they never bore me. Those compositions are so perfectly done, that I want to sing and dance to them all the time. I just felt in love with that snake and feel terrible that I do not have much time to play it now. But I actually can't recall any game that gave me so much fun. It's just pure type of joy, cathartic type and mybe even regressive in some way, but don't get me wrong. This game is not for kids, even if it might look like that for some. It requires advanced spatial orientation and fully developed manual skills. So the fun is not all. You will get real challenges and will feel super rewarded when you overcome them. You will get this feeling not by unlocking an achievement, but every time just after climbing that block, passing this moving platform or getting this hidden coin. Not many games can provide that. If you want to have all this, buy this game. I bought it on sale but already feel like it is worth the full price. [stream of consciousness].

Easily the most original and innovative platformer I've played in years. You master the art of squirming and sliding around obstacle courses, exploring your environment and picking up collectibles. The music is fun and relaxing, the characters are adorable and the art style is vibrant. The level design is generally good, however some levels get tedious and borderline infuriating towards the end of the game.
Controls are simple but extremely difficult to master. Unlike any other platformer I have ever played before.
You will be frustrated at some point, no doubt. Sometimes Doodle (the snake's little bird friend) will get in front of your camera and cause you to die, but you can't stay mad at him for long. He's just too darn cute. Occasionally your camera will have a mind of its own, shifting where you don't want it to shift, causing you to die. Often times I found myself getting impatient with the snake mechanics, causing me to die. Dying in this game is inexplicably aggravating, so be prepared to take a break every once in a while.
The main story can be completed in under 5 hours, but there are a ton of optional collectibles if you're a completionist. I would definitely recommend this on a sale, but it may be worth the full price to you if you really, really enjoy being a snake.
I really hope this game gets a sequel at some point, if for no other reason than to tighten up the controls and polish the level design. Still a fun and enjoyable experience.

This is truely the pennicle of the genere in my opinion. More polished and fun than the original X-com and more detailed and challenging than the "Enemy Unknown" remake, this game really scratches my itch for turn based tactics and global scale strategy.  It's not as pretty as a lot of other games, but that is well balanced by the addictive "one more turn!" gameplay.
Of course, there are a few niggling details that are bothersome. Even at lower difficulties, this game can be punnishingly, frustratinly hard. When you're first starting out, it plays more as a rougelike with frequent restarts or save loads until you can get your initial base(s) established and have figured out a good order to unlock the tech tree. Additionally, the maps get reused more often than I would like, though there are workshop projects that remedy that complaint. Hell, even the difficulty ends up adding to the charm (and nostalgia) of this game.
Seriously, though, if you're even remotely interested in this kind of game, you're doing yourself a diservice if you've not already aded Xenonauts to your cart.

For example, corners turn out to provide 0 cover and there is no clearly defined cover system. This means that a guy crouched in a doorway with a riot shield is actually completely exposed from 45 degree angles. And the game is full of things like this. Where did you toss that grenade? At the alien? Or is it at your feet? You'll find out soon..
The game is full of small bugs, poor design, and crashes every once in a while.
The menu system is also extremely clunky, and could've been much better. A huge amount of the game is spend managing through the menu system that is simply painful to use, especially for the outfitting of soldiers.
And soldiers are completely depersonalized except for a portrait and their origins. No matter what backround or gender a soldier comes from, they will appear on the map as a faceless white guy. There is no dialog or anything.. just feels like a missed opportunity.
I love the game for the strategy and the cold war art style, but I just can't recommend it to anyone who isn't a hardcore strategy fan

Initial impression? Surely there are already too many cute and colourful farming resorce-management female-protagonist wildlife-rescuing vacuum-gun-wielding chicken-worrying slime-exploitation-based first-person exploration games set on a ranch on another totally bizarre planet out there? This genre needs something new... ;)
Even though it's Early Access (and more expensive than most games I buy these days) it looked interesting so I gave it a try. 5 hours later, and I think I've got to the stage I can comfortably close it and go do something else.
In actual fact, it looks like I'm nearing the end of the current content*. Although given the nature of the game, you can never be
done. There are plenty of optimizations I'd still like to make to my ranch and slime population. And starting over now I know what's going on looks attractive too.
Is it too expensive in its current state? Well, I could have bought a DvD instead. Which would have lasted a fraction of the time. And most likely I'd not have had anywhere near as much fun. Plus there is massive potential for Slime Rancher to improve greatly with more content and features.
I'll not give away any spoilers, as working out how the world works is one of the best bits. But I will say I initially felt the tutorial was shockingly brief and didn't tell you anything besides how to use normal FPS-style controls. Now, however, I really hope that was completely deliberate, and that they leave it like that. The discovery of the environment, creatures, mechanics and what you need to do really is the bulk of the game. (At the moment at least - who knows what'll happen once more stuff is in there.)
Sure, there are some ballance issues. And 'not much' content (although still more than I've bothered with in many games). And I really don't like the linear layout of the game world, as opposed to using a more open environment. But what is there is so pollished, bug-free, and wonderfully captivating that it already has been worth the purchase, imo.
[Edit: * Found another area I'd not realised you could get to yet. Another 4 hours gone, re-arranging everything for the new slimes. So yeah; great value overall.]

GGxRD - Revelator can be seen as a *very important* upgrade of Sign providing a more "balanced" meta.
But, for me, this is the best fighting game since a while, despite that some players can be reluctant to the "gatling" combo style.
For people wondering its accessibility, GGxRD-R is still loyal to its creed: "Easy to play, hard to master".
You'll only need a couple of hours to understand and enjoy nearly all the game mechanisms! But the deeper you wanna go, the more time consuming the game becomes. Try it yourself, you will see the overall quality and depth! And now with 23 playable characters with *unique* gameplay, the roster is more than decent.
Regarding online mode, there are really good players on GG licence, and thus, it is hard to come as a "newbie". BUT, take a tour to the lab, learn some matchup, and you'll made a lot of progress in few time :)
Moreover, the training section bears a special mention. It is just amazing how Arc System revisited the classical training (when fighting games deign to implement one...) to bring a lot of fun and interactivity in it. So far the best training that I've encountered.
Plus the story, the 3D cell-animation anime like, the musics, the diversity of gameplays... Well, this is definitely a must have !

One of the things that sells a game to me on PC, is the option for higher resolutions, especially a belated release. I have a gfx card that can run this on at least 1440p@60. The game doesn't support an internal render resolution higher than 1080p.
What you get in this release is:
The option for PS4 resolution, max.
4 sliders in your graphics settings for some post processing.
That's it. That's legit it. It's not enough to justify the price to me. No, no.
For everyone who wants to try Guilty Gear, this is the best iteration out there, I highly recommend it.
For you who already own the PS4 copy, don't waste your time if you think this edition is going to bring anything new to the table, - cause it really won't.
P.S.: Ofc. you can run gedosato and hack the internal renderer, but that's really not what the issue is here. The issue is that you're paying 66% extra on top of what you would atm. on PSN, and you are NOT getting anything different.

For example, corners turn out to provide 0 cover and there is no clearly defined cover system. This means that a guy crouched in a doorway with a riot shield is actually completely exposed from 45 degree angles. And the game is full of things like this. Where did you toss that grenade? At the alien? Or is it at your feet? You'll find out soon..
The game is full of small bugs, poor design, and crashes every once in a while.
The menu system is also extremely clunky, and could've been much better. A huge amount of the game is spend managing through the menu system that is simply painful to use, especially for the outfitting of soldiers.
And soldiers are completely depersonalized except for a portrait and their origins. No matter what backround or gender a soldier comes from, they will appear on the map as a faceless white guy. There is no dialog or anything.. just feels like a missed opportunity.
I love the game for the strategy and the cold war art style, but I just can't recommend it to anyone who isn't a hardcore strategy fan

Day 1 hour 2: Slightly disturbed by pink slimes hopping desperately to get chickens. Built walls higher. Ventured into the wilderness.
Day 2: Made a sizeable profit wandering about collecting slime poop. Admired the shiny golden hue of spontaneously appearing phosphor slimes. Admired how much their poop went for on the open market. Decided to take some home.
Day 3: Phosophor slimes spontaneously combust in broad daylight. Goal of raising free range phosophor slimes put on hold while I quarantine the next batch in my primary vacpack slot.

They ignore the copious amounts of fruit I'm throwing at them for some mildly disturbing displays of coprophilia. They swell into giant pink Amy the hedgehogs and beat my face into my own♥♥♥♥♥harder than Amy's hammer swing. Officially done with Sonic metaphors.
Day 4 hour 16: Run from killer pink/rock hybrids. Find a valley of adorable kitten slimes. Pick one up. Get booped in the face. Kind of cute. Watch in bemusement as they proceed to chase down and devour a family of chickens, leaving behind even more valuable droppings. Pink slimes, as they are wont to do, eat everything including kitten poop. Turn into giant pink kittens. Remain sweet and adorable... until night falls... phosphor slimes gather and I vacuum up several for safe-keeping. Pink/kitten hybrids proceed to eat the valuable phosphor poo before I can grab it, transform into swirling rainbows and muck. Eat everything in sight. Seem to prefer the taste of me.
...I run for my life ignoring the squeals of horror and ghosts of the dead...
Day 5: Notice a slight dip in the price of pink poop. Also find my chickens may be suffering from PTSD. I discard pink slimes and gather some purebred vegetarian rock slimes instead. The chickens seem happy. I persist only mildly bruised.
Day 6: Expand the farm and dump colony of phosphor slimes into it. They seem pretty happy, all things considered. I decide I may need to feather my nest egg and start stocking up on kitten poop. As usual, night ends battling a rapidly growing army of black tar trying to eat me. Could throw them into the ocean, but far more enjoyable to shoot them in the face like a ghostbuster.
Experiment with breeding slimes for higher production value. Settle on kitten/rock hybrids. Can't tell whether they want to boop me or kill me. Just in case, lock the first subject in a cage on auto-feeder/auto-poop-harvest and watch it make me money.
Day 8: Purchase expansion pre-loaded with native chickens and fill it with kitten slimes. Free range kitten poop dreams achieved. Quietly ignore the plaintive cries of free range chickens slaughtered by free-range gelatinous carnivores. Perhaps for this reason I have gone 8 in-game days without in-game sleep. I fear the in-game nightmares awaiting me.
Day 11: Learn to ignore the startled cries of dying chickens. Turn my face away just so from the bouncing kitten/rock hybrids rattling about in their plasma cage. Is this what I got into slime ranching for? What would Slime God think of my slime breeding ways? Gather up a new stock of fresh chickens to throw into the kitten slime pit. Try to talk myself into moral legitimacy by claiming it's just nature.
...And yet, nature creates tars...
Day 12: Race deep into the jungle to gather new breeds of slime. Valuable. Profitable. And yet, dangerous. Rebuild the farm to contain, capture, and control. Convince myself I'm preserving them for posterity... just like the chickens. Just like the chickens. I load an auto-feeder full of them into a box made of light and pain so I don't get blasted into gibs by the boom slimes.
It's for science, I think. It's for the good of humanity. The galaxy. It's to preserve them from the inevitable entropy of their own uncontrollable hungers, the endless cycle of slime, tar, death.
Oh, Slime God, if slimes even HAVE gods, what am I doing...?
Day 13: I empty all of my cages. Send the carnivores back into their homes. Let the free-range chickens be free. I WILL do better than this. Because I AM better than this. Also, honey poop is ridiculously valuable and those dudes eat fruit.
Day 14: My kitten slime friends have all hybridized into kitten/pink largos. They still try to boop me when they see me. I load a vac canister with water from a fresh spring, partly to feed the puddle slimes back home, partly for the inevitable entropy of a nighttime walk, a sudden surge of phosphor slimes, and their poop just waiting for my former kitten slime friends to nibble on.
It was them or the chickens. I can be a sanctuary of civilization in the Far Range, but I can't save the world. Not without selling a lot more poop.

Round 1: Everyone spawns, everyone is friendly. Ammo? Plenty. Weapons? loads. Zombies with broken legs? Few. Manage to kill them all.

Honestly, I love the concept of this game, but the execution needs a lot of work.
TL;DR - Needs lots of work, but would still recommend.
-I can run a modded-out skyrim on ultra high on my computer, but I'm lucky if I get 20 fps on low settings with this game. If I try to run with High or Ultra settings, it crashes completely.
-The combat is pretty... lame. There's only one attack motion for each weapon, and the zombies MIGHT react to attacks if you're lucky. It's honestly a button-mash until it dies sort of situation.
-It's hard to tell when you get hit. You may get a little blood splat every third hit, but thats about it. I've died a couple times because I just didnt realize I was getting hit.
-Starvation and Thirst set in really fast. If I wanted to drink water every 15 seconds to prevent myself from dying, I'd play Fallout:Dust.
-Looting system is sorta... eh. I just feel like there would be a lot more variety in weapons than just scissor shanks and mechanics wrenches. Other items aren't super hard to come by, you just need to know what you're looking for.
-Crafting is a serious pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ You actually have to go out and find blueprints before you're able to craft anything. I feel like that's a bit unrealistic.
-I love the concept of the shop, but I have no idea how they've got it set up. You can only sell some items, so if you go out and gather a sh*t-ton of loot, you MIGHT find one thing you can sell. It's a bit aggravating.
-That damn desert goes on forever. Traveling from place to place is really boring because there isnt a lot of filler content in the world. Makes me get bored going from place to place.
-Other players can be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s sometimes. But you get that everywhere.
HOWEVER, even though this game needs a lot of work, I really thing it could be a really good game.
-It reminds me a lot of DayZ, Dying Light, and State Of Decay style games with the very open-world do your own thing sorta gameplay. Its a lot of fun.
-Ragdoll zombies are fun sometimes. They just sorta fal straight down when they die. Reminds me of a lot of older games.
-Even with the low quality graphics, it's pretty fun. It's sorta like games from the mid-late 2000s.

I bought Swap Blocks because I'm a fan of similar games. I hoped that the versus mode would be fun enough to play with my brother. Swap Blocks met that expectation and passed others. However, there are other ways in which the game falls short.
Swap Blocks is similar to other puzzle swapping games. You swap two blocks with each other in order to match blocks and clear items. The mode you play changes what happens when blocks are cleared. In marathon and timed modes, the blocks are immediately replaced with more blocks. In other modes, the blocks are either replaced slowly or not at all. Those modes are unlocked as the player collects stars. Stars are collected by beating each mode on easy, medium, and hard. Each mode level has three stars available, all of which are attained by points. Versus mode also has multiple modes, all of which are accessible the moment you purchase the game.
Pros:
- Graphics are smooth and clear.
- There are two mode of play - normal mode and cross mode - both of which are challenging in their own ways.
- Point values needed to unlock stars are in the bottom left-hand corner.
- Multiple tile styles are available. None of them have to be unlocked.
- The chosen tile style shows up on the main menu. You can see how the tiles look prior to actually playing a level, so it's easy to pick which option is going to be best for the player.
- Audio is easy to turn down/off.
- All achievements can be gotten during solo play.
- Local multiplayer.
- High replayability.
Cons:
- Graphics are simplistic in comparison to other swapping block games.
- Challenge mode doesn't seem to work. Either the goal of the challenges are not clear or they aren't functioning right now. Nothing about this problem in updates or news, unless I missed it. (As of Sept. 10th, 2017.)
- Challenge mode also has no reset button. You must back out of challenge menu entirely in order to restart the challenge.
Swap Blocks is a good block swapping game if you're looking for something to play with your friends. Definitely worth the price on that front. But with challenge mode not working correctly for me, I can't recommend it for solo play just yet.

Very very difficult to come back with negative thoughts on this game, because on the one hand I absolutely applaud the developers for trying something new. On the other hand...
I feel like we've all run into the frustrations of having a fun, relaxing, puzzle-based game be very reliant on the game's physics-based objects working just the way you need them to. Noodle ends up being much of that issue.
I definitely felt like I understood the controls of the game, and I can't say I noticed camera issues the way some other people are reporting. But, even with a solid understanding of the principles, I just couldn't seem to get Noodle to continue doing just as I wanted. The main gap here is, while Noodle's head (or, front) end is highly responsive and can even be directed in some slightly physics-defying manner, his tail end (or, back) often fails to follow through dutifully. Carefully wrapping yourself around one small piece of a branch will grant you some good grip positioning, but then the slightest move forward afterward will cause his entire back end to unwind as though it were a limp piece of rope.
To Sumo Digital's credit, their physics simulation of snakes seems really dead-on. They definitely paid attention to the actual workings of snake muscles to avoid giving players a game where you can float around based on Snake Magic. Ultimately, I feel like good realism kind of got in the way of giving players a fun, relaxing experience, which is mostly what I had planned for when sitting down with a game with such cartoony style and gentle music.
You may actually still enjoy this game if you're a bit more patient than me, and don't mind "hacking the physics" a bit on occasion to get where you're trying to go, like stretching waay out to touch the ledge rather than actually coiling towards it. It's definitely a unique enough idea, you might want to try it just based on that if you want to try something new. Unlike a lot of "physics-based challenge games" its failings aren't totally based on glitchy ragdolls or objects getting stuck or flying off, but simply the limited control of your complex-shaped character.
To close on a positive note, Sumo Digital also made Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed, which is a better cart-racing game than Mario Kart. You should check it out.

I think this idea has potential.
But it is absolutely not met here.
Laundry list of complaints:
1. Pacing feels way too slow. The act of basic movement is often a chore
2. Physics don't quite feel consistent & such lead to weird scenarios where something completely unexpected happens
3. Camera is very unfriendly and often gives you really bad angles to work with resulting in cheap deaths
4. The occasional linear level feels out of place compared to the more broad, exploratory levels; point 1 worsens the impact this has on the level design
5. The wind mechanic introduced in the last few stages is outright bad. Like genuinely ruins the last three levels outright.
6. Moving platforms and the snake physics often don't behave well together resulting in really tense and vaguely unfair situations
7. Unskippable cutscenes at the start or end of some levels, usually going on for over a minute too
8, Environments are all kind of samey; lots of grass, stone ruins, and bamboo. Bamboo everywhere.
9. Grip mechanic does, as far as I'm aware, absolutely nothing? I have never seen it work or be useful in any scenario and 100%ed the game without ever really using it
Presentation wise the game looks great and the music is decent though tends to get repetitive with how long some levels can drag on, especially near the end of the game. And there are genuinely a lot of moments of pretty solid level design, aside from the occasional bad moment the real fault of the game is the controls not quite being there. Maybe in a sequel they could refine and improve this idea but I honestly don't know if it would make for a fun game even if they did.
Because that's just the real failing here... due to the slow pace and frustrating controls, the game just isn't fun. I did not enjoy playing this game. Oh well.

The game is, I suppose, "fun" if you're interested in nothing but a strait rehash of the original XCOM series. And by that I mean if you're a fan of fustration and like having your butt handed to you on a platter on a consistent basis. I played through, all the way, on 'normal' mode (which is actually easier than what it's supposed to be played on, which is veteran) and the sheer unfairness of it all was mind boggling.
Grunts that would have something like a 17% chance to hit at point blank range, the absolute worst RNG ever (consistent misses, also at point blank range, with shotguns when you've got like a 90% chance of hitting). Aliens that can see across the screen when you *can't*, absolutely insane maintenance costs that basically mean that if you don't optimize your initial base you'll basically never be able to make another base. Which is a problem because you *need* at least 3 or 4 bases in total if only to get radar coverage of the whole world map. To say nothing of the extreme cost putting hangers and fighters in those locations.
TLDR- Horribily unbalanced combat in favor of the aliens, horribly implemented and unbalanced economy. When it's literally impossible to make a second base because your funding is so low you can't even afford to *start construction* there is a problem. Especially since the odds are extremely good that once you hit that critical point where you aren't making enough money you'll basically stay there for the rest of the game.
I recommend this game only for die hard purists of the original XCOM. In every other way however the newer XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within is a superior use of your money. That and if you're really a die hard purist of the original XCOM then you could, you know, just buy the original XCOM since it is also on Steam.

Before I bought this game, I didn't know what genre to expect, since you're a snake and you slide/slither across instead of jumping like you do in most, if not all, platformers. So I was sort of dumbfounded about it, but now I know! Clearly, it's a 3D platformer. Why? The horrendous, atrocious camera and controls that have plagued most 3D platformers since the early 32-bit console days are present here, in full glory. And in my case, they're without a doubt, the absolute worst I've come across since the PSX era.
The camera intentionally obscures what's around you and instead focuses on the ground most of the time. This is to try and make the game "challenging" somehow, otherwise they simply would have included a locked camera mode, as an option at least, with an isometric angle when it gets too close to the character or an object. The controls too get in the way, 'grip' for instance doesn't do what it's supposed to and it's a struggle and a chore just to get over a small obstacle or climbing a short pole or stick, this is exacerbated by clipping issues and off course, the drunk, inept, camera sabotaging every move and action.
A big disappointment, a pity really. The game is indeed charming, and the music is great and it makes you happy, at least when you're in the main menu, cause instead of being a relaxing and a chill game like you thought it would be, it ends up being extremely infuriating and exasperating. You always end up fighting the camera and controls, nothing enjoyable in the slightest.

Snake Pass is a proof of concept game, that concept being how you would navigate a 3D platformer without any arms and legs. Snake Pass is super dedicated to the whole snake thing – any expectation for remotely conventional controls should be quickly discarded as the bizarre, ungainly physics based controls ARE the game. Rather than jumping or climbing, you have to coil and slither around bamboo poles and fling yourself from platform to platform while managing your clumsy, limbless mass. Even moving along the ground requires a sidewinding motion. The main lesson I’ve learned from Snake Pass is that being a snake is a massive pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥
Thankfully, while this is a game that defies many genre conventions the structure of the game is actually very simple – every level consists of collecting three thingies and getting to the exit. There are optional other thingies to collect along the way if you’re a completionist. The 15 levels should last you about 5-8 hours depending on how rubbish you are, which means it doesn’t outstay its welcome. This is assuming you get that far and don’t ragequit and set your computer on fire. Don’t let the cutesy, twee art style fool you – you will either get good at Snake Pass, or you will perish like a dog.
There are three stages of Snake Pass grief – fascination, frustration and mastery. How long it takes to get from stage 2 to stage 3 will largely determine whether you enjoy the game or feel constant uncontrollable, incandescent rage. The first four levels are a fairly gentle introduction, but the game expects mastery of its unconventional controls very quickly and level five sees a massive difficulty spike- Snake Pass loves to dangle you above bottomless pits between sparse checkpoints, and it does not take long for this to begin in earnest. If you can clear level five and six without throwing your controller at the cat, the rest of the game should prove a challenging, entertaining and above all original experience.

Feb 15, 2016  (v0.2.4b)
It's still in Early Access, so this review might change.  At the moment, I would say that I love the idea but am disappointed in what is there currently.  TL;DR it's a good concept, but wait a patch or two before buying.
The game is exactly what it sells itself as: you're a slime rancher collecting and raising slimes.  You run into the outside world, collect slimes and raise them.  When fed, they will produce 'plorts' to sell, which in-turn allows you to expand your ranch and buy upgrades.  Different types of slimes can be combined, which will produce multiple types of plorts, and different slimes excel under different conditions.
I want to love this game, and I do.  However, after a couple hours, I feel like I have seen everything in the current version of the game.  I've explored the map, which includes some fenced-off areas that haven't been fully developed yet.  I've expanded the ranch to it's current maximum, though I have not bought every upgrade.  I haven't completed every in-game achievement either.  But, I would prefer the orgranic gameplay to be a bit better; bigger maps, more slimes, etc.
Slime Rancher also has a day-night cycle.  However, I don't think that there is a large purpose to it at present.  At night, tar slimes will appear, and will attack you and eat your slimes.  Running around at night hasn't been dangerous and remaing in your ranch at night is financial suicide; risking the loss of slimes before you can save them.  I think a risk-reward system for nighttime play would probably make the day-night cycle much more interesting.  At the moment, it's a hinderance.
The upgrades also feel a bit mixed in terms of usefulness.  Items such as increased vac space work well if you are making a large run collecting 'wild' plorts, fruits or vegetables.  But, the jetpack isn't really necessary at this point, and health/energy upgrades become a nice-to-have once you figure out how to avoid damage and make better use of your time (respectively).
Despite wanting more, the game I have now isn't terrible by any means.  I haven't come across any bugs.  I adore the art style.  The slimes are pretty entertaining (especially when you are first starting out).  The map is smaller than it first appears.  But, there are a decent number of entrances marked "coming soon" that may make the map much larger and enjoyable in a future update.
In short, I love the idea of the game and have enjoyed what I've received.  However, I am eagerly waiting for the next updates to give more content.  And, if you are on the fence about Slime Rancher, I would advise you to wait until the next major update (or further).

The game is, I suppose, "fun" if you're interested in nothing but a strait rehash of the original XCOM series. And by that I mean if you're a fan of fustration and like having your butt handed to you on a platter on a consistent basis. I played through, all the way, on 'normal' mode (which is actually easier than what it's supposed to be played on, which is veteran) and the sheer unfairness of it all was mind boggling.
Grunts that would have something like a 17% chance to hit at point blank range, the absolute worst RNG ever (consistent misses, also at point blank range, with shotguns when you've got like a 90% chance of hitting). Aliens that can see across the screen when you *can't*, absolutely insane maintenance costs that basically mean that if you don't optimize your initial base you'll basically never be able to make another base. Which is a problem because you *need* at least 3 or 4 bases in total if only to get radar coverage of the whole world map. To say nothing of the extreme cost putting hangers and fighters in those locations.
TLDR- Horribily unbalanced combat in favor of the aliens, horribly implemented and unbalanced economy. When it's literally impossible to make a second base because your funding is so low you can't even afford to *start construction* there is a problem. Especially since the odds are extremely good that once you hit that critical point where you aren't making enough money you'll basically stay there for the rest of the game.
I recommend this game only for die hard purists of the original XCOM. In every other way however the newer XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within is a superior use of your money. That and if you're really a die hard purist of the original XCOM then you could, you know, just buy the original XCOM since it is also on Steam.

Many of the mechanics are similar to  XEU like constructing the base by expanding locations and selecting what to build. Combat is also similar turn based and using cover, changing weapons, etc. But I just have no fun with this game. Here is what I dislike.
The combat in XEU is implemented much better. For example,  in XEU line of sight works is carefully implemented. In Xeno it seems they use a random factor to simulate it and it doesn't work well. For me combat was the most fun part of XEU and it is the worst part of Xeno. Xeno relies low hit rate to simulate difficulty. Chance is not a replacement for implementing strong combat elements like line of sight. XEU adds chance on top of strong combat elements, that is fun. Xeno adds chance as a replacement to implement strong game elements, that is not fun.
I will stop purchasing games with low production values like Xeno. This seems implemented for the 1980's before dedicated graphic cards were implemented.

One of the most satisfying gaming experiences I've had in a awhile.  Xbox 360 gamers may have played the indie game Miner Dig Deep, and this game is very much like that, only with somewhat more focused gameplay and a faster pace.  This isn't a minecraft style game or anything like that, but rather a simple, straightforward sort of action game where you dig for ore, sell it, get better equipment, and just keep going deeper.  Eventually the game gets harder and slightly more complex in that getting around and getting all of the ore and Orbs (a special currency) begins to take a bit of smarter planning to get.  While there are straightforward goals (keep digging until you reach a room that has your next major upgrade), the levels also have randomly placed "puzzle rooms" where you have to use your abilities to survive or figure out a challenge to gain access to some Orbs and valuable ore.  Extremely well crafted and paced just right so that it feels like every time you think you've mastered a particular part of a level, as you go deeper it throws more difficulty curves at you.  I can't recommend it enough.
I should point out my whole game time was just over 7 hours to find all the ore, orbs, completing every room and buying every upgrade.

Physics puzzle platformer where instead of jumping around, you slither and coil around obstacles as a snake.
The controls are very simple. you can move forward, lift your head (to start going upward) or "grip" to coil around something more tightly.
The challenge comes from mastering how to manouver your snake. Stages are large open areas that have various wooden poles and spokes to coil around to reach stuff, the more points of contact your body has with the surface, the better. Trying to move forward without properly adjusting yourself might leave too much of your body mass hanging free and you'lĺ fall to your death.
The camera has some issues and wants to go too far away to give you a better view, often putting some background object in the way so you can't see. Same goes for tight spots where the camera might not give you a good enough view of the layout, requiring you to adjust it.This hasn't been an issue TOO often, but can be annoying.
Each stage has you hunt down required "key stones" to beat it, while also harboring tons of optional collectibles.
Controling the snake is fun and unique. I recommend this game

Platforming on bamboo goes one of two ways, you can either tediously wrap Noodle around each shoot, or you can gamble it and try to balance a cylindrical character on top of another cylinder to try and finish in a reasonable amount of time. The game is fond of having you twirl Noodle around a pole to gain height. It gets old fast. The mere act of flipping a switch is annoying. No cutscene can be skipped, and with a game this light on story that's inexcusable. The brightness setting the game recommended caused switches in the fire levels to blend into the background. Speaking of the levels, every one looks the same. Just minor differences in lighting and sometimes there's flowers in the grass or hot ashes on the ground. Because of Noodle's down-to-earth stature, the camera doesn't like to point up. Particularly frustrating if you're trying to see the beacons in the sky that denote keystone positions.

Slime Rancher is a farm-type game where you tend to slimes and explore the planet in search of new slimes. You can gather slimes and resources with your Vac-Pack (Think, a gun that's also a 4 container vacuum cleaner) and then bring them to your ranch to tend to them, all to strike it rich with a resource only slimes produce: plorts.
First off, allow me to note that I wouldn't normally review an Early Access game unless it left a solid impression, and man did this game leave a strong impression.
Now, the game's simple mechanic that is made obvious right away is how you tend to slimes, and it works really well. You bring slimes to ranch, you feed them, you collect their plorts, you sell their plorts, all the while making sure all your other resources are doing well or if you have to go out and about to get more. It's a nice relaxing feel, that I haven't exactly felt in a game in a long time. Just going around and tending to the slimes, then exploring to bring more home with me just is a nice way to relax.
The relaxing part is aided by the beautiful soundtrack. Each area has its own music, and every song is simply suiting and relaxing, and it makes the world just a bit more lively.
The graphics are beautiful as well. Everything is colorful without being eye-searing. The pallettes all work well together, and it leaves a beautiful image that is fun to simply traverse and admire. Not to mention the slimes are made to be extremely cute, if you couldn't tell by the trailer already. Overall the visuals give the game a nice sense of charm and gives the game it's own unique style.
Gameplay is also pretty interesting, and does something I wish more games these days would do: Not hold your hand. Sure, it teaches you the basic controls, but that is literally it. It's up to you to figure out what is and isn't possible, either by observing the world around you, or going through the "Slimepedia" (Basically a booklet explaining what things you've found do). It leads to a nice sense of discovery, learning what does and doesn't work, and what you want your dream slime ranch to be, as well as dangers of what happen if you screw up.
One final note that I applaud the developers for: Interacting with the community. I've been to their forums, and they not only actively show progress but work with fans to come up with new and brilliant ideas. Few devs seem to do this these days and it's nice seeing game developers not trying to hide behind closed doors.
That all said, there are a few issues, namely that money becomes a bit too easy to get for no real reason. Granted, this is Early Access and from what I've read they seem to plan something about this but as it stands once you get a ranch going you never can really run out of money unless you try. I've seen people reach 100k in about 10 in game days, so it's not terribly tough.
There also isn't much in terms of exploration for now, though they clearly have a lot planned in that regard as well.
Finally one big issue I have is the slow speed it takes to grab and sell plorts from machines. Put it nicely, if you hold about 50 of a kind of plort, it takes about 30 seconds (real time) to empty them into the market. Thing is, it's not tough to get about 200 per run, assuming it's ONLY a single run you are doing, and it just kills the pacing of the game, as I sit at my desk holding my mouse button down waiting for it to be done just so I can go do something else (if you don't sell them, they can easily start to overflow).
Overall, a brilliant early access game that is fun and relaxing. Great atmosphere, and looks amazing. Definitely suggest getting it if you're into relaxing games.

WHAT IS THIS GAME?
This game is all about mastering the wonky controls of a snake protoganist in order to collect items throughout obstacle courses.
WHAT THIS GAME *IS NOT*
This game doesn't involve solving any puzzles; the levels are designed like obstacle courses, not puzzles.  Also, it's *not* particularly relaxing; you'll often find yourself tightening your grip on the mouse/controller and cringing as you try not to slip off ledges.
WHAT GENRE IS THIS GAME?
It's not quite an adventure in the spirit of Banjo-Kazooie.  I would actually liken it more to Mirror's Edge.  Like Mirror's Edge, the game is based entirely around your skills with a particular set of moves/controls.
HOW DIFFICULT IS THIS GAME?
There's a steep learning curve at the beginning, but about an hour or two into the game, you'll realize that the game is pretty easy to complete.  However, the game is significantly more difficult if you try to collect all the collectibles and *especially* if you try to collect all the Steam achievements.  This game is good for both casual gamers and "serious" gamers alike.
IS THIS GAME WORTHWHILE?

Slime Rancher is a farm-type game where you tend to slimes and explore the planet in search of new slimes. You can gather slimes and resources with your Vac-Pack (Think, a gun that's also a 4 container vacuum cleaner) and then bring them to your ranch to tend to them, all to strike it rich with a resource only slimes produce: plorts.
First off, allow me to note that I wouldn't normally review an Early Access game unless it left a solid impression, and man did this game leave a strong impression.
Now, the game's simple mechanic that is made obvious right away is how you tend to slimes, and it works really well. You bring slimes to ranch, you feed them, you collect their plorts, you sell their plorts, all the while making sure all your other resources are doing well or if you have to go out and about to get more. It's a nice relaxing feel, that I haven't exactly felt in a game in a long time. Just going around and tending to the slimes, then exploring to bring more home with me just is a nice way to relax.
The relaxing part is aided by the beautiful soundtrack. Each area has its own music, and every song is simply suiting and relaxing, and it makes the world just a bit more lively.
The graphics are beautiful as well. Everything is colorful without being eye-searing. The pallettes all work well together, and it leaves a beautiful image that is fun to simply traverse and admire. Not to mention the slimes are made to be extremely cute, if you couldn't tell by the trailer already. Overall the visuals give the game a nice sense of charm and gives the game it's own unique style.
Gameplay is also pretty interesting, and does something I wish more games these days would do: Not hold your hand. Sure, it teaches you the basic controls, but that is literally it. It's up to you to figure out what is and isn't possible, either by observing the world around you, or going through the "Slimepedia" (Basically a booklet explaining what things you've found do). It leads to a nice sense of discovery, learning what does and doesn't work, and what you want your dream slime ranch to be, as well as dangers of what happen if you screw up.
One final note that I applaud the developers for: Interacting with the community. I've been to their forums, and they not only actively show progress but work with fans to come up with new and brilliant ideas. Few devs seem to do this these days and it's nice seeing game developers not trying to hide behind closed doors.
That all said, there are a few issues, namely that money becomes a bit too easy to get for no real reason. Granted, this is Early Access and from what I've read they seem to plan something about this but as it stands once you get a ranch going you never can really run out of money unless you try. I've seen people reach 100k in about 10 in game days, so it's not terribly tough.
There also isn't much in terms of exploration for now, though they clearly have a lot planned in that regard as well.
Finally one big issue I have is the slow speed it takes to grab and sell plorts from machines. Put it nicely, if you hold about 50 of a kind of plort, it takes about 30 seconds (real time) to empty them into the market. Thing is, it's not tough to get about 200 per run, assuming it's ONLY a single run you are doing, and it just kills the pacing of the game, as I sit at my desk holding my mouse button down waiting for it to be done just so I can go do something else (if you don't sell them, they can easily start to overflow).
Overall, a brilliant early access game that is fun and relaxing. Great atmosphere, and looks amazing. Definitely suggest getting it if you're into relaxing games.
