This is what I think X-COM Enemy Unknown should've been like: a balanced turn-based-strategy game that rewards your intelligence and punishes your mistakes, and ONLY your mistakes. It's challenging without finding the need to cheat.
The gameplay is almost exactly like Enemy Unknown. But the few differences that are there make the game a lot more fun and a lot less frustrating. For starters, enemies no longer get a free move when you spot them, evening out the playing field. Their advantage instead comes from other abilities they have, such as regenerating damage, teleporting, flight, and psychic attacks (the latter of which has cost me more than one mission). These make them hard, but unlike X-COM where I found the game boiled down to "shoot them until they died", this game instead forces me to prioritize targets based on potential threat from things other than how big the aliens are and how big are the guns they're carrying. Each enemy unit merits a different approach, as it should.
Your soldiers don't get specialized abilities like they do in Enemy Unknown, but they're no longer arbitrarily placed into categories by whatever confusing algorithm turned all of my soldiers in to snipers and nothing else. Their effectiveness in combat boils down to what equipment you arm them with vs. how well suited they are for that type of combat according to their stats.
The air-to-air combat is FAR superior here than Enemy Unknown. There's an actual strategy element to it not that gives you more direct control of combat, allowing you to snatch victory from a 96% chance of defeat with some creative flight control and use of weapons.
The world map is also much improved. Rather than build satellites to watch over whole continents, you instead build bases at points where you can cover the most land with your limited radar. And aliens can always attack your bases, setting you back and possibly costing you the game if they're not properly defended. The limited space you have to build aircraft will more often than not force you to guess which ships pose more of a threat than others, until later in the game when you can build an intel array to spell it out for you.
Eventually, your equipment will outmatch that of the aliens', but said equipment is costly and takes far more time than is practical to build. What makes this and pretty much every other step forward in Xenonauts work, though, is that your triumphs only come after numerous successful missions and God knows how many soldiers lost to the enemy.
And, lastly, f**k those f**king Reapers.

A phenominal X-Com remake that overstays its welcome.
This crowd-funded game has everything I look for in an x-com remake, and if you prefer classic x-com with TU's and stun rods and destructable terrain to the newer, friendlier, class-based game, this is the remake for you. UFO interceptions become their own fun little minigame, base building (and defending) is just like X-Com original, and the turn-based tactical gameplay, while not the same, is very close to the original, with less of a budget for explosions. If you're interested in this game, you know what you want, and this game will deliver it.
One thing I should mention that really hurt my enjoyment, though, was how much of an unfriendly slog this game is, due 100% to its economy. Provided you keep all your funding nations happy, you'll make enough money for base upkeep, but not really enough for expansion, research, and building new weapons to replace your old ones. You can make some money (but gain no alien resources) by destroying downed UFO's from the world map, or you can send your soldiers on ground missions to make about twice as much money. While this ensures that you'll want frequent ground missions (that is, the whole point of the game) the fact that UFO hulls are one of the few objects that aren't subject to destructable terrain means that each time, you'll have to breach and clear UFO's through their own single-path construction, which is the least fun thing, and takes the most time. Every alien bridge is accessible from only one direction, often through two doors that are placed so that anyone on the bridge can get reflex fire on any soldiers entering. Psi isn't restricted to seen targets only, like the original x-com, and alien psykers will always stay in their invulnerable UFO bridges, and there's no psi defense like the original x-com, so you basically get soldiers berzerking and falling under alien control with no defense right up until you win the mission. All in all, this game took me 77 hours. I was done with the core gameplay at maybe 45 or 50.
Buy it if you like X-Com or Jagged Alliance; no other remakes have done it for me (the newer friendlier X-Com has excellent gameplay to be sure, it's just not the same kind of excellent gameplay). It may be sad that fans keep chasing the X-Com (or JA) dragon, but there's a reason for that: They're brilliant games.

Okay, how should I say this? OMG, it's one of the most exciting zombie video games of all time!!!
No More Room In Hell was a multiplayer-based Half Life 2 mod that was released in 2011 which has been in development nearly 7 years. The game has been released on Steam in 2013 as a full game, and that means Steam users don't need Half Life 2 to play the game.
The game has two modes, an objective-based mode and a survival mode, The objective-based is a simple point to point level which needs players to fight hordes of zombies in their way while they're going to the main objective, while the survival mode puts players in a scenario which players have to survive and kill some waves of hungry zombies.
There are three types of zombies : normal, flesh-eating, Romero-type "Walker" zombies, running zombies, and children zombies.
You can also have the ability to play the game in single player mode (just go to the create server menu with no other players and just dive in into the game).
The game's tense and dark atmosphere made the game's very fun and scary to explore, especially if you wander alone like a lost explorer. Most maps are pretty dark so you need flashlight to explore the game's levels (you can also use a lighter, but it can only lights a bit of an area).
Weapons in this game are pretty badass. From pistols to SMGs, knives to machetes, baseball bats to sledgehammers, and semi-automatic rifles to shotguns. The game also have some types of ammo, which firearms with a same ammo type can be used.
However, there are still some flaws in this game, which sometimes made the experience a little bit boring and annoying. One of 'em is the stiff, wooden, and unrealistic character animations, the lack of body deformation features on zombies, the lack of allied bot support on single player mode, and the depiction of children zombies. There are also no extra game modes other than the objective and survival modes, and the fact that the game didn't have some character and weapons customization features.
Still, it is one of the most exciting and scariest zombie survival video games of all time!!!
I gave NMRIH 8.7/10 :)

PROS:
Be a snake!  It's fun to slither around and climb on things, exploring and collecting hidden items.  The game is pretty and the music is nice.  Obstacles are generally straightforward-- the most difficult ones are much easier if you take a specific approach, but most can be solved by intuitive slithering.
CONS:
The physics and controls can be a bit frustrating, especially with the fatigue of having to press the slither button 90% of the time.  Highly recommended you switch to the "easy" control settings, and only switch back to default when you need the extra finesse of having a dedicated slither button.  Even then you may need an adjustment period to get used to the physics.  The camera is pretty bad, too.  All cutscenes are unskippable, hopefully the developers will change this.
Cautious recommendation.  I hope you like snakes.

An incredibly lovely game. It feels so refreshing in this day and age dominated by grimdark naturalistic titles all around (which I also love, don't get me wrong; it can just feel a bit stifling) to play such a vibrant, innocent game so reminiscent of old-school platformers. The music, too, is super catchy (not gonna lie, I was singing along to the tunes at least half the time). I don't really understand people who say it's difficult; sure, the controls are finicky and very different from what you're used to, but for good reason. I wasn't even playing with a gamepad (which I do believe would have made the experience a lot smoother but alas I don't own one) yet I quickly got used to them and within a few levels was ssslithering around like a true ssssneaky snek. Finished the game in 10 hours with all the collectibles found (no cheatsies!) so I can attest to the fact it's more relaxing than a nerve-wracking challenge, especially what with the re-passable checkpoints.
As regards performance issues, let's just say my rig isn't what it used to be - NVidia GTX 960 + 4-core AMD Phenom II X4 running Windows 7. My gameplay experience was as smooth as Michael Fassbender's backside in Shame and that is all I have to say about that.
8.5/10 camera can get annoying in tight spaces (maybe 1st person view would be better there?) and it's a shame the game is quite short other than that it's bomb.
(SIDENOTE: The game also made my graphics driver crash several times. However, I can't tell whether that's because of Snake Pass or because of my card getting old/dusty, so I won't hold it against the devs. It was never a big issue, anyway.)

I am really impressed by this game so far.
It still is early in its development phase so if you are not fond of early access you might not like that.
I bought it on sale and it really feels like a steal.
Let's go with the classic pros and cons:
Pros:
-It has dinosaurs!
-It has already five classes
-the multiplayer is good, i have not experienced any lag so far.
-It looks rather good, it could be better but it is really far from ugly.
-It has a lot of loot, and an interesting crafting system.
-it has a decent amount of weapons and this will get better with time.
-it can be pretty intense with 4 players
-it is objective based, i mean yes it is a simple horde game, but you know why you are camping: to defend a harvester
wich makes me think of the one in the command and conquer serie so i can't really complain.
-You will fight against a T-rex and many other bosses ;)
Cons:
-Poorly optimised, i can run it on max settings at around 40 fps with a gtx970, which is a bit annoying, especially if you have even worse hardware. The game looks good but not good enough to justify the low fps i am getting.
-Grindy, well yes it was to be excpected but still pretty damn grindy.
Pretty boring when playing solo.
-It needs more variety especially class wise and gear wise, but it is early access so it should be expected.
-It can be repetitive, but well it is an horde game so you know what you are buying right ;)
-3rd person view, i personaly hate that as i prefer the fps style, but you can also switch with a top down view if you think it is unbearable.
Tl;DR:
This game has a lot of potential, i recommend buying it on sale, but if the devs keep on working on it as they started this could become a classic.

I'm so diappointed in this game! I came across it by accident, but it looked promising, so I checked out the discussion page to see if the game had native controller support. It must have been my lucky day, because according to a post from the developer, it had just been added.
I bought the game today and installed it immediately, but after half an hour of gameplay, I'm giving up. The
are cute but not impressive, and the
has an annoying
effect that grates easily. What really makes me want to return the game for a refund, though, is the
.
The controls make you feel like the character is sliding around on ice all the time. Jumps are inconsistent, meaning that sometimes you jump after a button press, and sometimes you don't. When the jump doesn't execute properly, the character will instead just slide around and glide off the numerous narrow cliffs that make up the platforming aspect of the game.
The distances and heights that your character jumps when a button press results in an actual jump are also inconsistent and actually made worse when simultaneously pressing a directional joystick. I can't even use the potions in my inventory, becuse the cursor just keeps scrolling over the whole inventory landing on some obscure potion I wasn't trying to get to in the first place.
I strongly urge the dev to revisit controller support for the XBox 360 and perhaps tighten up other aspects of the game as well. I'd be glad to give it another try at that point.

I wanted to update my review to let readers know that the developer has reached out to me and is taking steps to fix these issues. I spoke with him extensively about what I was experiencing on both wired XBox 360 and Steam controllers and also shared my specs with him so he could troubleshoot. It's my understanding that the developer intends to remove the controller support notation from the store page until issues are resolved, and I've made myself available for further runthroughs. This is exactly the kind of developer that I like to meet, because while a perfect review would be lovely, a specific critical review is just as valuable.

Gosh do I love this game. The way I see it, this game has the potential to be literally the best game fathomable. Here's why:
-It has soo much variety in playstyles, guns,environments and enemies
-It's creative as hell
-Tons of hilarious writing
-It's very atmospheric at times
-Very unique mechanics; I especially love the badass rank mechanic
-Tons of content when you get the DLC
-It's infinitely replayable and you WANT to play it again
However, every game has its problems, and boy does this game have a lot
-First of all, the story is very mediocre. There was clearly more effort and thought put into other elements of the game than the story. It can feel like a more colorful version of COD at times sadly
-Second, the game CAN be boring depending on the person. I personally can't stand playing as Axton But others might find that Gaige is lame or that Krieg isn't fun. So, depending on who you are, you won't be able to get the most out of the 6 total characters available.
-3rd, the game has a clear bias on coop. It definitely supports single-player but it's the kind of game that's meant to be played with friends, and I personally like to play alone.
-4th, and this is by far the biggest problem, the game can be relentlessly frustrating at times. While the variety is nice and certainly makes it more interesting than other shooters, you are limited by the variety in a way. For example, You won't be able to rely purely on sniping or corrosive damage weapons because some enemies flat out say no to those type of playstyles. Another thing is UVHM. UVHM, when you start it right after TVHM, is an absolute NIGHTMARE. It flat out requires you to have the very best weapons your class can utilize, and sadly healing weapons are not given much variety in terms of where you can get them. It's either Moxxi or the grog nozzle, you HAVE to have one item from them at all times in UVHM or your build isn't viable. There are other things like the AI on enemies being♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when you're trying to get a kill in FFYL mode, any flying enemies being stupendously difficult to hit (except Rakk), and sometimes, out of nowhere, you find that your build simply isn't viable against a certain boss. It's also annoying when you have to farm for certain items because it can take considerable time for them to drop. Yeah, as you can see, I have a lot of complaints about stuff I personally believe is rather BS.
Overall though, this game is a blast at normal mode, TVHM, and to some extent, UVHM. Get it and you will love it

Sonic Adventure DX is an upgraded port of Sonic Adventure for the Sega Dreamcast. It features enhanced graphics as well as numerous other changes from the dreamcast version.
The story follows Sonic and his allies as they try and stop Dr.Eggman and his new weapon Chaos from collecting all 7 Chaos Emeralds and conquering the world.
The game features 6 playable characters all with unique play styles.
Sonic the Hedgehog
Sonic's stages focus primarily on reaching the end of the stage.
Miles "Tails" Prower
Tails' stages are very similar to Sonic's except you have to race sonic to the goal.
Knuckles the Echidna
Knuckles' stages focus on exploring the area to hunt down shards of the Master Emerald.
Amy Rose
Amy's stages focus on reaching the goal while trying to avoid Eggman's robot E-100 Zero.
Big the Cat
Big's stages focus on fishing for his lost friend, Froggy.
E-102 Gamma
Gamma's stages focus on reaching the end of the stage and defeating the boss at the end within a time limit.
The graphics are a fair improvement from the dreamcast version. All satges and characters recieved updated textures and, 4 of the 6 playable characters (Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, Amy) recieved updated models.

Sonic Adventure DX... DX stands for Directors Cut, and if this is the updated version... Oof. My memory of playing the Sonic Adventure on the Dreamcast must have been simply being impressed with the progression of 3d games.
But enough of my prejudgment. Sonic Adventure DX is a a Port of the orgional Sega DreamCast game, Sonic Adventure DX was released in 2011 and features many upgrades visually... but I'm not so sure about mechanically. The origional Sonic Adventure for the Dreamcast was released in 1998... So... just be prepared for what you're about to get yourself into. If I might make a kind suggestion: Sonic Adventure 2 built on many themes in Sonic Adventure and turned out a much better product in my opinion. (but Sonic Adventure still works... ...mostly!)
Here we are again with another "Sonic Story" review section. The story can be summed up in one sentence: "Sonic is trying to stop the "Evil" Doctor Robotnik (or Eggman)."
The plot has only grown more complicated since the original games release in the 90's. This time you get to play as Sonic, Tails, Knuckles, Amy, Big the cat, and E-102 Gamma. Each Character has a different "Gimmick" and the worst is that stupid purple cat and his fishing mini game.
I could go into a lot of different directions, but you know what? I'm going to keep it simple and just skip to the point: After you play through each character you unlock the final true ending of the game and they all lived happily ever after... until the next game dropped.
As said earlier in this review, each character has a different gimick to their gameplay: Sonic "runs fast", although I played with a keyboard and mouse... which this game wasn't very well optimized for.
Rather then moving with good 'ol WASD, you move with the arrow keys, you turn the camera with Q and E, S is your jump button, and A and D are your action buttons. You can do some key rebinding and configure the game when the launch Sonic Adventure DX from the steam library.
Sonic Adventure is a mix of a lot of other game genre's, when you're playing as Sonic, Tails, or Amy, it's basically a 3d platformer. When you're playing as Knuckles it's an egg-hung / Marco-polo game with chaos emerald shards. As Big it's a fishing game. As E-102 Gamma it's a FPS.
A consistent factor in Sonic Adventure is the use of a hub world to travel from location to location. This would be engaging and entertaining if it wasn't so difficult to navigate in 3d space with this game.
I've been stuck stuck a few times in the game, a couple times for bosses, a few times for the fishing mini games, and the longest time being stuck was trying to figure out which level to go to next.
Just a pro tip: grab the wind rock in front of tails workshop, and later grab the ice rock from the back alley way. Those are keys to get to the next levels. - You're welcome.
I wouldn't say Sonic Adventure, or Sonic Adventure DX is a bad game. ...I probably should, and in the past I might. ...but I've played some really worthless garbage in my steam backlog now.
I will say that Sonic Adventure hasn't aged very well, and isn't very well optimized for PC.
But if this game is your childhood, don't let me stop you, play Sonic Adventure DX, relive your childhood, enjoy those pleasant memories; most of us do that anyway!
Thanks for taking the time to read my review!

If you were a fan of the original series, get this game. If you're new to the genre, you may have some trouble.
Pros: Base Building. Deeper simulation. Solid tactical experience. Sweeter learning curve.
Cons: Virtually No tutorial or guidance. Have to save a lot. Air-to-air combat mechanics are funky.
It's almost impossible to talk about this game without comparing it to the latest X-COM remake, so I appologize for that. While the new X-COM feels like a modernized interpretation of the series, Xenonauts feels like a direct modernized sequal to the original series. If you're a fan of the original, it'll feel very similar, but you'll notice a number of subtle design improvements which are virtually impossible to detail here.
Ground combat feels pretty solid and similar to the X-COM series. The cover mechanics take a little getting used to, but the UI is quite straight forward. As with all X-COM games, there's still perma-death for any unfortunate soldiers. If you're a hardcore simulation fan, you'll enjoy the difficulty. If you're like me, and can't stand the loss of your beloved soldiers, you're going to have to save and load a lot. This makes for a bit of a stutter-stop experience, but from having loved the original series and the remake, I'm pretty used to it.
Xenonauts uses an "action points" system similar to the original, that determines how much stuff each of your units can do per round. This inclueds the usual move-n-shoot, but also encapsulates rooting around in your inventory, crouching, reloading, and so forth. Conversely, the X-COM remake did away with this sytem in order to steamline the ground combat mechanics. While well executed, I appreciated the added complexity, especially around planning a soldier's loadout.
Xenonauts retains most of the base management mechanics from the original X-COM series, such as base layout, inventory, and staffing. Having this added amount of customizability really adds to the sense that this is YOUR base, executing on YOUR plans to save the world. While the X-COM remake again simplified this experience deftly, I still very much enjoy the added control that Xenonauts gives back to the player.
There are two major areas in which I feel Xenonauts falls short. One is the air-to-air mechanics. Now, when engaging an enemy ship, you can choose to enter this mini-game, in which you can control speed, limited maneuverability, and whether or not you want to retreat. Although you can pause the action at will, you don't have enough control of your aircraft for it to really matter. In the end, it's mostly a real-time battle. This feels like a disconnect in that the rest of the game is a tactical take-your-time-and-think-it-out type of experience. Even so, the game allows you to autoresolve these battles, so you don't need to worry about it if you're like me.
It's possible that this mini-game is much richer and that I'm missing out on some key mechanics, which leads me to the next area in which Xenonauts falls short; no tutorials. There is almost no explanation of how to play the game. At some moments, such as the first time you initiate an air-to-air battle, you get a big block of text, that doesn't really tell you how to succeed. Due to the similarity with the original X-COM games, I didn't have too much of a problem figuring everything out, except when it came to brand new mechanics (ie: air combat), but I can imagine it is exponentially frustrating if you're new to the series.
In the end, Xenonauts is an excellent executition of the original game complete with a mess of improvements and sweeter difficulty curve. It might not be as enjoyable if you're new to the genre, but if you loved the original, this is a must-have in your library.

Failure is an unavoidable fact of life. Its devilish claws knock you down when you least expect it, but it's how you react to disappointment that's important. Super Meat Boy is the digital embodiment of the idea that pleasure can spring from pain, but although death is pervasive in this 2D platformer, it does not define the experience. There is an incredible sense of satisfaction when you clear a particularly nasty level that makes the setbacks you endured to reach that lofty goal well worth it. It's the feeling you get when you miraculously squeeze through two slicing blades unscathed or leap in the air to snatch a dangling bandage that seemed impossible to reach only moments earlier that continually pushes you forward to tackle the next challenge. Super Meat Boy is an extraordinary game that makes you work for every inch you gain, which makes success taste so much sweeter when you finally get there.
Everything in Super Meat Boy begins with the controls. Within seconds of diving into the first few levels of this daunting adventure, it's clear that your onscreen movement is amazingly responsive. The titular hero jumps with such precision that you're always in complete command of your actions. Wall jumping is particularly impressive. The extreme nimbleness of your character makes it a cinch to quickly leap straight up one wall, bounce smoothly between two adjacent ones, and even contort your trajectory in midair to avoid an obstacle while you make your ascent. Super Meat Boy can sprint with the best of them, and though it might seem crazy to hurl yourself at breakneck speeds through these deadly traps, it's not a problem here. Because he responds to your every command immediately, you can tear through levels as fast as Meat can run without worrying about the controls slowing you down. Just be warned: Using the keyboard will throw a hurdle in your path to victory. A controller is the preferred option here because the keyboard does not offer the exactness needed to overcome these daunting obstacles.
The level design in Super Meat Boy is absolutely stunning. The usual tricks you would expect in a 2D platformer are here--such as spinning saws, lava pits, and shooting blades--but they are positioned in such intelligent ways that the game is extremely challenging without ever feeling cheap. There is a delicate balance on display that ensures you're pushed to the limits of your skill without becoming frustrated. One of the most impressive aspects of Super Meat Boy is how you learn and adapt while you play. The first time you enter a level, you may be presented with a jump that seems impossible. You may try and fail a few times, maybe even a few dozen times, without any idea what you're supposed to do. But once you figure out the timing to succeed, you can pull off even the toughest moves with a good degree of consistency. Being able to conquer levels that previously seemed impossible is an exhilarating feeling, and the ease with which you become proficient is a testament to how precise the controls are and how meticulously designed the levels are.
Death is commonplace in Super Meat Boy. When you reach the harder levels, you may end up dying a dozen times before you pass the first pit, and more than a hundred before you reach the end. With failure such an expected occurrence, you might think this game is frustrating. It rarely is. Although you will inevitably be frustrated at times, Super Meat Boy goes a long way toward lessening your irritation. The precise controls and imaginative level design go a long way toward alleviating any throw-your-controller reactions, but the reason frustration is avoided goes even deeper than that. The upbeat soundtrack does a great job of keeping your energy at a high level without ever distracting you from the carnage that lies ahead. Each song also changes slightly, so even if you're stuck at a particularly wicked stage for an hour or more, the catchy riff never gets repetitive. The lack of extreme punishment also helps a lot. Although you die if any obstacle hits you, you do have infinite lives. Also, because levels usually last less than 30 seconds, even though you have to start from the beginning each time, you never have to retrace much ground. Finally, the extreme focus needed to pass these difficult stages ensures that you're zeroed in on completing your task rather than beating yourself up for falling short. This is an amazingly well designed game that avoids the frustration of failure by insulating you from your own aggravation.
The core mechanics and level design are absolutely superb in Super Meat Boy, and the wealth of content ensures you'll be playing this excellent platformer for quite a long time. There are more than 300 levels in all, most of them optional, and many of them are hidden. To reach the end you need to play through all of the light world levels, which include traditional platforming challenges along with a few clever boss fights. You have as much time as you need to pass each level, but if you reach the end under a specific mark, you unlock a dark version of that same level. This is when things get really difficult. The dark world puts a cruel twist on the light levels, and it can take all of your determination to rise above these daunting tests. It's a good thing the dark world is optional, so you can play through the slightly easier light world before you dive into the furnace. But the bonus content doesn't stop there. There are warp zones hidden in certain levels that whisk you to a three-level obstacle course that's a bit easier than standard levels but gives you a finite number of lives to make it through alive. On top of that are glitch world levels, which are as hard to unlock as they are to finish, and the goofily named Teh Internets, which is updated periodically with new levels. It takes lots of hours to plow through all this content, and you'll be glued to the edge of your seat the whole time.
Super Meat Boy is an extremely difficult game, but that doesn't mean it lacks a sense of humor. The setup is just as preposterous as the traps you have to overcome, setting the stage for a daunting adventure that always has a smile on its lips. Meat Boy's girlfriend, Bandage Girl, has been kidnapped by Dr. Fetus. You may wonder how an unborn baby could possibly have a medical degree, but the bigger question is: What is he wearing? He struts around in a mechanical suit clad in a spiffy tuxedo with a top hat on his dome. Certainly the sign of an evil individual. At the completion of each boss fight, a cartoony cinematic rolls, and these are a great reward for your hard work. The cutscenes are sometimes funny, sometimes poignant, but always entertaining. It's amazing how many emotions play out without any dialogue, but that's part of the beauty of this incredible game. It never lets its simplicity hold it back from greatness.
It's impossible to point to just one element that makes Super Meat Boy such an extraordinary game. From the intense-though-always-fair difficulty and the inspired level design, to the pinpoint controls and catchy soundtrack, all of the different aspects converge into something that is truly outstanding. When you hear stories of the unrepentant dangers that stand in your path, it's easy to get intimidated by such a daunting prospect. But don't be. The beauty of Super Meat Boy is that it always plays within the rules, and the smooth difficulty curve gives you plenty of time to become acquainted with everything before the true tests are unleashed. Death is always just one misstep away in Super Meat Boy, but the rush of winning is so supremely rewarding that you won't be able to tear yourself away.

This game can be quite a mixed bag.
As many have probably heard from anybody who isn't blinded by the nostalgia factor or pure Sonic fandom, this game is very...well, at a loss in focus. For example, one moment you may be running at a fast pace as a character through the levels designed for speed and the next moment you could be controlling a slow fat-legged mutant looking for his frog and fishing in the pond.
Can't really rate the story in this as it is just a Sonic platforming game, which means the story isn't all hard to follow, there are no twists, turns or surprises; it's simple. Some things here and there don't make any sense, but that's the world that this game is just based in. One thing that really bothers me and always has even after all this years of being familiar with this game is the presentation. It's mind-boggling how somebody could have possibly looked at this game's lip-syncing and god-awful animations for characters and said "nah, this looks fantastic!", it's really probably one of the worst in its league. I suppose you can put it into the so bad it's good category, but I did cringe quite a couple of times at some of the voice acting sequences, so generally for me it was more painful to watch for me than funny.
Nevertheless, as unfocused as gameplay is in this game; the separate characters don't control bad. In fact, I believe in this game the characters control the most realistic compared to their sizes and they actually speed up and slow down as they probably would in the real world (god I hope I never get to see a real life Sonic). Some sequences I feel are very, VERY unneccessary. Big the cat is probably one of the most infamous characters for just his lack of any reason to be in the game. He wasn't an original character, he has never been established before, yet here he is. What Big the cat does best for this game is ruin the flow. You need to beat all the stories in order to get to the final sequence, and yet his story revolves around running 3 meters in a level and fishing out some fish and a...frog. Needless to say the challenge in this game is quite satisfying. At the point of writing this review I had already collected all of the medals for all heroes and have digged into Chao garden to try and unlock Metal Sonic. I would definitely recommend this game to platforming fans if you could get past the terrible presentation of character interaction. In other cases, the music in this game is quite solid and the colourful graphics definitely do live up even for their dated polygon count.
I would give this game a 7/10.

I've played a number of X-Com games... and in fact X-Com Apocalypse is my favorite game of all time, and I really wanted to like this game.  The game artwork is sorta mediocre, but the gameplay graphics are more than adequate although not anywhere near the quality X-Com Enemy Unknown.  What is most important to me in this type of game is the gameplay, and this is where Xenonauts falls woefully short.  Let me give a couple of examples.
I started the game on the default "normal" difficulty, chose my starting base, and proceded to "fast forward" towards the first enemy encounter... Seconds later, a target is spotted and I send both my aircraft out to intercept the bogey.  Once they get close to their prey, they violently circle around the target at dizzying speeds until eventually they run out of fuel and have to return to base... hmm... okay.. no problem.. I will just start over.  This happens again and again over the next 3 or 4 restarts (from scratch choosing a different start location each time).. Apparently they didn't play test this part, or apparently I was very unlucky about ship positioning.
Okay... Finally I get a non-spin cycle encounter, and I heroically down the bogey with barely a scratch... Time to send in the troops !   My troop ship lands and my 8 ground agents are ready to kick some alien butt !   I deploy my troops from the landing craft in pairs, being sure to reserve some Time Units for a shot or two in case aliens are close.  From past experience, I also make sure to "kneel" and take advantage of cover whenever possible.  My last troops out of the ship are Joe & Bob... and I deploy them kneeling side by side behind a nearby fallen tree trunk and I End My Turn.  The hunt is on !  Seconds later during the Enemy Movement phase, I strike it rich !... My planning has paid off !   An unwary alien has appeared direectly in front of my two would-be heros, and Bob carefullly lines up a shot with his Sniper Rifle using his extra Time Units that he saved.... HEAD SHOT !... Not the Alien... but Joe crouching 90 degrees off to his right one square away  :(
Twice I removed the game from my hard drive, and twice I reloaded it in hopes that it was a quirk experience... But these experiences happened each time.   I sincerely hope that the developers/programmers work to correct these problems, and I hope I have the opportunity once again to try to play this game, but as for now, it will be removed again, and I cannot recommend it to anyone.

Maybe I'm calling this too early, but I'm not feeling it. In a game where the entire challenge is built on delicate movement, things are too unpredictable, and the terrible save system only compounds those issues.
Your body is a physical object that is constantly being pulled down by gravity. This is the core of the challenge in the game - getting around obstacles cleanly enough and quickly enough that you get around them without either falling off or being pulled off by your poorly supported body. This is a very cute in theory but in practice your constantly unspooling body changes how you move throughout an obstacle, rapidly changing how your snake reacts to the controls.  Adding to these are some serious camera issues, particularly with the way the head moves in relation to the camera. Your head will often move in the opposite direction you intended, or at a wildly different speed.  In the key moments of this game - piloting through precarious challenges or attempting to fix mistakes - your body won't behave as you expect and these moments quickly become very frustrating. Essentially this game is hundreds of attempts at threading a needle when the thread doesn't move in a consistent manner.
To make matters worse, this game has a very poor save system. The game is built around collecting various doodads (blobs, coins and gems) in often precarious situations, but makes no effort to save your progress within the game. You must return to checkpoints continously to update your collection and avoid losing several minutes work to a misjudgement on a cliff face. While the levels aren't very large, your snake doesn't move very quickly (even with enthusiatic speed-boosting slithering) and the checkpoints are somewhat stingy, so journeys too and from checkpoints are quickly tiresome. Especially when travelling back from a checkpoint for the 100th time to reattempt a particularly difficult coin.
To add to this, you cannot save progress within a level! Exiting a level midway will not only result in all your collectibles progress being lost, but the unskippable cutscenes will all return. It's maddening. One of the key strengths of a game like this is how it enables come-and-go gameplay but the save system completely nullifies that.
Don't get me wrong, the movement of the snake in the 'meat' of the game - basic movement through the space and defeating the basic obstacles - is very smooth and it's a novel idea, well executed. But things fall apart once you move onto anything that poses real challenge and risk, and those difficult puzzles make up half the game and certainly the most engaging portions of it.
It's cute and colourful and a really novel idea that is very successful on the surface, but the game falls apart the moment any pressure is placed on those systems. It makes me sad but I can't recommend it.

This will be a basic review as I've not played the game enough to know everything yet.
The game is adorable, the visuals are great, I love all the little slime animations and interactions.
The background music and the sound effects fit the game perfectly. Some of the noises the slimes make remind me of lemmings (yep, I'm old enough to talk about lemmings >.>).
The game play is fairly simple; you're a rancher in first person view with a vacuum/launcher that catches slimes in the wild, you build holding pens for then and little gardens or coops for their food and you take care of the little critters. Your income comes from collecting their crystallized poop and selling it to a vending machine. There is a miniquest vending machine as well.
There are a few areas still locked for me, as I only played the game for a little while, so I'm not familiar with everything yet.
The engine of the game runs very smoothly on my machine even though it's not exactly brand new, I love that the game does not require DX11 as my card can't handle that, there's a lot of things I can control in the options menu including the shadows and textures, so I'm sure if anyone has some issues with the game running smoothly they can tweak those, I have even streamed the game and had no issues with that.
Obviousely I haven't seen everything in the game yet, but I still get the impression that there isn't a lot of content in it, I hope more things get added soon, I would like to have some steam achievements as well, and maybe have some more customization available for my farm, including the house and things beside the corrals and holding pens. This game would benefit greatly from some kind of coop mode, that would greatly enhance the gameplay on it's own.

- Adorable little game

- No Multiplayer (I really hope this changes)

Well, here it is. Why I can't recommend the game. It's definitely the makings of a tragedy; the biggest work from the developer so far, yet it's praises go completely unsung. To me there just isn't a game here, only mechanics strung together. I should love this game. Dinsosaurs? Check. Explosions? Check. LOOT? Check. However, tossing this all togther doesn't a game make.
The trouble starts when you try to join a game. Single player? I'll pass, I know horde games. Survival isn't an option for a rookie straight off the boat. So multiplayer it is. Now to choose a server. Easy, medium or hard? OK, I get that, no explanation required. Item level, 1, 100, 500, 10 000 000? OK, this is getting out of my water. Modes? No clue at this point, just lemme shoot something.
Then onto the next hurdle. Welcome to this planet. We call it this planet because we don't know what it is, where it is, or why we're here. Oh, nevermind, this is why you're here. Protect this toaster while it shines light on these rocks. Now I'm engaged! /s.
Difficulty? Well, if you're starting at the bottom you are Rookie from Hell! The Rookinator. Rooknan the Gun Toting Barbarian. Seriously, you're shooting fully automatic laserplasma beams at cute little bunny dinosaurs, with cute little nicknames to boot. I don't need loot, I'M UNTOUCHABLE.
Oh, loot you say? Well, here is a bunch of . . . stuff. You know . . . things. They do stuff, definitely. That's why they're there. Dinosaur bones? Oh yeah, grab those. Goo! Oh yes, I want some goo. Can I wear it? . . . nope. Shoot it from my assault rifle? . . . nope. OK, screw this, this isn't loot. I'm just cleaning up after things now. I hate cleaning.
Finally! We made it, wave 5 complete! We've paved the planet with the corpses of a handful of helpless bunnysaurs, and it only took us 20 seconds! Semperfi! Now what do we do? Wait? A minute you say? I guess the next tiny wave of bunnysaurs needs to steel themselves, so we can hurry up to the next coffee break between ripples- er waves.

The emotional response garnered by the plot was much better than many other games out there, and the characters had a good amount of depth, especially after playing through the first game.  However, the lack of satisfactory animations during any sort of interaction hurt the depth of character interplay. The new characters were less developed and much shallower than legacy characters, but this was a problem with the original as well.
As far as actual gameplay goes, the guns are not so frustrating in the early game as the original's were. There is always something viscerally satisfying about shooting an enemy in Gearbox games, and this one did not disappoint. Unfortuntely, the combat is quite repetitive, and the enemies in later modes (TVH, UVH) become meatshields with ridiculous damage output more than they become legitimate strategic challenges. this detracts from the fun of replaying the game. After all, why not just use a worse gun and shield in normal mode if that's all the challenge it gives you. The combat is fairly bland, and seems to attempt to repeat the success of the original's quite innovative feeling. It falls short, and ends up with something that feels derivative, and doesn't really bring anything new to the table.
Overall rating: 7/10. A great game to play through in a very casual setting, but I would not consider it worth the original asking price. Now that it's on sale, buy away and blow up some bandits.

Huge XCOM fan.  I did wait quite a while on Xenonauts.  Missed the kickstarter.  Missed a few of the other sales.  Overall, I'm in two minds about this game even though I am going  to give it a postive review.
If you really enjoyed the original XCOM (1994), as I did, then this game is worth looking into.  The mechanics and the game itself are a near intentional copy of XCOM (1994).  They've just changed a few minor things.  Sectoids don't seem to exist.  Cyberdisks are smaller.  You can freely change weapons on the tanks between misisons.  Most enemies feel a lot like mutons.
This game is a good copy.  They've also made a number of changes that frankly XCOM (1994) needed to see many years ago.  It's more than just a copy.  It's a copy that's been updated tastefully, and that's great.  More games like this.  More developers that listen when fans say this is exactly what we want don't strap on 100 DLC's and a broken multiplayer.
The only bad things I'll say about this game is that it is 2015 and there is XCOM (2012) longwar mod.  With the popular longwar mod; XCOM has finally brought into the 21st century.  There is also a sloppyness in Xenonauts.  XCOM (1994) had a certain something assocaited with its balance.  It worked so well.  Who knows how they got it working with little playtesting, but it worked so well.  Every so often I suspect that the balance in Xenonauts is a bit skrewy.  The economic game sometimes seems unwinnable, and you start off fighting basically muton level guys for no good reason.  It's still a great game, but it needs more playtesting and balancing, which the developers fully support with mods.
I would say get this if you really like XCOM (1994).  If you've never played XCOM (1994), then get XCOM (2012) and longwar.

Seeing how there are already plenty of thorough reviews out there, I will keep this short and sweet.
First off, this is probably one of the best turn-based strategy games I've ever played.  Although it's a reboot of the X-com franchise, I find it to be more fun.  A lot of the tediousness has been taken out without sacrificing or dumbing down the strategy.  An example would be not having to reload ammo clips every single time your team returns from a mission.  The combat part of the game is more or less like a game of chess, easy to learn but can be hard to master; especially at higher difficulty settings.  Though easy mode is almost too easy.
Overall, I’m very pleased.  After 40+ hours in only a couple of weeks, this game gets two thumbs up.  Pick this one up.  You won’t be disappointed.

Sonic Adventure is like a car crash. It's terrible, and you know you should not look, but somehow, despite deep down knowing how terrible it is, you can't help but be fascinated by it.
Just for the record, I've got no nostalgia for this game. I did not play it when it was new, but I did play games back in 98/99. And frankly, I can't really see why anyone would have chosen to play this, unless they had a shortage of other games.
Oh boy. I don't know exactly where to start with this one. While low poly models and quite flat shading is something you would expect from a late 90's game, the animation quality in Sonic Adventure is really sub-par, even by that times standard. Facial animations look grotesque, and the characters with less developed facial animations look a lot better than those who they spent a lot of time animating. Sonic in particular just looks terrible when he speaks, while some of the lesser characters are not so bad.
The actual art style is not too bad though. The game is colourful and apart from a lot of wonky animations (character speed & animations not matching, animations cutting out mid animation and so on), it's not that bad looking. Sadly the overall really poor, even by late 90's standards, animations pull down the entire game.
In terms of sound, I can't believe the person in charge of the sound mixing can have had much in the way of hearing. Some sound effects are really low, some I think are even missing (during the first Robotnick fight, his craft explodes, yet it makes no sound!), and some are far too loud. It's as if they did not even try to get sound right.
Voice acting is universally atrocious. Not a single one sounds good, and some of the voices are just annoying. It sounds like a high school project.

Believe it or not, but this game has a story. It's told from the perspective of 6 different characters, all with their own campaign, and all of them show their side of the same set of events. This is a pretty good idea, but in practice it does not work well. You end up having events happen that just seem to come out of nowhere with the first character you play through the game with (which most likely will be Sonic). The story does make more sense once you've played through it with 3 characters, but the harm the structure does to the story for the first 2 campaigns makes it not worth it. Not that the story is good, in fact it's atrocious, but it could have been better told at least.
There's a water creature called Chaos who's being controlled by Dr. Robotnick, and Robotnick plans to destroy the city. He needs chaos emeralds for that, and it's up to you to find them. That's the gist of things.

Each character has their own gameplay style, so there's a lot of variety to the game. At its core it's a 3D platformer, but each character brings its own thing to the table.  One thing that's a problem with all though is the camera, which swings wildly depending on where the devs thought it should swing wildly (which results in cheap deaths), and sometimes it just ends up inside a wall.
Sonic
Sonic is of course all about speed. He has the longest campaign, and he's the fastest character. The goals of his levels are to get to the end. The controls for sonic are not great, and he feels very slippery, making him a pain to control. He can attack enemies with a homing attack, a homing attack that loves to home in on thin air, which causes some cheap deaths. Overall, the campaign is very easy though, and that's a good thing, considering how poor the controls are.
Tails
Tails can fly, and this opens up some new possibilities, but he actually plays surprisingly similar to Sonic. He's fast (just not quite as fast), and he attacks by jumping on enemies. No homing attack though. Most of his levels are races to the end, which in practice just introduces a time limit to levels that otherwise play quite similar to Sonic's levels. With tails the lack of testing of the levels really starts to show though, and there are plenty of spots that simply lack collision detection.

Knuckles
Knuckles can climb, glide in the air, and find holes in the level geometry. He's actually the most fun character to play (apart from the fact that the levels are so poorly tested that there are places where you can fall through). Knuckles have some terrible scavenger hunt levels though, which really pulls down the experience. Shame, because Knuckles is actually fun to control
Amy
Amy is slow, but have a big hammer. Her levels all have her being chased by a robot, and they are probably the second easiest set of levels in the game. Actually controlling Amy is really boring though.
Big the Cat
Big is the most unique of the lot. His levels are like the fishing minigame from games like Zelda OOT, only they're atrociously bad. Not much more to say, Big is terrible, and everything about his campaign is terrible. The game is not fascinatingly bad anymore, it's just so bad it's painful.
Gamma
Gamma is a robot, and once again we have a pretty fun character to play. He's a bit slower than most, and his weapon is really overpowered, but the main threat on his levels are the time limit. You need to chain-kill enemies to extent it. They're pretty fun, but also far too easy. Gamma's campaign is in fact a real pushover. The second to last boss has the worst camera of any place in the game though, and it feels like the devs intentionally made it bad, because that thing can't have been accidental.
Sonic Adventure is atrocious. But in a fascinating way. It does so many things wrong, I can't believe it's a game with any kind of a budget. But can I recommend it? Absolutely not! Not unless you find it really cheap, and want to see a game that's just broken at a fundamental level. Terrible camera, horrible sound mixing, awful voice acting, bad levels, annoying mechanics, there's really nothing that truly works here. And that's what makes it so fascinating.

As a proud player of BW since ~2014, I'm happy to see the developers taking their game in this direction. It's a little buggy and has some issues as of now, but that's to be expected from an early access game that just recently released. So far, I'm absolutely blown away by what they've done with this version.
First of all, the graphics! Play any world on the iOS version, then play it here. Worlds on this version look absolutely stunning. There's even skyboxes that change the lighting!
Second, the UI. The new UI looks really cool so far and definitely works better for PC. They haven't changed the building interface yet, but I imagine when it's done it'll work really well for PC.
Now, I do have some complaints and suggestions that I hope will be taken into consideration. No game is perfect, after all.
When in build mode, you can only move the camera while holding right click, and moving the camera with WASD is fast. Like, insanely fast. Having to hold ctrl every time I want to move the camera so I don't overshoot by a few miles is pretty annoying.
The controls could use some improvement. Since this is PC, there are a lot of keys at your disposal, so there should be an event for when a certain key is pressed, instead of using IJKL and the arrow keys for the existing buttons.
To those of you saying they should merge iOS version accounts with Steam accounts, I don't think they can do that. iOS accounts are connected to your game center account, so it's very unlikely that they can merge them.
And to anyone saying the game is bad or isn't as good as the iOS version, just know that this game is in early access and released 4 days ago. (as of me writing this) Many things are incomplete or haven't been added yet, but the developers are working hard on making sure they will be there in the finished product.
All in all, I'm really enjoying this new Steam version so far, and I'm looking forward to future updates. Don't expect it to be as good as the iOS version now. Expect it to get better as time goes on. Way better. Even better than the iOS version, maybe.

It's a plattformer but with very unusual controlls. Well you are a snake.
Getting used to the controlls is a bit tricky but quite fun to learn. It reminds me of Donkey kong Jungle Climber where you were constantly improving with the unusual control scheme though Snake Pass is much more relaxed. It has its challenges, but nothing one can't manage. It never gets frustrating and with amazing David Wise soundtrack, beautiful level design with different quirks and ideas make it an very enjoyable experience. The controlls are very well made and you really feel like controlling an actual snake when playing the game!
Unfortunately devs didn't finalize all ideas they had with the game due to time contrain so the game doesn't have the length it had planned and story is so barebones that some cutscenes should have been just cut out as well. However the length of the game is still alright especially for that price.

Haven't played it very long, but already the mechanics are pretty cool. I'm sure you can already tell by the videos how it works, but it really feels cool and new. The atmosphere is something like an old Rare game, like Banjo Kazooie. It's really relaxing and enjoyable, yet it will challenge even regular platforming veterans due to its unique control and navigation. As far as cons,  I can tell the game is a little less optimized than I had hoped. Very high settings do not run at a constant 60 fps on my GTX 1060 at 1080p, but this can be solved by swapping down to lower settings, which don't even affect visual quality that much. As well as that, the game is a bit on the short side, as any percent playthroughs seem to last 6 hours. Completionists will get more time out of it, but regardless that's a bit short for $20. If anything, pick it up on sale because the quality of the game itself is really high,  and you can tell they really worked hard to bring this idea to life.  I'll update this review once I've beaten it to give my playtime, or if they update it with more levels. Regardless though, I recommend it.

This game has been out forever, and I just beat it for the first time ever a couple weeks back. To be completely honest, I LOVE this game, but I am going to weigh the pros and cons.
Pros:
- Multiple properties can be bought where you can save your progress.
- There are SO MANY missions to keep you occupied.
- Obviously, the character customization was a new-ish concept that was pulled off incredibly.
- The storyline is so interesting; it was very well-written.
Cons:
- The choice of playing the game either with a keyboard/mouse or a controller is a no-brainer. Keyboard config sucks.
- Don't expect to be able to jump into this game right away with a modern rig. The game is locked on 25 FPS unless you turn off the Frame Limiter in the settings. Do that, though, and the game becomes unplayable unless you edit the game's 3D Settings from your video card software. The cars' back axes will rock back and forth, the handbrake is constantly applied while driving, you swim at snail pace and can't dive, etc.
- There is a game-crashing bug where the game shuts off after a nearby explosion occurs. This is easily fixed by going to the "GTA San Andreas User Files" folder in your Documents, then deleting the "gta_sa.set" file. After a while, it'll start happening again. Repeat as needed.
Honestly, the cons are unavoidable, as this game is incredibly old. No one should expect a game this old to run even sub-par. Hell, Max Payne required a damned sound patch to even hear what's going on. This is a classic, and if you can run it, you'll love it! Cheers, Rockstar!
